Subject: Finally figured out this aphid situation
Hi Sarah,
I hope you are having a wonderful week and that your tomato plants are thriving. I am writing to you today because I finally cracked the code on the aphid infestation that has been plaguing my rose bushes last month. It has been an absolute nightmare trying to keep them under control, but after reading through quite a few forums and asking around at the local nursery, I think I have established a routine that is actually working. I know you have been dealing with similar issues in your back garden, so I wanted to share what has made the difference for me.
The first thing that really helped was switching from a generic insecticide to a neem oil spray. I used to reach for the strong chemical sprays whenever I saw a cluster of little green insects, but that seemed to upset the balance of beneficial insects in the garden. By using neem oil, which I mixed at a lower concentration than the label suggested, I was able to target the pests without wiping out the ladybugs that I know are natural allies. It is a bit messy to apply, and you really have to cover the underside of the leaves thoroughly, but the results have been much more sustainable in the long run.
I also started hand-picking the worst offenders in the early mornings when the bugs are less active. It sounds tedious, but walking around with a bucket of soapy water and knocking them off the stems has cleaned up the initial populations so effectively. I found that combining this physical removal with the neem oil treatment created a double barrier that the pests just could not overcome. It does require a bit of patience and a steady hand, but there is something deeply satisfying about physically seeing the problem disappear bit by bit rather than just spraying and hoping for the best.
One other tip that cannot be overstated is to ensure your plants are not under stress from poor soil conditions. I noticed that the aphids always attacked the weakest plants first, so I took the time to compost around the base of the roses and improve the drainage. Healthy, vigorous plants seem to be more resistant to infestations generally, which means I am spending less time on emergency treatments now. It is a slow process, but investing in the soil health has reduced the frequency of these outbreaks significantly.
Let me know if you want me to drop off a small bottle of the neem oil mixture or if you have any questions about the specific timing for the application. I would love to hear how your garden is doing and if you have found any other tricks that work for you. Maybe we can schedule a visit next weekend to check on the damage together and perhaps pour a cup of tea in the process. Looking forward to hearing from you.
Best regards,
Alex

Sandwich (horse)

Sandwich (1928 - after 1941) was a British Thoroughbred racehorse that won the classic St Leger Stakes at Doncaster Racecourse in 1931, for owner Earl of Rosebery. By 1931, Archibald Primrose, 5th Earl of Rosebery had died, making this a win for his son, Harry Primrose, 6th Earl of Rosebery. Sandwich was a half-brother to Manna, winner of the 1925 Epsom Derby, and as well as his 1931 St Leger success also won the Chester Vase and King Edward VII Stakes.

Sandwich was a bay stallion, bred in Great Britain by the Irish breeder, James J. Maher. He was sired by the 1924 Epsom Derby winner, Sansovino. His dam Waffles was unraced but had previously produced the Derby winner Manna. As a yearling, he was purchased by Lord Rosebery for 3,600 guineas and was sent to trainer Jack Jarvis.

As part of the Rosebery stable, Sandwich was trained by Jack Jarvis. Jarvis was noted for being the first trainer to be knighted for his service and contribution to horse racing. Jarvis' reputation for training horses was to work them hard, and he found success with his approach.

Sandwich was slow to mature and after finishing unplaced in his only races as a juvenile in 1930 he was well beaten in both the Craven Stakes and the 2000 Guineas the following spring. When moved up in distance he showed immediate improvement: in May, ridden by Billy Nevett, he won the Chester Vase, a major trial race for the Epsom Derby. In June Sandwich, ridden by Harry Wragg he started at odds of 8/1 for the Derby. After being hampered early in the race and losing his position he finished strongly to take third behind Cameronian and Orpen. Jarvis said that the colt was "beaten by the bad draw". Later that month he won the King Edward VII Stakes at Royal Ascot at odds of 1/3. When matched against older horses for the first time in the Eclipse Stakes he finished third behind the 25/1 outsider Caerleon. The St. Leger race is the oldest of the five British Classic races, the last in the year to be run, and it is also the longest. To: All Staff, Department of Earth Sciences 
From: Dr. Elena Ramirez, Lead Volcanologist 
Date: 8 October 2026 
Subject: Current Understanding and Monitoring Practices for Active Volcanic Systems

The purpose of this memo is to provide a concise overview of the scientific principles governing volcanic activity and to outline the standard procedures we employ for monitoring active volcanoes within our regional network. Volcanic eruptions are driven by the ascent of magma, a complex mixture of melt, crystals, and volatiles, from the mantle to the surface. The physical properties of the magma, especially its viscosity and gas content, dictate whether an eruption will be effusive, producing lava flows, or explosive, generating ash plumes and pyroclastic density currents. Recent studies have emphasized the role of magma recharge events in reactivating dormant conduits, a factor that must be considered in hazard assessments.

Our monitoring program relies on a combination of seismic, geodetic, gas, and visual observations. Broadband seismometers detect low-frequency tremor associated with magma movement, while continuous GPS stations quantify surface deformation that signals pressure changes in the underlying magma chamber. Gas emissions, particularly sulfur dioxide, are measured using both ground-based spectrometers and satellite retrievals to infer changes in magma degassing dynamics. All data streams are integrated in real time through the central volcano monitoring platform, which generates alerts when thresholds for anomalous behavior are exceeded.

Interpretation of these signals follows a tiered framework. Initial anomalies trigger a heightened observation level, prompting more frequent field inspections and the deployment of portable instruments. If multiple parameters show concurrent escalation-such as increased tremor amplitude, rapid inflation, and rising sulfur dioxide flux-we advance to an advisory level, issuing public notices and coordinating with emergency management agencies. The final decision to declare a warning rests on a multidisciplinary review of all available evidence, taking into account the volcano's historical behavior and current contextual factors.

Training for field personnel emphasizes safety protocols during high-risk periods, including the use of personal protective equipment, real-time communication links, and predefined evacuation routes. Continuous professional development is supported through workshops on the latest remote sensing techniques and numerical modeling tools that improve our predictive capabilities.

Please ensure that all team members familiarize themselves with the outlined procedures and incorporate the latest data into their daily workflows. Your vigilance and adherence to these guidelines are essential for protecting communities and advancing our scientific understanding of volcanic processes.

raw:
bike repair

Winter is approaching, and many cyclists are facing the inevitable: a chain that has stretched past its serviceability. Ignoring this simple issue leads to accelerated wear on your cassette and chainring, components that are far more expensive to replace than a new chain. Checking chain wear takes less than five minutes. Use a chain checker tool to measure a twelve-inch section. If the tool slips into the gap at the wear mark, it is time for a swap. Do not wait until the chain skips under heavy pedaling, as that indicates you have already caused unnecessary damage to your drivetrain. Keeping a spare chain in your tool bag is a cheap insurance policy that saves you from roadside frustration.

Brake performance often degrades quietly before it fails completely. Inspect your brake pads for remaining material. If you can see the metal backing plate, or if the brake calipers are throwing the pads, the system needs immediate attention. For disc brakes, check for wobbly rotors. A slick, clean rotor is essential for consistent stopping power. If your pads are squealing, clean them with isopropyl alcohol and a lint-free cloth. Grease contamination is the enemy of braking performance, and even a tiny drop of oil on a disc pad can render your brakes ineffective until they are professionally re-bedded.

Tire pressure is not just about comfort; it is a critical component of safety and efficiency. Under-inflated tires roll slower, increase rolling resistance, and are significantly more prone to pinch flats. Over-inflation creates a harsh ride and reduces traction on rough surfaces. Check your pressure every time you go for a ride. A quick release valve can waste seconds, and a leaking presta valve can waste minutes. Keep a compact pump with a pressure gauge in your car or at your doorstep. Consistent pressure ensures your tires maintain their intended geometry and contact patch.

The hub is a sealed unit in many modern bikes, but bearings still fail. A grinding noise from a wheel that is spinning freely is a clear sign that the bearings are done. Modern sealed bearings are cheap and easy to replace if you have the correct bearing pullers. If you hear clicking or feel play when you rock the bike, the axle or dropouts might be the culprit. Torque your wheels to the manufacturer's specification. Under-torqued wheels can wobble, while over-torqued wheels can crack carbon frames or bend axles. This is a precision issue, not a matter of brute force.

Ultimately, consistent maintenance is less about fixing major breakdowns and more about preventing minor annoyances. Lubricate your chain regularly, especially after riding in the rain or mud. Dry lube is sufficient for dry conditions, while wet lube is necessary for damp environments. Clean your bike after every wash, paying close attention to the drivetrain where grime accumulates. A clean bike is a reliable bike. By spending twenty minutes a month on these routine checks, you ensure that your bicycle remains a trustworthy companion rather than a source of stress on your commute or trail rides.

raw:
office relocation

When a company decides to move its headquarters, the announcement can feel like a mixture of excitement and anxiety. A fresh address often promises more space, better amenities, or a location that aligns with the brand's growth strategy, yet the reality of packing desks, wiring servers, and re-creating the daily rhythm in a new setting can quickly become overwhelming. Understanding the full scope of an office relocation-not just the physical move but the impact on staff morale, client perception, and operational continuity-sets the tone for a smoother transition.

The planning phase is where the project either succeeds or stalls. It begins with a thorough audit of current assets: furniture inventories, technology equipment, and any items that can be donated or recycled. From there, a realistic timeline is drafted, taking into account lease expirations, vendor lead times, and the calendar of the business itself to avoid peak periods. A dedicated relocation team, often comprising members from facilities, IT, HR, and finance, should meet weekly to track milestones, assign responsibilities, and flag potential bottlenecks before they become crises.

Logistics turn the abstract plan into concrete action. Selecting a reputable moving company that specializes in corporate moves is essential; they will handle delicate office furniture, secure transport of confidential documents, and ensure that the new space is prepared for a "plug-and-play" setup. Parallel to the physical move, the IT department must coordinate server migration, network cabling, and phone system reinstallation, often scheduling these tasks during off-hours to keep the business online. Simultaneously, the facilities crew prepares the new floor plan, confirming that workstations, meeting rooms, and break areas match the design approved by senior leadership.

Communication is the glue that holds the process together. Employees need clear, frequent updates about what to expect, where their new desks will be, and how the move will affect their daily commute. Clients and partners should receive a courteous notice well in advance, outlining any temporary service interruptions and providing the new contact details. A simple FAQ on the intranet, complemented by town-hall meetings and reminder emails, can dispel rumors and keep the team focused on the benefits rather than the inconvenience.

On moving day, the emphasis shifts from preparation to execution. A central command center-often set up in a conference room of the old office-monitors the progress of each zone, from packing to loading to unloading. Having a "go-live" checklist helps ensure that essential services such as internet, phone, and security systems are verified before employees return. A small welcome kit on each new desk, perhaps containing a map of the floor, a list of nearby lunch spots, and a note from leadership, adds a personal touch that eases the transition.

After the doors close on the old location, the focus moves to post-relocation fine-tuning. A quick walk-through with department heads reveals any missing supplies or ergonomic adjustments needed for comfort and productivity. Surveys collected a week later provide insight into lingering pain points, allowing facilities to address issues before they affect performance. Celebrating the successful move-through a launch event, a photo tour of the new space, or a simple thank-you email-reinforces the collective effort and signals that the company is ready to thrive in its new environment.

raw:
Minuscule 257

Minuscule 257 (in the Gregory-Aland numbering), α 466 (Soden), is a Greek minuscule manuscript of the New Testament, on parchment. Palaeographically it has been assigned to the 14th century. Formerly it was labelled by 302a and 260p. Scrivener by 250a and 300p. It has marginalia.

The codex contains the text of the Acts of the Apostles, Catholic epistles, and Pauline epistles on 116 parchment leaves (24.3 cm by 17.5 cm). The text is written in one column per page, 39 lines per page. The text is divided according to the κεφαλαια (chapters), whose numbers are given at the margin, and the τιτλοι (titles of chapters) at the top of the pages. It contains prolegomena, lectionary markings at the margin, Synaxarion, Menologion, subscriptions at the end of each book, with numbers of στιχοι. It has also some Psalms. The Greek text of the codex is a representative of the Western text-type. Aland did not place it in any Category.

The manuscript was written by Joseph, a scribe. Heinrich Brugsch brought it from Cairo to Berlin. It was held in Königliche Bibliothek Gr. Quarto 43. Gregory saw it in 1887. Formerly it was labelled by 302a and 260p. In 1908 C. R. Gregory gave the number 257 to it. At the end of 1943 year has increased the frequency of the bombing of Berlin. The Prussian State Library sent many collections out of Berlin to be sheltered in Silesia for safekeeping. As the result of postwar border changes some of these collections were found in Poland (among them minuscule 257). They were moved to the Jagiellonian University Library. It was cited only once in the Novum Testamentum Graece (Nestle-Aland 27 ed.) - in 1 Cor 11:23. The manuscript is currently housed at the Biblioteka Jagiellońska (Fonds der Berliner Hss, Graec. qu. 43) at Kraków.

raw:
budget planning

Effective budget planning starts with a clear picture of where your money currently flows. Most people underestimate the value of a simple spreadsheet that tracks every expense for a month, from rent and utilities to that daily coffee habit. By documenting each outflow, you reveal patterns that are often hidden in the noise of day-to-day spending. This baseline becomes the foundation upon which realistic goals can be built, allowing you to see exactly how much is available for savings, debt repayment, or discretionary use.

Once you have your baseline, the next step is to set priorities that align with your short-term and long-term aspirations. Ask yourself what matters most: building an emergency fund, paying down a high-interest loan, or saving for a down-payment on a home. Assign a percentage of your net income to each priority, keeping the allocation flexible enough to adjust as circumstances change. It helps to think of your budget as a living document rather than a rigid contract; occasional revisions are normal and often necessary.

A common pitfall is neglecting irregular expenses such as car maintenance, insurance premiums, or holiday gifts. To avoid surprise shortfalls, estimate these costs on an annual basis and spread them evenly across the months. By creating a "sinking fund" for each category, you ensure that money is set aside before the bill arrives, smoothing out cash flow and reducing stress. This approach also encourages you to plan for future upgrades or investments, rather than reacting impulsively when the need arises.

Technology can simplify the budgeting process, but the core principles remain unchanged. Automated transaction alerts, rule-based categorization, and goal-tracking dashboards can keep you accountable without demanding constant manual entry. However, it's important to review the data regularly, verify that categories are accurate, and adjust your allocations when life events-like a salary increase or a new child-alter your financial landscape.

Finally, remember that budgeting is as much about mindset as it is about numbers. Treat your budget as a tool for empowerment rather than restriction. Celebrate milestones, such as hitting a savings target or paying off a debt, and use those successes to reinforce disciplined habits. Over time, consistent planning and thoughtful adjustments will turn a modest budget into a robust roadmap toward financial security and peace of mind.

Assign a percentage of your net income to each priority, keeping the allocation flexible enough to adjust as circumstances change. It helps to think of your budget as a living document rather than a rigid contract; occasional revisions are normal and often necessary.
A common pitfall is neglecting irregular expenses such as car maintenance, insurance premiums, or holiday gifts. To avoid surprise shortfalls, estimate these costs on an annual basis and spread them evenly across the months. By creating a "sinking fund" for each category, you ensure that money is set aside before the bill arrives, smoothing out cash flow and reducing stress. This approach also encourages you to plan for future upgrades or investments, rather than reacting impulsively when the need arises.
Technology can simplify the budgeting process, but the core principles remain unchanged. Automated transaction alerts, rule-based categorization, and goal-tracking dashboards can keep you accountable without demanding constant manual entry. However, it's important to review the data regularly, verify that categories are accurate, and adjust your allocations when life events-like a salary increase or a new child-alter your financial landscape.
Finally, remember that budgeting is as much about mindset as it is about numbers. Treat your budget as a tool for empowerment rather than restriction. Celebrate milestones, such as hitting a savings target or paying off a debt, and use those successes to reinforce disciplined habits. Over time, consistent planning and thoughtful adjustments will turn a modest budget into a robust roadmap toward financial security and peace of mind.

Memorandum

To: All Engineering Staff
From: Manufacturing Operations
Date: October 12, 2023
Subject: Introduction to 3D Printing Processes and Best Practices

Additive manufacturing, commonly known as 3D printing, involves creating three-dimensional objects from a digital model by depositing material layer by layer. Unlike traditional subtractive methods such as machining, which removes material, this technology builds up components from a liquid, powder, or filament base. This method allows for complex geometries and rapid prototyping that would be difficult or impossible to achieve with conventional tooling. Understanding the fundamental differences between these processes is essential for selecting the appropriate technology for specific part requirements.

The most common material extrusion technique utilizes a heated nozzle to melt thermoplastic filaments. The build platform moves in X, Y, and Z axes to deposit the molten material in precise paths. This method is widely used for prototypes due to its low cost and speed. However, parts produced this way often exhibit visible layer lines and anisotropic mechanical properties. Strength varies significantly depending on the orientation of the load relative to the print layers.

Surface finish quality is a critical consideration in additive manufacturing. Depending on the technology and material used, raw prints may require post-processing to meet aesthetic or functional standards. Techniques such as sanding, resin curing, or chemical fusing can smooth surfaces and enhance durability. Engineers must evaluate whether the functional requirements justify the additional time and cost of post-processing. Always consult with the materials team to determine the optimal finishing procedure for your specific design.

File preparation is equally important before initiating any print job. Standard file formats include STL and 3MF, with the latter being preferred for its support of color and metadata. Slicing software converts these models into machine-readable instructions, defining layer height, infill density, and support structures. Poorly sliced files can lead to print failures or suboptimal mechanical performance. Ensure that all models are watertight and free of non-manifold edges before exporting them to the printer queue.

Finally, material selection dictates the final properties of the manufactured part. Common materials include PLA for general use, ABS for heat resistance, and nylon for flexibility. Each material has a specific melting point and expansion rate that must be accounted for in the printer settings. New employees should undergo a hands-on training session with the materials coordinator to familiarize themselves with the available stock and their respective applications. Proper handling and storage are required to prevent moisture absorption, particularly for hygroscopic materials.

File preparation is equally important before initiating any print job. Standard file formats include STL and 3MF, with the latter being preferred for its support of color and metadata. Slicing software converts these models into machine-readable instructions, defining layer height, infill density, and support structures. Poorly sliced files can lead to print failures or suboptimal mechanical performance. Ensure that all models are watertight and free of non-manifold edges before exporting them to the printer queue.

Finally, material selection dictates the final properties of the manufactured part. Common materials include PLA for general use, ABS for heat resistance, and nylon for flexibility. Each material has a specific melting point and expansion rate that must be accounted for in the printer settings. New employees should undergo a hands-on training session with the materials coordinator to familiarize themselves with the available stock and their respective applications. Proper handling and storage are required to prevent moisture absorption, particularly for hygroscopic materials.

Subject: Update on upcoming FAA Part 107 changes
Hi Sarah,
I hope you are having a productive week. I am writing to share some important developments regarding the new aviation regulations that will affect our commercial drone operations next quarter. The Federal Aviation Administration has released the final rulemaking document, and it includes several stricter compliance measures that we need to address immediately to avoid any service disruptions.
The most significant change is the mandatory requirement for Remote ID broadcasting on all commercial aircraft flying in Class G airspace. Our current fleet of industrial inspection drones does not yet feature the integrated broadcast module, meaning we will be grounded if we do not upgrade the hardware by the end of the month. I have already requested quotes from our primary vendor and expect to have a finalized purchase order ready for your review within the next two business days.
In addition to the hardware upgrades, the new guidelines mandate annual recurrent training for all Pilots in Command. The previous refresher course we used is no longer compliant with the updated curriculum standards, which now place a greater emphasis on automated conflict detection and emergency landing protocols. I am restructuring our internal training schedule to ensure all flight operators complete the new certification module before the regulatory deadline takes effect.
We also need to revisit our standard operating procedures for night operations. The rule now requires additional anti-collision lighting intensity that our current models struggle to meet in high-wind conditions. I recommend we temporarily suspend scheduled aerial mapping projects in open rural areas until we can verify that the upgraded lighting systems meet the new photometric requirements. This precautionary step will help us maintain our safety record and ensure full regulatory compliance.
Please let me know if you want to hold a brief call this Thursday to discuss the budget implications of these upgrades. My goal is to have the procurement and training timeline fully locked in by Friday so we can start executing the necessary changes without delaying our key client deliverables. Thank you for your support in managing this transition smoothly.
Best regards,
James Miller
Operations Director

Mingdao High School

Home | About | Contact

Mingdao High School is a private secondary school located at 497, Sec 1, Zhongshan Road, Wuri District, Taichung, Taiwan 41401. The school serves grades 7-12. There are 7,510 students. The school is served by the Ming Dao high school bus station. Mingdao teaches 7 major subjects: Chinese, English, math, science, social science, information, and liberal arts.

Mingdao was founded in 1969 by Wang Fu-Lai and Wang Kuang-Ping. Mingdao is now composed of a junior high school, senior high school, comprehensive high school and adult school at night, with a total of 7,510 students.

There are more than 150,000 volumes in Mingdao library, including its Complete Library of the Four Treasuries (Siku Quanshu). The library building also includes both of its Classical Chinese Literature Classrooms, molded after ancient Chinese classrooms, and its Contemporary Literature Museum, which offers the complete works of many modern writers.

Subject: Updated Recycling Rules Effective May 1
Dear Residents,
We are writing to inform you of several updates to the recycling program that will take effect starting May 1. These changes are designed to improve the quality of the material we collect and reduce contamination, helping our community meet its sustainability goals.
Only clean, dry paper, cardboard, glass bottles, metal cans, and certain plastics may be placed in the blue bins. Food waste, soiled items, Styrofoam, and broken ceramics should be disposed of in the regular trash, as they interfere with processing.
Before you recycle, rinse containers to remove food residue and flatten boxes to save space. Caps and lids belong with their respective containers, while plastic film and bags belong in the designated collection points at the community center. This small effort makes a big difference.
The curbside pickup will occur every Wednesday for the blue bins and every Friday for the green compost bins. If you miss a collection day, you may leave your recyclables at the depot no later than 5 p.m. the following day. Please do not leave items on the street.
We appreciate your cooperation as we transition to the new system. If you have any questions or need clarification, please contact the facilities manager at (555) 123-4567 or email facilities@city.gov. Thank you for helping keep our neighborhood clean and green.
Best regards,
Jordan Lee
Facilities Manager
City Waste Services
Phone: (555) 123-4567
Email: jlee@city.gov

Subject: Urgent need for protected infrastructure on Main Street
Hi Councilmember Hayes,
I am writing to you directly because the current conditions for cyclists on Main Street have become genuinely dangerous. Last week, a near-miss involving a delivery driver and a commuter almost resulted in a serious accident. This incident feels like a symptom of a larger, systemic failure in our urban planning. We cannot continue to treat two-wheeled traffic as an afterthought in our downtown grid.
Protected bike lanes are not a luxury item or a political favor. They are a critical piece of safety infrastructure that works. Cities that have implemented physical barriers between cars and bikes report a drastic reduction in collisions and an increase in community health. The revenue generated by boosted local commerce often outweighs the initial construction costs within a few years of operation.
Our current painted lines offer zero protection. A speeding sedan can cross that white stripe with absolutely no consequence to the driver and catastrophic risk to the rider. We are sending a clear message to everyone who chooses not to drive that they do not matter. This approach alienates potential customers and drives families away from our struggling storefronts. We need to do better.
I urge you to prioritize the budget allocation for the Main Street pilot program in the upcoming session. Let us lead by example rather than waiting for legislation to change. Your constituents are watching this debate closely, and many of us are tired of hearing promises without action.
Please consider my feedback seriously as you draft the final transportation bill. I look forward to seeing tangible progress rather than vague assurances about future studies.
Best regards,
Alex Miller

Shi Yomi district

Shi Yomi district is one of the 28 districts of Arunachal Pradesh state in northeastern India. Shi-Yomi district was created on 9 December 2018 by dividing the West Siang district when northern areas along the Tibet border were made into a newly created Shi-Yomi district and the southern areas remained the part-truncated West Siang district. It has its headquarters at Tato.

Shi Yomi district is home to the people of Adi (Bokar, Libo, Ramo), Tagin, and Memba tribes. Religions practiced in the valley include Donyi Polo, Tibetan Buddhism, and Christianity. Scheduled Tribes are 12,202 (91.68%) of the population. At the time of the 2011 census, 71.83% of the population speaks Adi, 17.33% Bhotia, 3.77% Tagin, 2.17% Monpa, and 2.08% Hindi as their first language. The languages spoken in Shi-Yomi district are Adi, Bokar, Libo, Ramo, Tagin, and Memba.

Prior to the Trans-Arunachal Highway construction of the modern road, the only access was via an airstrip, used by the Indian Air Force to supply goods to local people. Another strategic road was constructed by BRO in 2017 in the Kurung Kumey district between Huri (which is already connected to Koloriang) and Sarli after heavy construction equipment was heli-airlifted from Ziro, which will enable Koloriang-Huri-Sarli-Taliha-Daporijo connectivity by facilitating the construction of the remaining Sarli-Taliha section. Once Taliha-Daporijo, Taliha-Nacho, Taliha-Tato, headquarter of Shi Yomi district, were completed, all of which were under construction in February 2021 while facing land acquisition issues, it will provide the strategic frontier connectivity from Seppa-Tamsang Yangfo-Sarili-Koloriang-Sarili-Nacho (and beyond to Daporijo-Taksing)-Tato (and beyond to Mechuka-Gelling and Aalo). The Indian Air Force maintains an airstrip, known as the Advanced Landing Ground (ALG) in Mechuka. The airstrip is used frequently to bring in vital supplies from cities in Assam via Antonov-32 aircraft and helicopters. The runway was renovated, strengthened, upgraded to a concrete runway, and extended to 4,700 feet in 2017 by the government. The area has a significant military presence, which also creates some employment opportunities for civilians. There is a twice-a-week helicopter service under the UDAN scheme. Government of Arunachal Pradesh has invited bids from private airlines to operate a 9-seater fixed-wing air service which will not be under the UDAN scheme.

Shi Yomi district's Mechuka is gradually becoming a popular tourist destination in Arunachal Pradesh due to its scenic beauty, exotic tribes, gentle hills, snow-capped mountains, and Siom River. The Siyom River, which flows through Mechukha also provides a scenic view of the valley. raw:
knitting patterns

Knitting patterns are the essential guide for any successful project. They transform a vision into a tangible object, directing knitters stitch by stitch, row by row. Without a reliable pattern, even experienced crafters would struggle beyond a basic swatch. These detailed instructions provide the roadmap, ensuring yarn transforms into the desired garment with precision. They are truly indispensable tools for all makers.

The world of knitting patterns is incredibly diverse and expansive. You'll find everything from simple dishcloths to intricate lace shawls, complex cabled sweaters, and delicate baby garments. Sources range from free online resources to paid patterns by independent designers on platforms like Ravelry. This abundance means a pattern exists for every skill level, style, and project idea, often beautifully photographed.

A good knitting pattern is characterized by clarity and comprehensive detail. It clearly states the required yarn weight, yardage, needle sizes, gauge, and any special techniques. Instructions must be logically structured, easy to follow, and include sizing options. Quality patterns often feature charts for colorwork or lace, clear photographs, or video tutorials. Ambiguous language quickly leads to frustration, making a well-written pattern invaluable.

Choosing the right pattern is crucial before casting on. Consider your skill level; an overly complex design can be discouraging. Ensure your chosen yarn matches the pattern's specifications for gauge and drape. Read through pattern notes and difficulty ratings carefully. Browsing other knitters' project pages often offers insight into challenges, helping you make an informed decision.

Following a knitting pattern is more than executing instructions; it's a journey of creation and learning. Each completed row brings you closer to your goal, building confidence. Even when challenges arise, unraveling and re-knitting refines skills and deepens understanding. The satisfaction of seeing your chosen yarn transform into a beautiful, wearable item, guided by the pattern's wisdom, is profoundly rewarding.

The evolving digital landscape has made knitting patterns more accessible and collaborative. Designers connect directly with their audience, receiving feedback and iterating.

Effective password management is the first line of defense for our organization. When you receive a password reset notification, treat it with immediate urgency. Do not ignore the email or assume it is a phishing attempt without verification. Legitimate reset requests always originate from our official security portal, accessible only through the internal company intranet. If you receive a link via direct email, do not click it. Always navigate to the secure login page directly using your browser's address bar to initiate the recovery process safely.

The new password you create must meet strict complexity requirements to withstand modern brute-force attacks. Your credential should be at least twelve characters long, combining uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers, and special symbols. Avoid using personal information such as birthdays, pet names, or common dictionary words. Instead, consider using a random phrase of several unrelated words connected by symbols, which is easier to remember yet significantly harder for automated systems to crack. This approach balances security with cognitive ease.

Never reuse a password that was previously compromised or one currently used on other personal or professional accounts. Reuse creates a dangerous web of vulnerability where a single breach exposes multiple systems. If a service you regularly use has suffered a data leak, assume your credential is compromised. Change it immediately in all attached accounts. Our identity management system flags reused credentials, preventing you from logging in until you establish a unique, strong secret.

For high-value administrative accounts, additional steps are required. These users must utilize a hardware security key or multi-factor authentication device link during the reset sequence. Simply entering a new password is insufficient for privileged access tiers. Security Operations centers monitor these actions closely. If a reset is initiated from an unfamiliar IP address or location, an automatic verification call will be placed to the registered phone number. Responding to this verification is mandatory to complete the process.

Post-reset, you should verify your session stability across all devices. Log out and back in on workstations or mobile applications to ensure the change propagates correctly. Report any lingering access issues to the Help Desk immediately. Delays in reporting can extend the window of potential unauthorized access. Remember, strong passwords are just one component of a robust security posture. Maintain vigilance against social engineering tactics that target human error, which remains the most common vector for enterprise breaches.

The annual Riverside Community Craft Fair has concluded, marking its twenty-fifth successful iteration in the city's history. Organized by the Department of Cultural Affairs in partnership with local zoning boards, the event transformed three city blocks into a vibrant marketplace that attracted an estimated twelve thousand visitors over the weekend. The inaugural day saw particularly high foot traffic, with rain delays on Saturday giving way to bright sunshine that encouraged lingering and browsing. Merchants reported strong engagement, with several independent artisans noting their highest earnings of the year, validating the fair's role as a critical economic artery for small-scale creative professionals in the region.

Despite the overall success, several operational challenges surfaced that warrant immediate attention for next year's logistical planning. Traffic management around the northern perimeter proves increasingly difficult as the surrounding housing density continues to grow. The current two-way street closure caused significant congestion in side streets, leading to complaints from residents and localized spill-over into residential alleys by mid-afternoon. Survey data indicates that forty percent of attendees used personal vehicles rather than public transit, a shift from previous years that correlates with the expansion of the downtown parking structure. Security teams note that the influx of cars created blind spots in camera coverage, necessitating a review of surveillance placement and patrol routes to ensure comprehensive monitoring of both merchandise and pedestrian pathways.

Vendor feedback highlights the need for improved infrastructure support within the designated craft zones. Many pottery and glass artists expressed frustration regarding the uneven ground conditions near the riverbank, which impacted the stability of their display cases and the safety of their fragile goods. Furthermore, power access remains a bottleneck; the increased demand for electric lights and heating elements has strained the temporary grid, resulting in intermittent outages during peak evening hours. The department will allocate additional funding for reinforced flooring preparations and supplementary generator rentals. We will also be revising vendor application criteria to include specific requirements for equipment that draws high power, ensuring that the electrical load is managed more effectively and sustainably across the fairgrounds.

Financial performance data indicates a marginal decrease in total expenditure following the sharp rise in entry fees and vendor booth costs. While revenue from concession stands and light food vendors increased by fifteen percent, the overall spending per visitor dipped by approximately eight dollars compared to last year. This trend suggests that attendees are becoming more selective about their purchases, prioritizing quality interactions over impulse buys. To counter this, marketing efforts for the forthcoming edition should focus on promoting unique, high-value craft categories and exclusive artist meet-and-greets. Digital pre-registration discounts could also incentivize early commitment, helping to stabilize projected financial models and reduce the uncertainty associated with weather-dependent attendance fluctuations.

The organizing committee extends its sincere gratitude to the hundreds of volunteers who dedicated their time to maintaining cleanliness, guiding visitors, and supporting vendor setup and teardown. Their resilience was particularly evident during the sudden wind gusts on Sunday afternoon, which required rapid coordination to secure loose materials. As we transition into the post-event review phase, all stakeholders are encouraged to submit detailed written feedback by the end of next month. These reports will form the core of the strategic planning document for the upcoming season, ensuring that the craft fair continues to evolve as a cornerstone of our community's cultural identity and local economic vitality.

Subject: Maintenance Issue in Unit 402 - Persistent Leak Under Kitchen Sink
Dear Property Management Team,
I am writing to formally report a recurring maintenance issue in my apartment, Unit 402, specifically concerning the plumbing under the kitchen sink. Over the past two days, I have noticed a consistent drip from the connection point where the main supply line meets the sink drain. While the leak was initially minor, it has escalated significantly since this morning. I noticed a small puddle forming on the floor of the cabinet whenever I used the hot water tap, which indicates that the seal on the gasket or the compression nut is failing. I have placed a bucket underneath to catch the water, but it is now nearly full, and the cabinet floor is becoming waterlogged, posing a risk of mold growth or structural damage to the wood if not addressed immediately.
The urgency of this matter is heightened by the fact that the temperature in the building has dropped considerably over the last night. Given the current cold snap, I am concerned that the moisture continuing to accumulate inside the closed cabinet could lead to frozen pipes more quickly than usual, or cause the existing joint to crack under pressure. I have already shut off the main water valve for the kitchen sink as a temporary mitigation measure to prevent further flooding, but this means I am unable to use the sink for basic hygiene tasks or dishwashing, which is becoming quite difficult to manage in my daily routine. I understand that you receive many requests, but I wanted to emphasize that this is not a cosmetic issue but a functional failure that threatens the integrity of the unit.
I have inspected the visible components myself and can confirm that the nut appears to be stripping at the threads, suggesting that standard tightening tools will not resolve the root cause. Replacing the washer or the entire adapter may be necessary. Since I am not licensed to perform heavy plumbing repairs and do not have the specialized tools required for a proper replacement without risking further damage to the pipes, I must ask for a professional technician to be dispatched as soon as possible. I am available to be home for the repair any time between nine in the morning and five in the afternoon starting tomorrow, though I can accommodate an earlier slot if your schedule allows. Please let me know if there are any specific instructions I should follow before the technician arrives, such as clearing out the cabinet entirely to provide better access.
I would also appreciate it if you could confirm whether this repair falls under the standard maintenance coverage or if there are any associated costs I should be aware of, although given the nature of the wear and tear on the existing fixtures, I assume this is a standard landlord responsibility. If the leak has already caused any damage to the subfloor or the cabinet itself, I kindly request that this be included in the assessment and repair scope. I have taken a few photographs of the leak and the water damage to the cabinet floor and can attach them to this email upon your request, or I can forward them separately if that works better for your system. Please treat this matter with priority, as I am currently limited in my use of one of the essential fixtures in my home.
Thank you for your prompt attention to this matter. I look forward to receiving a confirmation of the scheduled visit time so I can plan my day accordingly. If there is any delay in getting a technician out, please inform me immediately so I can arrange alternative living accommodations if the situation becomes unsafe or uninhabitable. My contact number is listed in your records, and I will be checking my email frequently for updates. I appreciate your assistance in resolving this issue efficiently and respectfully hope to have the problem fixed before it escalates into a more significant and costly emergency. I value living in a well-maintained building and trust that this will be handled swiftly.
Sincerely,
Alex Meridian
Unit 402
(555) 019-2834
alex.meridian@email.com

2008 Oregon Ballot Measure 62

Home | About | Contact

Oregon Ballot Measure 62 (2008) (formerly IRR 41) appeared on the November 4, 2008 general election ballot in Oregon. It was an initiated constitutional amendment dealing with the issue of where a percentage of profit from the Oregon State Lottery should go. The initiative, if it had passed, would have required that 15% of net lottery proceeds be deposited in a public safety fund. 50% of that fund would have been distributed to counties to fund grants for childhood programs, district attorney operations, and sheriff's investigations. The other 50% of the fund would have gone to Oregon State Police criminal investigations and forensic operations. It is expected that most of that money would have been diverted from schools. It was rejected with around 60% of the votes statewide; every county except for Josephine saw majority rejection.

The official ballot title is: Allocates 15% Of Lottery Proceeds To Public Safety Fund For Crime Prevention, Investigation, Prosecution Measure 62 has become unofficially known as the "Oregon C.S.I. Measure".

20% for grants to counties to fund early childhood programs for children who are at risk; 50% to fund the criminal investigation and forensics operations (including crime lab) of the Oregon State Police to assist law enforcement throughout the state; 15% to provide grants to countries to supplement existing county appropriations for the operations of District Attorneys; 15% to provide grants to counties to supplement existing county appropriations for investigation and field operations of county sheriffs.

The state's Financial Estimate Committee prepares estimated fiscal impact statements for any ballot measures that will appear on the ballot. The estimate prepared by this committee for Measure 62 says:

Measure 62 would require public safety spending from the state lottery fund of $100 million in the first year, increasing in subsequent years depending on how much money goes into the state lottery fund from the sales of tickets in the Oregon state-sponsored lottery.,

More money going into crime investigations will help reduce the backlog of investigations. Currently, some crimes in Oregon aren't investigated using modern forensic techniques because the resources don't exist. Rural counties especially need the help funding investigations. The money is needed to help stabilize funding for state police investigations.

It would divert money from the lottery that would otherwise go to schools. From the Oregonian's No on 62 endorsement: "Ballot Measure 62 is one more in a long line of gratuitous assaults on good government in Oregon. Ill-conceived and poorly crafted, the measure would rip millions of lottery dollars from where they are most needed -- Oregon classrooms -- and squander them in a hodgepodge of public safety causes."

Defend Oregon, as a committee, fought seven different ballot measures, and supported two others. As a result, it is not possible to discern how much of its campaign money was going specifically to defeat Measure 61. Altogether, the group raised over $6 million in 2008. Major donations to the Defend Oregon group as of October 8 included:

Oregon Ballot Measure 62 (2008) (formerly IRR 41) appeared on the November 4, 2008 general election ballot in Oregon. It was an initiated constitutional amendment dealing with the issue of where a percentage of profit from the Oregon State Lottery should go. The initiative, if it had passed, would have required that 15% of net lottery proceeds be deposited in a public safety fund. 50% of that fund would have been distributed to counties to fund grants for childhood programs, district attorney operations, and sheriff's investigations. The other 50% of the fund would have gone to Oregon State Police criminal investigations and forensic operations. It is expected that most of that money would have been diverted from schools. It was rejected with around 60% of the votes statewide; every county except for Josephine saw majority rejection.
The official ballot title is: Allocates 15% Of Lottery Proceeds To Public Safety Fund For Crime Prevention, Investigation, Prosecution Measure 62 has become unofficially known as the "Oregon C.S.I. Measure".
20% for grants to counties to fund early childhood programs for children who are at risk; 50% to fund the criminal investigation and forensics operations (including crime lab) of the Oregon State Police to assist law enforcement throughout the state; 15% to provide grants to countries to supplement existing county appropriations for the operations of District Attorneys; 15% to provide grants to counties to supplement existing county appropriations for investigation and field operations of county sheriffs.
The state's Financial Estimate Committee prepares estimated fiscal impact statements for any ballot measures that will appear on the ballot. The estimate prepared by this committee for Measure 62 says:
Measure 62 would require public safety spending from the state lottery fund of $100 million in the first year, increasing in subsequent years depending on how much money goes into the state lottery fund from the sales of tickets in the Oregon state-sponsored lottery.,
More money going into crime investigations will help reduce the backlog of investigations. Currently, some crimes in Oregon aren't investigated using modern forensic techniques because the resources don't exist. Rural counties especially need the help funding investigations. The money is needed to help stabilize funding for state police investigations.
It would divert money from the lottery that would otherwise go to schools. From the Oregonian's No on 62 endorsement: "Ballot Measure 62 is one more in a long line of gratuitous assaults on good government in Oregon. Ill-conceived and poorly crafted, the measure would rip millions of lottery dollars from where they are most needed -- Oregon classrooms -- and squander them in a hodgepodge of public safety causes."
Defend Oregon, as a committee, fought seven different ballot measures, and supported two others. As a result, it is not possible to discern how much of its campaign money was going specifically to defeat Measure 61. Altogether, the group raised over $6 million in 2008. smart home devices

Smart home devices have moved from a futuristic novelty to a staple of everyday life, and the market now offers solutions that cater to nearly every household need. From voice-controlled speakers that can dim the lights to thermostats that learn your schedule, the convenience factor is undeniable. Yet the real value lies in how these gadgets communicate with each other, creating an ecosystem that can adapt to the rhythms of a busy family or a single professional.

When choosing a hub, compatibility is the first question to ask. Many brands still rely on proprietary protocols, which can lock you into a single ecosystem and limit future expansion. Devices that support widely adopted standards such as Zigbee, Z-Wave, or Thread tend to integrate more smoothly with a broader range of products. This openness also makes it easier to replace a single component without overhauling the entire system, preserving both budget and flexibility.

Security concerns have kept some consumers hesitant, but manufacturers have responded with stronger encryption and regular firmware updates. A good practice is to keep the central hub on a separate Wi-Fi network from your primary devices, reducing exposure if a smart appliance is compromised. Additionally, opting for devices that offer two-factor authentication for their companion apps adds an extra layer of protection, ensuring that only authorized users can control your home environment.

Energy efficiency is another compelling reason to upgrade. Smart thermostats can cut heating and cooling costs by up to 15 percent by adjusting temperature based on occupancy patterns and weather forecasts. Likewise, smart plugs and power strips can monitor usage in real time, allowing you to shut down idle electronics with a tap on your phone. Over time, these savings not only lower your utility bills but also reduce your household's carbon footprint, making sustainability a tangible benefit of the technology.

The user experience continues to improve as artificial intelligence becomes more embedded in home automation. Voice assistants now understand context better, allowing you to issue multi-step commands like "Set the movie night mode," which can lower blinds, dim lights, and start your streaming service in a single phrase. As these AI capabilities evolve, the promise of a truly intuitive home-one that anticipates your needs before you voice them-edges closer to reality.

Ultimately, the decision to adopt smart home devices should balance convenience, security, and long-term value. Start with a few core components that address your most pressing needs, and expand gradually as you become comfortable with the system's capabilities. By selecting interoperable, regularly updated products, you can build a resilient network that not only simplifies daily routines but also enhances the safety and efficiency of your living space.

Subject: Updates and Tips for Your Marathon Training
Hi Jamie,
I hope you're feeling strong after our last long run. I wanted to share a quick rundown of what we've covered so far and a few adjustments to keep the momentum going. The key this week is to focus on steady mileage while incorporating a couple of speed intervals to boost your lactate threshold. Remember, consistency beats occasional bursts of intensity, so stick to the schedule we've outlined.
Your current weekly mileage sits at 42 miles, which is right on target for the mid-phase of our plan. Make sure you're logging each run in the app, noting how you felt during the hills and any aches that lingered. If you notice any niggling soreness, especially in the calves or shins, take an extra day of rest or swap a run for low-impact cross-training like swimming or cycling.
Nutrition is another pillar we can't overlook. Aim for a balanced intake of carbs, protein, and healthy fats, and experiment with fueling during longer runs. I've found that a 30-gram gel at the 10-mile mark works well for most runners, but feel free to test different options during your weekend long run. Hydration is equally crucial; carry a handheld bottle or use the water stations strategically placed on the course.
Sleep and recovery will make a huge difference as the mileage climbs. Try to get at least seven to eight hours of quality sleep each night and incorporate stretching or foam rolling after each session. If you can, schedule a short yoga session once a week to improve flexibility and core strength. These habits will help you stay injury-free and keep your energy levels high.
Let me know how the next two weeks feel, and if you have any questions about the upcoming taper phase. I'm confident you'll hit the marathon with confidence and a strong finish line. Keep up the great work!
Best regards,
Alex Rivera
Head Coach, RunStrong Training Group

Kolisch Quartet

The Kolisch Quartet was a string quartet musical ensemble founded in Vienna, originally (early 1920s) as the New Vienna String Quartet for the performance of Schoenberg's works, and (by 1927) settling to the form in which it was later known. It had a worldwide reputation and made several recordings. The quartet disbanded in the United States during the early 1940s.

Othmar Steinbauer (1921-1922) Herbert Duesberg (1922-1923) Marcel Dick (1924-1927) Eugene Lehner (1927-1939) Jascha Veissi (1939-1941) Kurt Frederick (1941-1942) Ralph Hersh (1942-1943) Bernhard Milofsky (1943-1944) violoncello:

In the early 1920s, the Viennese violinist Rudolf Kolisch began to study composition with Arnold Schoenberg, who also put Kolisch to work in the composer's "Society for Private Musical Performances" (Verein fuer musikalische Privatauffuehrungen). This led to the creation of a string quartet ("Neue Wiener Streichquartett") dedicated to performing Schoenberg's music, but also to performing the classical string quartet repertoire in a manner which would take into account the principles of Schoenberg's teaching. The quartet consisted initially of Kolisch and Fritz Rothschild (alternating first and second violins), Marcel Dick (viola) and Joachim Stutschewsky (cello). This ensemble began to concertize and tour in central Europe. By 1927, the membership of the ensemble had settled: Kolisch played first violin, Felix Khuner played second violin, Eugene Lehner played viola and Benar Heifetz played cello; this group became known as the Kolisch Quartet. Numerous works were written for them by composers including Alban Berg, Anton Webern, Arnold Schoenberg, and Béla Bartók. The Quartet's tours extended eventually to include all European countries including Scandinavia, and also (by the mid-1930s) North and South America. One notable aspect of the Quartet was that they generally performed from memory, including difficult modern works such as the Lyric Suite of Berg. This was not intended as a demonstration of any special powers of memorization, but rather of an approach which involved such careful rehearsal that by the time a piece was ready for performance, the musicians no longer required the score. The quartet used eye contact and were more able to respond musically to one another without music stands interfering. The Quartet was on tour in Paris in 1938 when Nazi Germany annexed Austria. Because of their association with Schoenberg (whose music had been banned by the Nazis) and because most of the members of the Quartet were considered Jewish according to the Nazi legal definition, they did not return to Vienna. They set up their headquarters in Paris and toured from there. Béla Bartók's String Quartet No. 6 is dedicated to the Kolisch Quartet, and it was they who gave its premiere at The Town Hall in New York City on 20 January 1941. They were on tour in the United States when that country entered the war and civilian transport across the ocean suddenly became unavailable. Rather than continue with the Quartet in the face of great uncertainty about the future, the cellist and violist soon took jobs with major U.S. orchestras (Philadelphia and Boston, respectively). The Quartet continued to play concerts with replacement players for some time, but when the second violinist left to join an orchestra in San Francisco, the Quartet finally disbanded.

The Kolisch Quartet recorded several albums of string quartets of Franz Schubert and Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart on 78s for the Columbia Records and RCA record labels. In 1937 they recorded the four string quartets of Arnold Schoenberg privately under the composer's supervision; these were re-issued several years later as LP recordings on the "Alco" label. All the commercial recordings of the Kolisch Quartet are currently available on compact discs.

Bartók: Quartet No. 5 Mozart: Quartet in C major, K 465; Jascha Veissi, viola; Stefan Auber, cello (Columbia M439) Mozart: Quartet in D major, K 575 'Cello' or 'Solo' (Columbia LX 337-8). Schoenberg: Quartets 1-4 Schubert: Quartet in A minor, Op. 29 (Columbia LX 286-9). Schubert: Quartettsatz in C minor (Columbia LX 289). Schubert: Quartet in G major, Op. 161 (Columbia LX 357-60).

Philosophers, Poets & Kings

Philosophers, Poets & Kings is the sixteenth studio album by English folk singer Kate Rusby. It features traditional folk music, original songs and covers of Fairport Convention and Oasis. The album was released by Pure Records, including on CD and on vinyl, on 17 May 2019. It garnered positive critical reception that praised the production and instrumentation. The final song, "Halt the Wagons", commemorates the death of 26 children in the Huskar Pit mining disaster.

The album features arrangements of traditional songs, songs written by Rusby or co-written with her father, two cover songs and a remix. Colleen Taylor of The Irish Echo reviewed that the album saw Rusby return to acoustic folk after recent experimentation with electronic. It is centred around Rusby's family and home in Barnsley, Yorkshire. Tonally, it features "jaunty, comic" songs like the lead song "Jenny" as well as more emotional tracks like "Halt the Wagons". "Bogey's Bonnie Belle" is a 20th-century Scots folk song that has been performed by Irish artists including Christy Moore and Cherish the Ladies. "Crazy Man Michael", a song by Fairport Convention, was a favourite childhood song of Rusby's. "The Squire and the Parson" was co-written by Rusby and her father many years prior to the album's release. It is based on a Barnsley legend about a drunken fight. "The Wanderer" is an original song by Rusby about a man in her community with Alzheimer's disease. The final track, "Halt the Wagons", was written for the 180th anniversary of the Huskar Pit mining disaster in which 26 children died, following which Parliament restricted underground work to people aged at least ten years old. The song and music video featured members of the Barnsley Youth Choir in the same demographics as the victims: aged seven to seventeen, with 15 boys and 11 girls. It was first performed by Rusby's mother at a local concert to commemorate the anniversary on 5 July 2018. Rusby performed it with the backing choir at the 2018 Underneath the Stars Festival.

Taylor said that it was "quickly winning the race to become my favorite Rusby album-perhaps my favorite folk album-to date". She praised that "Rusby can reinvent traditional songs better than anyone recording today", giving the example of "Bogey's Bonnie Belle", which Rusby modernises with electronic guitar and synthesisers. Taylor lauded "Halt the Wagons" as "gorgeous in its simple, subdued, yet affective brass instrument arrangement", and explained that "The Farmer's Toast" was her favourite song due to its "expert tune arrangement, joyous balladeering, and historical flare". Taylor concludes that Rusby transports the listener to the traditional village life of her music's tradition. Neil McFayden of Folk Radio praised the album's production. For instance, on "Jenny", the "understated opening" builds to a "singalong chorus" through the "beats and brass". McFayden enjoyed the cover of "Don't Go Away", as it was performed "superbly soft, beautifully sparse, and with an edge of plaintive appeal". He summarised that the album was "impressive" as Rusby "continues to apply her exquisite voice to a meticulous selection of songs, including her own". In Louder Than War, Mike Ainscoe positively reviewed songs such as "Until Morning", with its "exquisiteness", and "Halt the Wagons", after which "there won't be a dry eye in the house". Ainscoe called the cover songs a "surprise highlight" and said that O'Kane's guitar was "caressed with a touch so precise and sensitive that belies its potential dominance".

Kate Rusby - vocals Damien O'Kane - backing vocals Michael McGoldrick - backing vocals Sam Kelly - backing vocals Ross Ainslie - whistling Chas Mackenzie - electric guitar Duncan Lyall - double bass, Moog Nick Cooke - accordion Josh Clark - percussion Gary Wyatt - cornet Rich Evans - flugelhorn Ron Block - banjo

Mahesh Bhuriya

Mahesh Bhuriya (born 1970) is an Indian politician from Gujarat. He is a member of the Gujarat Legislative Assembly from Jhalod Assembly constituency, which is reserved for Scheduled Tribe community, in Dahod district. He won the 2022 Gujarat Legislative Assembly election representing the Bharatiya Janata Party.

Bhuriya is from Jhalod, Dahod district, Gujarat. He is the son of Somjibhai Bhuriya. He passed Class 12 in 2002 at M.S. High School, Gandhinagar and later discontinued his studies.

Bhuriya won from Jhalod Assembly constituency representing the Bharatiya Janata Party in the 2022 Gujarat Legislative Assembly election. He polled 82,745 votes and defeated his nearest rival, Anilbhai Garasiya of the Aam Aadmi Party, by a margin of 35,222 votes. He first became an MLA winning the 2002 Gujarat Legislative Assembly election from Limdi Assembly constituency representing the BJP. In the 2017 Gujarat Legislative Assembly election he lost to Bhaveshbhai Babubhai Katara of the Indian National Congress by a margin of 25,410 votes.

Vin Cronin

Vincent R. Cronin (September 7, 1906 - January 4, 1993) was an American basketball coach who was the head men's basketball at Boston University from 1949 to 1952.

Cronin born in Somerville, Massachusetts and was one of 12 children. He and raised by his older sisters after the death of his parents. He was a football and basketball star at Somerville High School and graduated in 1924. He then attended St. John's Preparatory School and Saint Anselm College.

In 1942, Cronin became the head boys' basketball coach at Somerville High. His teams won the Tech Tourney five times (1942, 1943, 1944, 1945, and 1949), the state championship twice (1944 and 1949), and the New England title once (1949). Many of his players went on to play in college, including Tony Lavelli and Ron Perry. In 1949, he became the head coach of the Boston University Terriers men's basketball team. He compiled a 23-29 record over his three seasons with the Terriers. While at BU, Cronin studied for his bachelor's degree in physical education, which he received in 1952. After graduating, Cronin became a teacher in the Somerville school system. In 1953, he returned to coaching at Mission High School in Roxbury. In 1954, he was hospitalized with a "stimulated nervous condition" and on the advice of his doctor, gave up coaching. He retired from the Somerville Public Schools in 1977.

Sunday Concert

Sunday Concert is Canadian singer Gordon Lightfoot's first solo live album, released in 1969 on the United Artists label. Lightfoot's last recording for United Artists, it was also his first live album and until the release of a live DVD in 2002 remained Lightfoot's only officially released live recording. The album was recorded at Massey Hall in Toronto. The album is notable as it includes performances of five previously unreleased tracks. It also contains the first recording of Lightfoot's hits "I'm Not Sayin'" and "Ribbon of Darkness" together as a medley. This medley would later feature on Gord's Gold and would become a concert staple. "Ballad of Yarmouth Castle" chronicles the fate of the SS Yarmouth Castle which caught fire and sank off the Bahamas in November, 1965. A 1993 CD reissue on Bear Family Records includes five studio recordings as bonus tracks.

In his Allmusic review, critic Richie Unterberger praised the album, writing "These then-new songs aren't among his classics, but are up to the general high standard of his '60s work, with the socially conscious "The Lost Children" and the poetic "Leaves of Grass" standing out as lyrical highlights."

New Suns: Original Speculative Fiction by People of Color

New Suns: Original Speculative Fiction by People of Color is a 2019 speculative fiction anthology edited by Nisi Shawl. The anthology received critical acclaim, winning the 2020 British Fantasy Award, Ignyte Award, Locus Award, and World Fantasy Award, all in the anthology and/or collected works category. The title is taken from a quote by Octavia E. Butler: "There's nothing new under the sun, but there are new suns."

"The Galactic Tourist Industrial Complex" by Tobias S. Buckell "Deer Dancer" by Kathleen Alcalá "The Virtue of Unfaithful Translations" by Minsoo Kang "Come Home to Atropos" by Steven Barnes "The Fine Print" by Chinelo Onwualu "unkind of mercy" by Alex Jennings "Burn the Ships" by Alberto Yáñez "The Freedom of the Shifting Sea" by Jaymee Goh "Three Variations on a Theme of Imperial Attire" by E. Lily Yu "Blood and Bells" by Karin Lowachee "Give Me Your Black Wings Oh Sister" by Silvia Moreno-Garcia "The Shadow We Cast Through Time" by Indrapramit Das "The Robots of Eden" by Anil Menon "Dumb House" by Andrea Hairston "One Easy Trick" by Hiromi Goto "Harvest" by Rebecca Roanhorse "Kelsey and the Burdened Breath" by Darcie Little Badger

Writing for Locus, Rich Horton praised the anthology, particularly the science fiction stories. Horton wrote that the strongest entries included "The Fine Print", "The Shadow We Cast Through Time", and "The Robots of Eden". The review praised the diversity of the selected authors, noting the value of "different histories, both personal and cultural, in informing the imagination." Horton concluded the review by calling the book one of the best original anthologies of the year. John Rieder of Los Angeles Review of Books called the book a "varied, rich, and delightful collection". Rieder examined the way in which the SFF literary community has become more diverse over the previous decades, beginning with Clarion West Writers Workshops of the 1990s and the publication of the Dark Matter anthologies in 2000. Rieder commented upon the way the genre has become more inclusive for women and writers of color, changing the genre for the better. Rieder noted that the stories included significant diversity of themes and genres, but commented that several stories examined colonialism from the perspective of authors of color. Cynthia C. Scott reviewed the anthology in Strange Horizons, also noting that the book follows in the footsteps of Dark Matter and later anthologies of authors of color. Scott noted that the fantasy stories were stronger than the science fiction offerings, but praised the breadth of themes explored in the collection: "race, gender, sexual orientation, and culture; there is literally something here for everyone." Mahvesh Murad of Reactor noted that the anthology is presented without an overarching theme, but that many stories examine the notion of "otherness". Soli IV

Soli IV is a brass trio written in 1967, the last of a series of four works by Mexican composer Carlos Chávez, each featuring a succession of solos. In contrast to the more traditional character of most of Chávez's large-ensemble work, the Solis belong to the more "experimental", high-modernist strand of his compositional output, which features an abstract, atonal musical language based on the principle of non-repetition. In the composer's own words, the objective is one of "constant rebirth, of true derivation: a stream that never comes back to its source; a stream of eternal development, like a spiral, always linked to, and continuing, its original source, but always searching for new and unlimited spaces".

Soli IV was commissioned by Mario di Bonaventura for the Hopkins Center Congregation for the Arts at Dartmouth College, in Hanover, New Hampshire. It was premiered in the Spaulding Auditorium of the Hopkins Center on 9 August 1967 by Robert Pierce, horn, Dominick de Gangi, trumpet, and Dean Werner, trombone.

Soli IV "has about it a rather special kind of 'atonality' (since the more 'tonal' intervals, such as fifths, fourths, major-thirds, minor-sevenths, and octaves, are seldom, or never used). Otherwise, melody and melodic counterpoint, proceed freely, each 'antecedent' producing a 'consequent' that in turn becomes the antecedent for a new consequent. It is music that continually evolves from itself. In this sense, the entire piece constitutes a single, long, main 'theme'". In Soli IV, the foreground is taken first by the horn, then the trumpet, and finally the trombone The instrumental solos, however, are often submerged in the ensemble interaction. Sections are created by tempo changes and subtle alterations of texture and style, and each section is introduced by either the trumpet or the trombone. Within a prevailing chromatic field, Chávez concentrates locally on smaller note groupings, primarily of four- or five-note chromatic sets. A slightly larger set of seven notes, E, E♭, D, C♯, G, G♯ F♯ in the trombone opens the work lyrically and at a moderate pace. Six more sections follow (beginning at b. 30, 43, 85, 92, 103, and 112). The evolving contrapuntal interplay is punctuated by vertical harmonies, almost always of the (0,1,2) chromatic trichord, sometimes preceded by an (0,1,3) trichord to form a cadence. The final cadence is also to a (0,1,2) trichord: trumpet and trombone on F5 and E♭5 over E4 in the horn.

Lee Thommock

Lee Hammock (November 28, 1976 - September 2, 2022), who changed his surname to Thommock later in life, was an American professional writer and game designer who worked on numerous products for various companies, including the NeoExodus: A House Divided role-playing game (Louis Porter Jr. Design), The Halo Graphic Novel and the Dawning Star Campaign Setting (Blue Devil Games).

Hammock was born on November 28, 1976 and raised in Georgia. At an early age he was diagnosed with a heart murmur, and although he was barred from organized sports, he still led an active life. In high school, Hammock became interested in videogames and role-playing games. The latter led him into the world of LARPing.

Home | About | Contact

Hammock worked creatively in the fields of graphic novels, comics, role-playing games and videogames for companies such as Bethesda Games, Paizo, Tripwire Interactive, and Blizzard Entertainment. Hammock co-designed the licensed Farscape role-playing game for Alderac Entertainment Group. He also co-designed the Dawning Star Campaign Setting with Justin D. Jacobson for Blue Devil Games, which was subsequently a finalist for "Best d20 Game" at the 2002 ENNIE Awards. Hammock worked for DC Comics. Hammock wrote the story "The Last Voyage of the Infinite Succor" for The Halo Graphic Novel. He described the process of writing the story as a "heady task" since he had to respect Halo fans' knowledge of the characters and canon, ensuring that "characters that [the fans] know as a part of themselves are portrayed aptly". Hammock described the basis of the story as a way to showcase the true danger of the Flood as an intelligent menace, rather than something the player encounters and shoots. Hammock also stated that the story would prove the intelligent nature of the Flood, and "hopefully euthanize the idea that they are just space zombies". Hammock co-designed the NeoExodus: A House Divided RPG for Louis Porter Jr. Design. He also co-designed the Arcane Tech book for the Fading Suns role-playing game. Hammock was lead game designer on Fallen Earth. On April 5, 2010, the Fallen Earth team announced that Hammock was leaving Fallen Earth to work as story designer on a new MMO title, Gargantuan.

After Hammock married Lindsay Thompson, they both legally changed their surnames to "Thommack", a portmanteau of "Thompson" and "Hammock". They had several children. He suffered a stroke on September 1, 2022, and died the next day, age 45.
