raw:
Gruffydd Robert

Gruffydd Robert (1527-98) was a Welsh Catholic priest and humanist scholar who in 1567 wrote a pioneering Welsh grammar while in exile in Italy with his uncle and fellow-writer Morys Clynnog.

Gruffydd Robert was born in Caernarfonshire (Gwynedd) to parents named in the sources as Robert and Catrin ferch Gruffudd. He was awarded an MA degree from Christ Church, Oxford in 1555 before taking office as archdeacon of Anglesey in 1558. Shortly after his appointment Mary I died and Protestantism was reaffirmed as the established religion of England and Wales with the Acts of Supremacy and Uniformity (1558) following the accession of Elizabeth I. Catholicism remained strong in Wales, and Gruffydd was among those who remained faithful to the old religion. Gruffydd Robert and Morys Clynnog chose to leave Wales for the continent after Elizabeth became Queen. By January 1563 they were in Rome, where Gruffydd was ordained priest. Both he and Morys Clynnog became chaplains to the English Hospice (which in 1579 would become the English College) in that city. By 1567, when the first part of his grammar was published, Gruffydd Robert was in Milan, in the service of Archbishop Cardinal Borromeo. Gruffydd was referred to as doctor by Anthony Munday and Morris Kyffin; he may have received a doctorate at Louvain, Belgium or perhaps during his time in Milan. Gruffydd was confessor to Borromeo and canon theologian to the Duomo (Milan Cathedral). During the plague of 1576-7 he was noted for his courage and assiduousness in caring for the sick. He remained in Milan in the service of Carlo Borromeo and his successors, Gaspare Visconti and Federico Borromeo. In 1582 Gruffydd Robert requested retirement from publicly preaching in the cathedral of Milan; there being no other position vacant, he received a diocesan pension. After Borromeo's death in November 1584 he would have had more time to work on his grammar. Gruffydd died on 15 May 1598 in the Archbishop's Palace in Milan.

The first part of Gruffydd Robert's groundbreaking grammar of Welsh was published as Dosbarth Byrr ar y rhann gyntaf i ramadeg Cymraeg ('A brief analysis of the first part of a Welsh Grammar') in Milan on Saint David's Day in 1567, probably at the press of Vincenzo Girardoni. The second, third and fourth parts are likely to have appeared post 1584. All of these are presented in the form of a dialogue between Gruffydd and Morys Clynnog, described as having taken place in a vineyard (possibly at Monti di Creta in Rome, which belonged to the Hospice). Clynnog himself is reported as having drowned c. 1582; St. Carlo Borromeo, who is referred to as Gruffydd's master or lord in the grammar, also died in 1584. The fourth part of the grammar discusses cynghanedd and the 24 strict metres of Welsh poetry. Also included with the grammar were the first published collection of Welsh poems and what remains of Gruffydd's literary translation of the Cato Maior de Senectute by Cicero.

T. Gwynfor Griffith, 'Italian Humanism and Welsh Prose' in Yorkshire Celtic Studies (vol. vi, 1953-58). D. Rhys Phillips, Dr. Griffith Robert, Canon of Milan (1922). G. J. Williams (ed.), Gramadeg Gruffydd Robert (University of Wales Press, Cardiff, 1939). This remains the standard edition of Gruffydd Robert's grammar, with an extensive introduction. M. P. Bryant-Quinn, 'Dyddiadau a Chefndir Gruffydd Robert, Milan: Gwybodaeth Newydd', Welsh History Review/Cylchgrawn Hanes Cymru, 29/4 (2019), 532-61.

Subject: Concerns regarding recent incidents on Maple Street
Dear Neighbors,
I am writing to you today to share some concerns about safety in our immediate vicinity. Over the past two weeks, I have noticed a disturbing increase in activity on Maple Street, specifically between the hours of 9:00 PM and 4:00 AM. Several residents have mentioned seeing unfamiliar vehicles parked in front of our homes for extended periods. These cars often have their windows tinted heavily, making it difficult to see who is inside. While I do not wish to panic anyone, the pattern feels repetitive and warrants our collective attention. It is unfair to assume the worst, but ignoring these signs seems to lead to negligence.
The most troubling incident occurred last Tuesday when my friend John reported a break-in attempt at his front door. The handle was visibly forced, though he was fortunate enough to arrive home just in time. He did not see anyone, but the sound of metal scraping against the wood woke him from a deep sleep. This was not an isolated event. Two days later, a different family on the corner reported that their back gate was left wide open despite being securely latched the previous morning. These minor signs of intrusion suggest that someone is scouting the area for easy targets.
Our current security setup is reactive rather than proactive. We have motion-sensor lights on the house, but they cover only the driveway. The side alley and the rear garden remain largely unlit, creating dark spots that could hide someone moving through the property unnoticed. I propose that we collaboratively fund a few additional high-powered floodlights for the shared green space and the alleyway. This would not only deter potential intruders but also improve general visibility for late-night walkers and cyclists within the neighborhood.
Beyond physical hardware, we need to strengthen our community watch efforts. I suggest we form a small group that takes turns walking through the lower half of the street between 11:00 PM and 1:00 AM. We can share our shift schedules via a simple shared calendar to ensure no night is missed. If anyone feels uncomfortable walking alone, pairs are encouraged to coordinate. We are not asking for anyone to act as a vigilante, but mere presence and awareness create a much safer environment for everyone living here.
Please reply to this email if you are willing to participate in either the lighting fund or the walking patrol. We can meet for coffee at the local cafe this Saturday at 10:00 AM to finalize the details. Let's work together to ensure that Maple Street remains a place where we can feel secure in our own homes. Your input and participation will make a significant difference in how we approach these emerging issues. Thank you for your time and consideration.
Sincerely,
Elena Vance
142 Maple Street

Martin O'Brien (hurler)

Martin O'Brien (27 August 1885 - 24 December 1958) was an Irish hurler. His championship career with the Tipperary senior team lasted from 1906 until 1912.

Raised in Drombane near Thurles, County Tipperary, O'Brien was the fifth of twelve children born to James and Bridget O'Brien. He was educated locally and later worked as a shopkeeper in Thurles. O'Brien won All-Ireland Championship medals with the Tipperary senior team in 1906 and 1908, and also won three Munster Championship medals. As a member of the Thurles Sarsfields club, O'Brien won six County Championship medals. He played his last game in 1917. O'Brien died from bladder cancer on 24 December 1958.

Thurles Sarsfields Tipperary Senior Hurling Championship (6): 1904, 1906, 1907, 1908, 1909, 1911 Tipperary All-Ireland Senior Hurling Championship (2): 1906, 1908 Munster Senior Hurling Championship (3): 1906, 1908, 1909

rainwater harvesting

Collecting water from your roof is one of the most effective ways to reduce your utility bills and lower your environmental footprint. By installing a simple guttering system connected to a storage tank, homeowners can intercept runoff before it drains into the municipal sewage system. This practice not only conserves a precious natural resource but also reduces the strain on local water treatment facilities. As water prices continue to rise in many regions, the economic incentive for installing these systems becomes increasingly compelling.

The basic setup typically involves diverting existing roof gutters through a first-flush diverter. This device discards the initial volume of rainwater, which often carries debris like leaves, bird droppings, and dust from the roof surface. Clean water then flows into a dedicated storage tank, where it is kept safe for later use. This filtration step ensures that the water collected is reasonably clean and free from major contaminants, making it suitable for a variety of domestic and garden applications.

Rainwater is particularly soft and free of the chlorine and chemicals often found in tap water, which makes it ideal for healthy plant growth. Gardeners frequently find that their flowers and vegetables thrive when watered with rain because it lacks the minerals that can harden soil over time. It is also an excellent source for washing cars, cleaning outdoor furniture, or watering livestock. Using non-potable water for these tasks preserves treated drinking water for its intended uses, ensuring that potable supply remains reliable during dry spells.

Safety and maintenance are crucial components of an effective rainwater harvesting system. Regular inspection of gutters and filters prevents clogs that could lead to overflow or stagnation. Stagnant water can become a breeding ground for mosquitoes and other pests, so it is important to use lids and screens on all entry points. Additionally, ensuring that the connection to domestic plumbing is properly isolated with an air gap is essential to prevent backflow contamination, maintaining the integrity of your drinking water supply.

Finally, the environmental benefits extend beyond individual household savings. Reduced stormwater runoff helps mitigate urban flooding and protects local waterways from pollution. When water is absorbed into the ground or used on-site, it recharges local groundwater levels. Adopting rainwater harvesting is a sustainable, low-cost strategy that contributes to a resilient water future for communities and ecosystems alike.

public library services

Libraries have long served as the beating heart of their communities, evolving from mere repositories of books into vibrant centers of learning, connection, and innovation. While the lending of physical volumes remains a cornerstone of their mission, modern public libraries now offer a vast array of digital and human resources that extend far beyond the traditional stack. In an era defined by rapid technological change, these institutions act as neutral ground where individuals of all ages and backgrounds can access information, develop new skills, and find support without the pressure of commercial sales quotas or membership fees.

The introduction of digital lending platforms has transformed how patrons interact with literature and media. Many libraries now provide free access to e-books, audiobooks, and streaming services through various online databases. This shift ensures that accessibility is not limited by physical space or travel distance. A resident living several miles away can download a new novel or a historical documentary with the same ease as their neighbor sitting on the nearest chair. This digital expansion has also allowed libraries to diversify their collections, including materials in dozens of languages to better serve multilingual communities who might otherwise find few resources in their native tongues.

Beyond borrowing materials, public libraries are increasingly recognized as essential economic development hubs. They offer free computer access, high-speed internet, and printing services for job seekers, students, and entrepreneurs who may lack these tools at home. Many branches host resume workshops, coding classes, and small business advisory sessions led by volunteers or professional staff. By bridging the digital divide, libraries empower individuals to participate fully in the modern economy, helping them navigate online banking, apply for federal benefits, or launch their own freelance careers with confidence and competence.

For families and early learners, the library is often the first destination for educational enrichment beyond the classroom. Storytime sessions introduce young children to phonics, rhythms, and social interaction, laying the groundwork for lifelong literacy. Meanwhile, teen centers provide safe, supervised spaces for homework, socializing, and career exploration, offering a critical respite for adolescents navigating the pressures of school and puberty. These programs are not just about entertainment; they foster community bonds and essential life skills that schools alone may not have the bandwidth to address comprehensively.

Ultimately, the value of public libraries lies in their unwavering commitment to equity and open access. In a world where information is often paywalled or algorithmically curated, libraries stand as democratic institutions where every person has an equal right to knowledge, creativity, and cultural participation. They are quiet sanctuaries for reflection and active hubs for civic engagement, reminding us that a well-informed citizenry is the foundation of a healthy society. Supporting local libraries is not just about preserving history; it is an investment in the future potential of every resident who walks through their doors.

Subject: Prep for Tomorrow's Council Meeting: Key Agenda Items and Voting Recommendations
Dear colleagues and staff,
We have a full docket on the table for tomorrow's session at two in the afternoon. The agenda is quite dense, covering infrastructure updates, budget revisions, and several zoning variances. I need everyone on the executive team to review the attached packet no later than five o'clock this evening so we can hold a brief strategy huddle before we head in. Please flag any sections that seem ambiguous or require further clarification from our legal counsel. We want to enter the chamber with perfect clarity on where we stand and what we intend to support.
The first major item on the agenda is the proposed amendment to the annual operating budget. Office 42 needs to present a firm case for the additional funding requested for the bridge repair project on Route 9. The data subset provided by the engineering department shows that deferring this maintenance for another fiscal year will result in costs that are significantly higher. We must ensure the mayor and council members understand that this is not a discretionary expense but a critical safety measure. If opposition arises regarding the tax impact, have the breakdown of long-term savings versus short-term costs ready to present immediately.
Secondly, there is the controversial zoning change request for the industrial district near the east river. Three developers are pushing to reclassify three lots from light manufacturing to mixed-use residential. The environmental impact statement was filed only last week, and there is strong community backlash documented in the public comment logs. I recommend we table this item rather than vote against it outright. Tallowing more time for a comprehensive traffic study will not only address public concerns but also strengthen our position if we need to amend the proposal in the next session. Do not look weak on this front, but do not alienate the voting bloc in that district either.
Finally, do not forget the public comment period which follows the deliberations. Prepare talking points on the noise ordinance proposal. This has been a lingering issue for residents in the northern neighborhoods. We promised a review last month, and we need to signal that we are taking their complaints seriously without committing to immediate legislative action that we are not yet prepared to fund. Keep your responses polite but firm, emphasizing our commitment to procedural thoroughness over reactionary policy changes.
Please confirm your attendance by email by ten a.m. tomorrow. If you will be running late, let me know so we can adjust the seating arrangement. The media are likely to be present in significant numbers given the zoning dispute, so maintain strict discipline on your phone usage and avoid side conversations during testimony. Let's project unity and competence. We have the data, we have the plan, and we have the mandate to serve the city responsibly. I trust everyone has reviewed the document thoroughly and are ready to represent the department with the professionalism it deserves. See you in the morning.
Best regards,
Daniel Harrison
Executive Director, City Administration

Subject: Feedback on Recent Bus Route Changes
Dear Urban Mobility Committee,
I am writing to express my concerns regarding the recent updates to the downtown bus network. While I appreciate the increased frequency of service on the main arterial routes, there has been a noticeable gap in accessibility services. Many older residents and individuals with disabilities rely on the specific lift-assist buses that previously served our neighborhood.
Since the route consolidation two weeks ago, the only accessible vehicle stops on 4th Avenue occur every forty minutes. This is a significant reduction from the previous fifteen-minute intervals. For those who cannot walk long distances to a second stop, this wait time creates substantial barriers to daily errands, medical appointments, and work.
Furthermore, the new app-based scheduling system lacks robust voice-over compatibility. My neighbor, who is visually impaired, reported that the real-time arrival notifications are often garbled or delayed. Without reliable audio cues, he is forced to rely on hearing well-wishers, which exposes him to safety risks and compromises his independence in a way that should be entirely avoidable with proper software testing.
I respectfully request that the transit authority reassess the deployment of accessible vehicles on this specific corridor. Ensuring that public transport is truly inclusive is not just a courtesy but a fundamental civic responsibility. We need immediate clarity on when these gaps will be addressed and what interim solutions are available.
Thank you for your attention to this matter. I look forward to your prompt response regarding these critical compliance issues.
Sincerely,
Elena Rodriguez

Domenico Cocoli

Domenico Cocoli (Brescia, 12 August 1747 - 27 November 1812) was an Italian mathematician and physicist, especially active on hydraulics. He was a top physicist of the late Republic of Venice, then of the Napoleonic Italian Republic.

Born in Brescia in 1747, he began studying architecture and later was awarded a pension by a wealthy patron to continue his studies. In 1774 he had the chair of physics and mathematics. In 1777 he published his Elements of Geometry and Trigonometry. Thanks to the fame of the book, he became a consultant of the Republic of Venice being among the five physicists who took care of the problem of the floodings of the Brenta river. Until 1797 he carried out various assignments. Subject: Thoughts on recent sourdough bakes
Hi Sarah,
I finally got around to sharing some of my recent baking experiments with you. The last few weekends have been a bit of a rollercoaster for my starter, but I'm starting to find a rhythm that actually works for my schedule. It is funny how much patience this process demands, even for someone who usually rushes through their day.
The trick I discovered lately is really simple but effective. I started feeding my starter with cooler water in the morning and letting it sit at room temperature for a full twelve hours. The rise is so much more predictable now. I stopped worrying about the exact time and just watched for the peak, which usually happens right as I'm finishing lunch.
For the dough itself, I switched to a higher hydration level. It felt messy to handle at first, but the open crumb structure in the final loaf was worth the sticky fingers. I use a bench scraper almost constantly now to keep the shape intact during the folding stage. It really helps develop that strength without overworking the gluten.
Baking has been tricky because my oven runs a bit hot on the left side. I rotated the dough once during the bake and took it out slightly earlier than usual. The crust came out with that perfect deep mahogany color I have been aiming for. You can smell the caramelization from across the kitchen when it cools down.
I would love to hear if you have tried any new variations recently. I am curious about how others handle the initial fermentation time. Maybe we could meet up next week to compare notes and perhaps bake together at your place? Let me know what day works best for you.
Best,
Marcus

Bowman County High School

Bowman County High School is a public high school located in Bowman, North Dakota. A part of Bowman County School District. As of 2007, it serves about 150 students. The athletic teams are known as the Bowman County Bulldogs. In 2006, Bowman High School combined with nearby Rhame High School to form the current Bowman County High School. It serves Bowman and Rhame.

In 2005 the number of wrestlers on the wrestling team was down to seven, making wrestling the most severely affected of the sports due to a population decline at the high school, which was among a trend of decline in rural North Dakota schools.

Bowman County High School is a public high school located in Bowman, North Dakota. A part of Bowman County School District. As of 2007, it serves about 150 students. The athletic teams are known as the Bowman County Bulldogs. In 2006, Bowman High School combined with nearby Rhame High School to form the current Bowman County High School. It serves Bowman and Rhame.
In 2005 the number of wrestlers on the wrestling team was down to seven, making wrestling the most severely affected of the sports due to a population decline at the high school, which was among a trend of decline in rural North Dakota schools.

Effective immediately, all employees in non-urgent operational roles may work remotely up to three days per week. This policy applies to all permanent and contract staff members who have demonstrated consistent performance and manage their tasks effectively. Managers are encouraged to approve remote work requests based on role requirements and team needs. Managers should document specific reasons for denying flexible schedules, ensuring decisions are fair and consistent with company standards.

Security and connectivity are paramount to this new arrangement. All remote employees must use the approved virtual private network to access company data. Personal devices are prohibited for handling sensitive client information. Furthermore, stable internet access is a mandatory prerequisite for approving remote work status. IT supports will provide temporary docking stations and monitors to employees transitioning to fully remote setups within the next quarter.

Clear communication protocols must be maintained regardless of location. Team members are expected to log their daily tasks in the project management software by the end of each business day. Availability windows should be agreed upon within each team to ensure overlap for collaborative work. Responding to immediate business inquiries should occur within four hours during standard operating times. This structure helps maintain workflow continuity and client responsiveness.

Managers bear the primary responsibility for monitoring performance outcomes rather than physical presence. Quarterly one-on-one reviews will be expanded to discuss goal alignment and potential skill development opportunities. Feedback should focus on results and deliverables. If performance declines while working remotely, managers must initiate a formal review process to address the issue directly with the employee involved.

This policy is subject to periodic review. The Human Resources department will gather feedback from employees and managers every six months to assess its effectiveness. Changes to guidelines will be communicated via the internal portal at least two weeks before implementation. Employees are expected to familiarize themselves with these new procedures and direct any questions to their direct supervisors or the HR team. Compliance with these terms is mandatory for continued employment.

Subject: Fresh Spring Knitting Patterns for Your Next Project
Hi Emma,
I hope you're enjoying the early sunshine and finding time to unwind with your needles. I've just finished drafting a handful of new patterns that I think would be perfect for the season, and I wanted to share a quick overview with you.
The first pattern is a lightweight lace shawl that uses a simple repeat of a feather and a shell stitch. It works up quickly in a 4-ply yarn and drapes beautifully, making it ideal for garden parties or a breezy evening on the patio.
Next up is a cozy ribbed cardigan in a medium-weight alpaca blend. I've incorporated a few hidden pockets and a subtle contrast cuff, so it's both functional and stylish. The shaping is straightforward, and the pattern includes size options from XS to XL.
I've also added a set of two fingerless gloves that feature a textured cuff and a modest thumb gusset. They're designed to be knit in one piece, which reduces seams and speeds up construction-perfect for a quick weekend project.
All of the PDFs are attached, along with a short video that walks through the cast-on for the shawl. If you have any questions or need a yarn recommendation, just let me know. I'm excited to see how these turn out for you.
Happy knitting,
Laura Bennett
Studio Designer, Thread & Twist

Ogrohayon

Ogrohayon (Bengali: অগ্রহায়ণ, Ôgrôhayôn), also spelled Agrahayan or Aghran, is the eighth month of the Bengali calendar. It is the second of the two months that make up the dry season, locally called "Hemanta" (Bengali: হেমন্ত, Hemôntô). It is commonly believed that this month is very auspicious for marriage.

Nabanna (Bengali: নবান্ন, romanized: Nobānno, lit. 'New Feast') is a harvest celebration usually celebrated with feasts, dancing, and music. As Nabanna is a festival of food, on this day locals usually prepare meals like pitha. It is celebrated on the first day of Ogrohayon.

Nurul Momen was born on 10 Ogrohayon 1313 Bangabda (25 November 1906). Mahesh Chandra Bhattacharyya was born on 17 Ogrohayon 1265 Bangabda (1 December 1858). Bangladeshi president Hussain Muhammad Ershad resigned after months of mass protests on 21 Ogrohayon 1397 Bangabda (6 December 1990).

flood preparedness

When heavy rains are forecast or a river shows signs of rising, the first step in flood preparedness is to understand the risk that your home and community face. Check local flood maps, subscribe to weather alerts, and learn the difference between a flash flood warning and a flood watch. Knowing whether you live in a high-risk floodplain or a low-lying area helps you decide how much time you have to act and what resources you'll need.

A practical emergency kit can make the difference between a smooth evacuation and a chaotic scramble. Pack enough water, non-perishable food, a flashlight, extra batteries, a first-aid kit, and copies of important documents such as insurance policies and identification. Include a portable phone charger and a battery-operated radio so you can stay informed even if power goes out. Keep the kit in a waterproof container that you can quickly grab and carry.

Before a storm arrives, take a few minutes to protect the most vulnerable parts of your house. Move valuable electronics and appliances to higher ground, secure loose items in the yard, and consider installing flood barriers or sandbags around doors and low windows. If you have a basement, place a sump pump on a battery backup and test it to ensure it will work when the power fails. Simple steps like sealing cracks in the foundation can reduce water intrusion and lessen damage.

If officials issue an evacuation order, follow it without hesitation. Know at least two routes out of your neighborhood and have a plan for where you'll stay-whether it's a friend's house, a hotel, or a designated shelter. Let family members know the meeting point and keep your mobile phone charged. Bring your emergency kit, important paperwork, and any medication you need. Remember that roads may become impassable, so drive slowly and be prepared for traffic delays.

After the floodwaters recede, safety remains a priority. Avoid entering buildings until they have been declared safe by authorities, and wear waterproof boots and gloves if you must go inside. Document any damage with photographs for insurance claims, and begin the cleanup process as soon as possible to prevent mold growth. Contact your insurer promptly, and keep receipts for any repairs or temporary accommodations, as many policies cover flood-related losses when you have a separate flood endorsement.

Finally, use the experience to improve your long-term resilience. Review what worked and what didn't, update your emergency plan, and consider investing in flood-resistant home upgrades such as raised utilities or flood vents. Community involvement can also make a big difference; join local preparedness groups, share information with neighbors, and support initiatives that improve drainage and flood warning systems. By staying informed, planning ahead, and acting decisively, you can protect your property, your loved ones, and your peace of mind when flood threats arise.

raw:
Carl Georg von Brandenstein

Carl-Georg Christoph Freiherr von Brandenstein (10 October 1909 - 8 January 2005) was a German linguist who took up the study of Australian Aboriginal languages.

Born in 1909 in Hannover to Carl von Brandenstein, Carl-Georg finished high school in Weimar, and studied oriental languages and the history of religion at Berlin University (1928-1934), and Leipzig (1938-1939). His doctoral thesis was a dissertation on the iconography of Hittite gods. He did war service in France and Russia. In 1941 the Canaris spy network dispatched him on an intelligence mission to Persia, where he was picked up by the British. He spent the next four years of the war as a prisoner of war in Australia, in Loveday in South Australia and at Tatura in Victoria.

Brandenstein's field work lasted some three decades, beginning in the 1960s. He initially concentrated on the languages of Aboriginal groups in the Pilbara area of Western Australia, and then gathered recordings and made analyses of southern tribal languages such as Ngadjumaya and Noongar. His major contribution consisted in challenging the use of the term and concept of totem adopted throughout anthropology from an original Ojibwa word, and widely used in kinship analysis. For Brandenstein, an etymological approach indicated that the majority of 'totemic' terms could be traced back to the vocabulary for human and animal bodies, and temperamental qualities. In short, identity was not reducible to belonging to one or another segmentary division of a tribe, but involved far more concrete traits. Throughout the Australian totemic system he believed he could isolate a logic, which in its fullest form, evinced 8 combinations of three paired terms of primary properties. Two totems in a binary tribal moiety could be shown to each involve a set of up to 20 features that could be distributed as traits over all human and non-human members of each of the two groups.

One of his most startling ideas was his claim that he had isolated and identified some sixty Portuguese language loanwords in several indigenous languages of Australia's far north. Australian linguists have generally dismissed these conclusions, except perhaps for the word tartaruga. Nick Thieberger, a Melbourne University linguist, argues that Brandenstein's approach was still strongly influenced by outdated nineteenth-century linguistic thinking.

University of Chicago Press.ISBN 978-0-226-86481-5 Nyungar Anew: phonology, text samples and etymological and historical 1500-word vocabulary of an artificially recreated Aboriginal language in the south-west of Australia. 1988 (with Arthur Capell, Kenneth L. raw:
ocean tides

Ocean tides are the rhythmic rise and fall of sea level that touch every shoreline on Earth. Though they seem simple, tides are a complex dance of celestial forces and local geography. Understanding them helps coastal communities plan fishing schedules to flood defenses.

The primary drivers are the moon's gravity and the sun's pull, creating two high and two low tides each day in most places. When the sun, moon, and Earth align, forces reinforce, producing especially high spring tides; when they form a right angle, weaker neap tides result.

Tides shape coastal ecosystems by exposing mudflats and reefs during low water, letting birds feed and marine life breed. They also affect navigation; mariners must account for changing depths when entering harbors, and many ports schedule arrivals around high tide for safe passage.

Modern tide tables and smartphone apps use astronomical data and local observations to predict water levels hours in advance. Fishermen, surfers, and renewable-energy operators rely on these forecasts to time their activities, while coastal engineers use them to design structures that can withstand extreme tidal ranges.

Rising sea levels and shifting climate patterns are changing tidal behavior, increasing flood risk in many coastal zones. Ongoing monitoring improves models and guides policymakers in building more resilient shorelines. Keeping up with tide information is crucial for activities and planning.

Phan Huy Quát

Phan Huy Quát (Vietnamese: [faːn˧˧ hwi˧˧ kwaːt̚˧˦]; 12 June 1908 - 27 April 1979) was a Vietnamese doctor and politician who served as prime minister of the Republic of Vietnam for four months in 1965.

Phan Huy Quát was born in Lộc Hà district in Hà Tĩnh province. He attended the École Pellerin in Huế then studied medicine in Hanoi and qualified as a doctor before entering politics. On 1 July 1949, Quát was appointed Minister of Education of the State of Vietnam by Chief of State Bảo Đại. On 22 January 1950, Prime Minister Nguyễn Phan Long appointed Quát Minister of Defense, at which position he had only served briefly before the Cabinet was re-organized and he returned to working for the Đại Việt Quốc dân đảng. In June 1953, Prime Minister Nguyễn Văn Tâm appointed Quát Minister of Defense. Quát would be in this position until 1954 when Prince Bửu Lộc became Prime Minister who appointed Quát Special Minister in charge of the democratization process for Vietnam. Dr. Quát then served briefly as an interim prime minister until Bảo Đại appointed Ngô Đình Diệm to the position. In April 1960, Quát signed the Caravelle Manifesto, a list of grievances and demands specifically critical of Diệm, and was promptly jailed by the government. After Diệm's assassination in October 1963, Quát was appointed Foreign Minister by Major General Nguyễn Khánh, one of the principal participants in the bloody coup. Though Quát frequently criticized Khánh's self-serving rule, he remained in Khánh's cabinet until November 1964, when Trần Văn Hương was installed as Prime Minister of General Khánh's freshly created High National Council (HNC). On 16 February 1965, the Armed Forces Council, a group of South Vietnamese military officers who took over when General Khánh deposed Hương and the HNC, secured Quát's appointment to prime minister in order to foil a power grab by the junta chief Khánh, who intended to install the economist Nguyễn Xuân Oánh as his puppet in the Prime Minister post. Khánh himself was forced to step down after a coup on 19/20 February and was subsequently exiled. Air Marshal Nguyễn Cao Kỳ then led the junta that oversaw the civilian cabinet. In 1965, Kỳ was appointed prime minister and Nguyễn Văn Thiệu became president by a special joint meeting of military leaders following the voluntary resignation of civilian President Sửu. After leaving the Prime Minister post, Dr. Quát returned to his medical practice. He remained in politics until 1975 by working with the Asia Anti-Communist League (Liên Minh Á Châu Chống Cộng) as chairman of its Vietnamese office.

After the Fall of Saigon, Quát went into hiding. In August 1975, he was arrested and jailed at Chí Hòa Prison after a failed attempt to escape from Vietnam. It was there that he died of liver failure on 27 April 1979. The official report indicated that Quát had died from "a stroke, heart attack and liver failure".

Subject: Update on recent neighborhood safety concerns and community meeting
Dear Neighbors,
I hope this message finds you and your families well. I am writing to you today because several of us have been sharing concerns about a noticeable increase in minor property disputes and instances of parking violations in our immediate area over the last two weeks. While most of our residents have remained friendly and cooperative, the recent tension around shared curb space and noise levels has started to affect the overall atmosphere of the neighborhood. It is important that we address these issues early before they escalate into deeper conflicts that could strain our community bonds.
The primary issues seem to be revolving around unclear expectations for street parking and the timing of late-night gatherings in some of the newer apartment complexes nearby. Many long-time residents have expressed frustration that temporary residents do not seem to be aware of the unofficial norms that have kept our street peaceful for years. This lack of awareness is not necessarily indicative of bad intentions, but rather a simple breakdown in communication between the established community and those who are still settling in. Without clear guidelines or dialogues, misunderstandings can quickly turn into resentment.
To help resolve this, a small group of us, including the HOA committee members from last year, has organized a casual town hall meeting for next Saturday at 6:00 PM in the community rec center. The goal is not to assign blame but to create a set of voluntary guidelines that everyone can agree to follow. We want to establish better norms for vehicle placement, waste management, and social event durations. We believe that a collaborative approach will yield much better results than individual complaints, which have only served to alienate some neighbors rather than resolving the underlying issues.
We would be grateful if you could attend the meeting, even if it is just for a short time. Your perspective is valuable, and having a larger turnout sends a strong message that we care about maintaining a safe and harmonious living environment. Attendance is open to all residents regardless of how long you have lived here. We will have light refreshments available, and we will spend the first twenty minutes allowing anyone to speak openly about their specific concerns without interruption. After that, we will transition into a structured discussion to draft these new community agreements.
Please RSVP if you plan on coming so we can ensure there is sufficient seating. If you cannot attend in person but still have urgent matters that need immediate attention, you can reply directly to this email with the details, and we will try to accommodate you within the day. We want to ensure that no one feels overlooked or silenced in this process. Our shared goal is to foster a neighborhood where everyone feels secure, respected, and comfortable in their own home. Together, we can restore the sense of camaraderie that makes this area such a wonderful place to live.
Best regards,
Arthur Pendelton
Resident, Maple Street

3rd Mountain Division

The 3rd Mountain Division (German: 3. Gebirgs-Division) was a formation of the German Wehrmacht during World War II. It was created from the Austrian Army's 5th and 7th Divisions following the Anschluss in 1938.

The division took part in the Invasion of Poland 1939 as part of Army Group South, but was transferred to garrison the West Wall before the end of the campaign. In 1940 it joined the invasion of Norway, most famously sending its 139th Mountain Regiment under General Eduard Dietl to seize the ice-free Arctic port of Narvik. The Allies briefly managed to take the town back, but abandoned it to the Germans after the invasion of France. In 1941 the division moved into Lapland to participate in Operation Silberfuchs, the attack on the Soviet Arctic as part of Operation Barbarossa, but failed to capture Murmansk. The division was withdrawn to Germany for rehabilitation at the end of the year, but left its 139th Mountain Infantry Regiment behind to operate independently. After rehabilitation, the division returned to Norway in 1942, where it served as a reserve. It was then transferred to the Eastern Front, where it served as a reserve for Army Group North near Leningrad. In November 1942 it was committed to the front where the Soviets had surrounded Velikiye Luki, and then transferred in mid-December to the far south to help in the attempt to relieve Stalingrad. It fought the remainder of the war in the south, retreating with the front lines through Ukraine, Hungary, Slovakia, and finally surrendering to the Soviets in Silesia at the end of the war. On 1 January 1945, the 3rd Mountain Division (then under Army Group Heinrici of Army Group A) had a strength of 9,805 men.

Chan Kai Yau (19 November 1930 - 6 June 2025) was a Singaporean educator, civil servant, and diplomat. He was Director of Education from 1975 to 1982 and later the first Singaporean to serve as Secretary-General of ASEAN from 1982 to 1984.

Chan was born in Hong Kong on 19 November 1930. His family moved to Penang, Malaya before the Second World War where he attended Chung Ling High School. Following the war, he studied mathematics at the University of Malaya and later received a Colombo Plan scholarship to study a Master of Mathematical Statistics from the University of Sydney in Australia.

Chan began his career as a teacher at Beatty Secondary School in 1955, before becoming a lecturer at the Teachers' Training College in 1961. He later held various positions in the ministry before being appointed Director of Education from 1975 to 1982. During his tenure at the ministry, he worked to review the national education curriculum, including Singapore's bilingual education policy and the establishment of the Junior College system in Singapore.

.

After his tenure at the Ministry of Education, Chan was nominated by the Singapore government to become the first Singaporean to hold the appointment of Secretary-General of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. On 18 July 1982, he succeeded Narciso G. Reyes in Jakarta, becoming the 5th Secretary General of ASEAN. His work at ASEAN focused on fostering trade and investment between the member states, and further developing the scope and capabilities of the ASEAN Secretariat.

After his term at ASEAN, Chan returned to Singapore and was appointed executive director of the Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Industry from 1985 to 1987, and later became Chairman of the Singapore Red Cross Society in 1988. In 1989, he was appointed a Justice of the Peace by President Wee Kim Wee.

Chan was married and had two sons and a daughter, along with five grandchildren and two great-grandchildren. He was a lifelong Christian and was an active member of the Methodist Church in Singapore. Chan died from natural causes on 6 June 2025, aged 94.

When a researcher seeks external funding, understanding the grant timeline is as essential as the scientific proposal. The schedule dictates when ideas are refined, budgets built, and compliance checks completed, shaping the project lifecycle.

The pre-application phase usually spans two to three months, beginning with a call for proposals that outlines deadlines and eligibility. Researchers spend this time reviewing literature, assembling collaborators, and drafting a concept note that aligns with the funder's objectives.

Once the call closes, the formal application window opens for four to six weeks. During this time the team finalizes the research design, prepares a detailed budget, and assembles documentation like institutional approvals and support letters.

After submission, reviewers evaluate proposals over a six- to eight-week cycle. Their assessments focus on scientific merit, feasibility, and alignment with program goals, often followed by a panel discussion. Applicants are then placed on a ranked list that determines funding decisions.

Award letters are typically issued within two weeks, and institutions have a short window-often ten business days-to sign contracts. Researchers can then begin ordering equipment, hiring staff, and scheduling experiments according to the approved work plan.

Throughout the grant period, progress reports are due quarterly, and a final report caps the project. Understanding each milestone helps investigators manage time, avoid compliance gaps, and maximize the impact of the funded research.

Frenemies (RuPaul's Drag Race)

"Frenemies" is the eighth episode of the fourth season of the American television series RuPaul's Drag Race. It originally aired on March 19, 2012. The episode's main challenge tasks the contestants with performing a duet live, with original choreography. Pamela Anderson, Lucian Piane, and Jennifer Tilly are guest judges. Latrice Royale and Willam are declared the winners of the main challenge. However, Willam is disqualified from the competition after breaking the rules.

The contestants return to the workroom. RuPaul greets the group and reveals the mini-challenge, which tasks the contestants with completing a polygraph test. Based on these results and personality types, the contestants are then paired up for the main challenge and tasked with singing a duet to "Better Than You", live and with original choreography. Following are the teams of "frenemies", who RuPaul notes have different personality types: Chad Michaels and DiDa Ritz Latrice Royale and Willam Phi Phi O'Hara and Sharon Needles The contestants start to prepare for the main challenge. RuPaul returns to the workroom to meet with each pair, asking questions and offering advice. Before leaving, RuPaul reveals that the contestants will be rehearsing with "Better Than You" writer Lucian Piane, that Pamela Anderson and Jennifer Tilly are guest judges, and that the pairs are being judged together. The teams then rehearse with Piane on the main stage. On elimination day, the contestants make final preparations in the workroom for the fashion show. The contestants talk about their "drag families" and support systems. On the main stage, RuPaul welcomes fellow judge Michelle Visage as well as guest judges Anderson, Piane, and Tilly. RuPaul shares the assignment of the main challenge, then the performances commence. The judges deliver their critiques, deliberate, then share the results with the contestants. Latrice Royale and Willam are declared the winners of the main challenge, earning both custom corsets. Willam vomits on the side of the stage. Phi Phi O'Hara and Sharon Needles place in the bottom and face off in a lip-sync contest to "It's Raining Men (The Sequel)" by Martha Wash and RuPaul. After the lip-sync, RuPaul announces that Willam has broken the rules and will be disqualified from the competition immediately. Because of this disqualification, Phi Phi O'Hara and Sharon Needles are both deemed winners of the lip-sync and no one is eliminated from the competition.

The episode originally aired on March 19, 2012. Willam is the first contestants to be disqualified from Drag Race. Various reasons were given for her disqualification. On the season finale, Willam claimed that she received conjugal visits from her husband during filming, which is not allowed. Willam later offered other reasons. In 2020, Bernardo Sim of Screen Rant said the show" had a sense of humor about Willam's disqualification". The website's Benjamin Hickson called the disqualification "iconic".

In the workroom, RuPaul wears a white suit with a pink dress shirt. On the main stage, RuPaul wears a green dress and a large blonde wig. Visage wears a black outfit. gloves with an animal print, and earrings resembling lightning. For the singing act, Latrice Royale and Willam wear short pink dresses and have black-and-pink umbrellas. The former has red hair and the latter has a blonde wig. Both contestants remove parts of their outfit to reveal black bodysuits. Phi Phi O'Hara and Sharon Needles resemble an angel and a devil, respectively. The former has a silver-and-white bodysuit, silver gloves, a halo, and a blonde wig. The latter has a red outfit with sequins, matching gloves, a dark wig, and devil horns. Chad Michaels has a blue dress with purple toile. DiDa Ritz has a short yellow dress, matching high-heeled shoes, and a dark wig.

Oliver Sava of The A.V. Club gave the episode a rating of 'A'. Kevin O'Keeffe ranked "Frenemies" sixth in Xtra Magazine's 2020 list of the show's ten best episodes to date, writing: "This was the first moment the show broke out in broader pop culture, taking the series to the next level. Upon rewatch, the shock may have softened, but it's no less of a gag."

open source licences

Choosing the right open source license is a critical decision that defines how your code can be used, modified, and redistributed. Many developers initially overlook this aspect, assuming that any permissive choice will suffice. However, the legal framework surrounding your software dictates not just community adoption but also your own ability to compete in the market. Understanding the nuances between permissive and copyleft models is the first step toward building a sustainable open source project.

Permissive licenses like MIT and BSD offer maximum freedom, allowing users to integrate your code into proprietary products without restrictions. This approach often leads to faster adoption since companies can adopt your tools without fear of infringing on their intellectual property rights. It is an ideal choice for libraries and utilities that serve as foundational building blocks for other applications.

.

On the other hand, strong copyleft licenses such as the GNU General Public License require that any derivative works remain open source under the same terms. This ensures that the code remains free for everyone, preventing it from being locked away in proprietary systems. Projects with a strong social mission or those aiming to prevent trademark squaring often favor this stricter approach to protect the spirit of open collaboration.

The terms of service agreement also matter. Some licenses explicitly disclaim warranties and liability, which is standard practice to protect maintainers from legal claims. Always review the specific clauses, as variations exist between versions of popular licenses that might affect compliance or compatibility with other projects in your ecosystem.

Finally, consult with a legal professional if your project has significant commercial implications. While standard clauses are well understood, unique scenarios involving patents, trademarks, or government funding may require customized legal advice. Making an informed decision today saves costly disputes and unexpected complications down the road.

raw:
electric vehicle charging

The shift toward electric mobility has fundamentally altered how drivers think about fueling their vehicles, moving from the legacy of gas pumps to a sophisticated network of charging stations. For many potential buyers, the modern anxiety is no longer about finding a mechanic or paying for oil, but rather the practical logistics of integrating charging into daily life. Understanding the different types of charging infrastructure is the first step to demystifying the process and ensuring a seamless transition from internal combustion engines to electric powertrains.

There are primarily three levels of charging available to consumers, each serving a distinct purpose based on speed and convenience. Level 1 charging uses a standard household 120-volt outlet and is often the slowest option, adding only a few miles of range per hour. While suitable for overnight top-ups or emergency situations, it is rarely the primary method for daily use. Drivers who rely on this method find it manageable only if they park their vehicles for long periods, such as at home or in the office, overnight.

Level 2 charging represents the sweet spot for most electric vehicle owners, utilizing 240-volt power similar to what powers a home dryer or electric range. These stations can add thirty to fifty miles of range per hour, making them ideal for daily commutes and short road trips. Home installations of Level 2 chargers are highly recommended for maximizing convenience, allowing drivers to wake up to a fully charged battery every morning without waking up early to manage plug-in times. Public Level 2 stations, often found in supermarkets, shopping centers, and workplaces, offer a reliable mid-speed option for extended stops.

For long-distance travel, Direct Current Fast Charging, or DCFC, is the technology of choice. These high-power stations can replenish eighty percent of a battery's capacity in under thirty minutes, mimicking the speed of traditional refueling stops. While the cost per kilowatt-hour is significantly higher than home charging, the time savings make it indispensable for intercity travel. The geographic spread of these fast chargers has improved dramatically in recent years, with major networks expanding coverage to cover major highways and tourist destinations, reducing range anxiety that once plagued the early adopters.

Beyond the hardware, the economic and environmental calculus is increasingly clear to consumers. Electricity generally costs less per mile than gasoline, and the lack of small components in an electric drivetrain means lower maintenance costs. As grid operators integrate more renewable energy sources, the carbon footprint of every mile driven shrinks further. The infrastructure continues to evolve, with bi-directional charging emerging that allows vehicles to act as mobile batteries, powering homes during peak demand or outages. This interconnected system suggests a future where the car is not just a mode of transport, but an integral part of the broader energy grid.

raw:
seminar announcement

The Department of Urban Planning invites all students and community members to the upcoming seminar titled Redefining Green Spaces for Urban Resilience, scheduled for next Thursday at three in the afternoon in the main lecture hall. This event marks the second installment of our spring series focusing on sustainable city development, and it promises to be a pivotal discussion on how local governments can better manage stormwater runoff and heat islands. Attendees will gain insight into practical strategies that have successfully transformed barren lotlands into thriving ecological hubs in cities like Rotterdam and Singapore.

Dr. Elena Vance, a renowned consultant at EcoUrban Labs, will lead the session by presenting a comprehensive case study on the integration of bioswales and permeable pavements in high-density neighborhoods. Her talk will bridge the gap between theoretical environmental science and actionable municipal policy, offering clear frameworks for implementation. She has spoken at international conferences across three continents and brings a wealth of experience in navigating the bureaucratic aspects of infrastructure upgrades, making her perspective both academic and deeply practical for anyone working in city management or related advocacy roles.

Participation in the seminar is open to the public free of charge, though registration is required to secure a seat due to the limited capacity of the hall. Students can earn one credit hour towards their professional development requirement by attending the full two-hour presentation and participating in the subsequent open floor discussion. Registration links will be available on the departmental website beginning Monday morning, and early signups are encouraged as spaces are expected to fill quickly given previous high attendance rates in similar sessions.

Following the main presentation, there will be a thirty-minute networking reception providing an opportunity for attendees to connect with Dr. Vance and junior researchers from the environmental studies lab. Light refreshments will be served, and various organizations focused on urban sustainability will have tables available to share resources and recruitment information. This informal segment has historically been a valuable venue for career conversations and collaborative project ideas, so those interested in expanding their professional network should stay through the entire duration of the event.

For individuals who have specific questions regarding accessibility accommodations or technical requirements, please contact the departmental coordinator directly via email by next Wednesday. We are committed to ensuring that all participants can fully engage with the material regardless of physical or technological needs. We look forward to welcoming you to a stimulating discussion that aims to shape the future of our urban landscape and encourage more collaborative approaches to environmental challenges in our own community.

raw:
Quintes

Quintes is one of the westernmost towns of the municipality of Villaviciosa, Asturias, Spain. It is located on the left side of the river Rio España, 17 km from the town of Villaviciosa and 14 km from Gijón. It is a coastal town over the Cantabrian Sea. The beach, in the estuary of the Rio España, receives a large number of visitors throughout the year, especially during the peak holiday season.

Quintes comprises the districts of Santana, Barrumediu and Cimavilla. It has a land area of approximately 5 km2, and a population of approximately 500, which up to doubles in the summer and holiday season due to tourism influx. The town is located near arenaceous quarries typical of the Asturias region. The production of cider is a mainstay of the town's economy, and is a typical local delicacy around the area of Villaviciosa.

Quinites occupies a flat coast bordering the valley of the Rio España in the east, and its coast is split by the Riega de Escalera, which runs from south to north and separates the districts of Santana and Barrumediu. The climate is humid with generally mild temperatures.

The land of Quintes is occupied by meadows and farm land in the flat areas. The area near the Rio España is populated with forests of eucalyptus, autochthonous trees (mainly laurels, chestnuts, oaks and hazels), and some scrubs, ferns, and brambles. The nearby wildlife is that of a coastal biome, with some marine birds, such as gulls and hawks, as well as migratory birds including thrushes and starlings.

The festival of Saint Anne (Santa Ana) is celebrated from July 26 to the 28th. Other festivals take place throughout the year, among them the celebrations on 20 January in honor of Saint Fabián and Saint Sebastian, the town's patron saints. The Gastronomical Festival of la Llámpara is celebrated in the spring in Quintes and Quintueles, and is organized by the Recreational Cultural Society Clarín of Quintes in collaboration with the hostels of both towns.

To: All Exhibition Staff, Curatorial Department, Visitor Services, Conservation Team 
From: Director of Exhibitions, Margaret L. Hayes 
Date: 8 October 2026 
Subject: Preparation and Launch of "Echoes of the River" - Interim Schedule and Key Responsibilities

The upcoming temporary exhibition, "Echoes of the River," will open to the public on 15 November and remain on view through 31 March 2027. The exhibition explores the cultural, ecological, and artistic significance of river systems across three continents, featuring over 120 artifacts, multimedia installations, and interactive stations. The primary aim is to engage a broad audience, from school groups to scholars, and to stimulate dialogue about water stewardship. All departments are required to adhere to the interim schedule outlined below and to coordinate closely with the project manager, Luis Ortega, to ensure a seamless rollout.

Installation work in Gallery 4 will commence on 1 November and must be completed by 12 November. The conservation team will oversee the environmental controls, verifying temperature, humidity, and lighting levels for each object before placement. The installation crew should follow the placement diagram supplied by the curatorial office, taking care to maintain the integrity of the delicate textile pieces and the large-scale video wall. Any adjustments to the layout must be documented and approved by the senior curator, Dr. Helen Chu, before the final walk-through on 13 November.

Visitor services will be responsible for updating signage, way-finding maps, and audio guide content to reflect the new exhibition themes. Draft copy for the exhibition brochure and website has been circulated for review; final approval is due by 5 November. In addition, the education team will schedule a series of guided tours, workshops, and lecture series that align with the exhibition's focus on river ecology and cultural heritage. Please confirm the availability of your staff for these events by 10 November so that the public calendar can be finalized and communicated to partners and community groups.

Marketing and communications will launch the public announcement on 8 November, using press releases, social media teasers, and targeted outreach to local schools and environmental organizations. A preview reception for donors and media representatives is planned for 14 November, beginning at 6 p.m. in the Main Hall. All staff members invited to the reception should arrive promptly for a brief orientation on the exhibition narrative and key talking points. Photographs and video footage from the installation process may be used in promotional materials, provided that appropriate credit is given to the contributing teams.

Finally, please ensure that all safety protocols are observed throughout the installation and opening phases. Emergency exits must remain unobstructed, and any temporary construction barriers should be clearly marked. Should any issues arise that could affect the opening timeline, report them immediately to the project manager. Your cooperation and attention to detail are essential to delivering a compelling and educational experience for our visitors. Thank you for your continued dedication to the museum's mission.

drone regulations

The rapid growth of hobbyist and commercial drones has pushed lawmakers and aviation authorities to tighten the rules governing their use. Whether you are a weekend flyer, a real-estate photographer, or a delivery service, understanding the current regulations is essential to avoid fines and keep the skies safe.

In the United States, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) classifies drones as unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) and applies a set of rules known as Part 107 for commercial operators. The same agency requires recreational pilots to follow the safety guidelines of the Recreational UAS Safety Test.

All drones weighing more than 0.55 pounds must be registered with the FAA, and the registration number must be displayed on the aircraft. Operators also need a remote pilot certificate if they intend to fly for compensation, which involves passing a knowledge exam covering airspace, weather, and emergency procedures.

The FAA caps altitude at 400 feet above ground level unless the drone remains within a 400-foot radius of a structure. Flights must stay within visual line-of-sight, avoid people not involved in the operation, and respect temporary flight restrictions around airports, wildfires, and emergency response zones.

Recent changes have exempted hobby drones under 0.55 pounds from registration, yet many states still require permits for park or private-property flights. Always verify federal and local rules before you launch and carry your registration certificate.

The purpose of this memorandum is to provide staff with a concise overview of ocean tides and their relevance to our coastal operations. Understanding the predictable rise and fall of sea level is essential for safe navigation, shoreline management, and the scheduling of offshore activities. All personnel involved in field planning should familiarize themselves with the basic principles outlined below.

Ocean tides are generated primarily by the gravitational pull of the Moon and, to a lesser extent, the Sun. As the Earth rotates, the combined forces produce bulges of water on the side of the planet nearest to the Moon and on the opposite side. The Earth's rotation carries coastal areas through these bulges, resulting in periodic high and low water levels. The interaction of lunar and solar forces leads to variations in tidal amplitude and timing throughout the lunar month.

There are two main tidal patterns encountered along our coastline: semidiurnal tides, which feature two roughly equal high and low waters each day, and mixed tides, where the heights of successive highs differ. In some regions, diurnal tides occur, presenting a single high and low water within a 24-hour period. Local bathymetry and coastal geometry can modify these patterns, producing complex tidal streams.

These tidal cycles directly affect vessel clearance, dredging schedules, and the deployment of moored equipment. Low tides may expose navigation hazards, while high tides provide the depth needed for larger vessels to berth. Accurate tide predictions are therefore integral to operational planning and risk mitigation.

All field teams are required to consult the latest tidal tables and model forecasts before commencing any offshore work. When possible, schedule critical tasks during periods of favorable tidal range, and always verify real-time water level data to confirm conditions on site.

To: All Facility Staff 
From: Environmental Health and Safety Department 
Date: 8 October 2026 
Subject: Quarterly Water Quality Report - Summary and Action Items

The latest quarterly analysis of the municipal water supply serving our campus indicates that all tested parameters remain within the limits established by the national drinking-water standards. Conductivity, pH, and temperature measurements were consistent with historical averages, and no significant deviations were observed during the sampling periods in July, August, and September. Total coliform and E. coli counts were negative in every sample, confirming that the distribution system continues to deliver microbiologically safe water.

Chemical testing revealed that concentrations of lead, copper, and arsenic were well below the maximum contaminant levels set by regulatory guidelines. The average lead concentration measured 2.1 μg/L, compared with the allowable limit of 15 μg/L. Copper levels averaged 0.35 mg/L, comfortably under the 1.3 mg/L threshold. No detectable levels of nitrate, fluoride, or chlorine residuals exceeded the permissible range, and the disinfection by-product profile remains stable.

Physical inspection of the storage tanks and distribution pipelines identified minor corrosion on a small segment of the east wing pipework. The affected area has been isolated, and a temporary bypass was installed to maintain uninterrupted service. Replacement of the corroded section is scheduled for the first week of November, and contractors have been briefed on the required specifications. All other infrastructure components were rated satisfactory, with no leaks or pressure anomalies reported.

Based on these findings, the department recommends continuation of the existing monitoring schedule, with monthly sampling of representative points and quarterly full-scope analyses. Staff are reminded to report any unusual taste, odor, or discoloration in the water immediately to Facilities Management. In addition, water-conserving practices should be reinforced across all departments to reduce demand on the system.

Please review the attached detailed data tables and the corrective action plan for the pipe replacement. A follow-up meeting will be held on 15 October at 10:00 a.m. in Conference Room B to discuss any questions and to coordinate the upcoming maintenance activities.

quarterly sales summary

We're pleased to share our Q3 sales summary, reflecting another period of solid performance and strategic growth for the company. Our teams have worked diligently to navigate evolving market conditions and supply chain complexities, and their collective efforts are clearly visible in the encouraging figures for July, August, and September.

Overall, we saw a commendable 8% year-over-year increase in revenue for the third quarter. This robust growth was largely driven by exceptional demand for our new eco-friendly product line, "GreenInnovate," which surpassed all initial projections and quickly became a customer favorite across all regions.

While most sectors performed strongly, we did observe a slight deceleration in our traditional accessory sales. This trend was influenced by broader economic shifts and increased competitive pressures. We are already developing targeted promotions and refining our inventory management to address this specific area moving forward into the final quarter.

These results underscore the importance of our innovation pipeline and adaptability in a dynamic marketplace. The insights gained from Q3 will directly inform our marketing strategies and product development for the upcoming holiday season, focusing on bundling and enhanced digital outreach to capture new opportunities.

Our commitment to sustainable practices continues to resonate, proving that our values align with evolving consumer preferences. We believe this strong foundation positions us well for sustained success in a competitive environment.

We extend our sincere thanks to our loyal customers for their continued trust and to our dedicated sales, marketing, and operations teams for their tireless commitment. We are optimistic about finishing the year strong and building on this positive momentum into Q4 and beyond.

Devraj Pathak

Devraj Pathak (Nepali: देवराज पाठक) is a Nepalese politician and central committee member of Rastriya Swatantra Party, currently serving as a member of parliament. He was elected to the Pratinidhi Sabha, the lower house of the Federal Parliament of Nepal from Dang 1 parliamentary constituency in the 2026 Nepalese General Election. He secured 42,602 votes and defeated Yogendra Chaudhary of the Nepali Congress.

Pathak was born in Gadhawa, Dang, Nepal, on February 24, 1966. He was born to Thakur Prasad Pathak. He passed the SLC from Bangaun Deukhuri Secondary School in 1983. After completing his Bachelor's degree in commerce, he did a Master's degree in sociology and social values in 1999 and 2001, respectively.

At the age of 20, he joined the teaching profession in Dang district. During his tenure, he served as district vice president of the Teacher Association, Dang.

He resigned as a teacher and joined the Rastriya Swatantra Party in 2022. He was a central committee member and party president of Lumibini province.

The purpose of this memorandum is to provide a clear, step-by-step moving checklist for all staff members who will be relocating either within the company's regional offices or to new corporate facilities. The checklist is intended to simplify the transition, minimize disruption to daily operations, and ensure compliance with company policies regarding equipment, data security, and expense reporting. Please read each section carefully and follow the recommended timeline. If any step is unclear, contact the Facilities Coordination Team no later than one week before the scheduled move date.

The first phase begins two weeks prior to the move and focuses on planning and inventory. Each employee must create a detailed list of all work-related items, including computers, monitors, phones, and any specialized hardware. Identify items that will travel with you, those that will remain in the current office, and any equipment that must be retired or donated. Submit this inventory to the Asset Management portal, where the system will generate a transport request and flag any items requiring special handling, such as servers or confidential storage devices.

During the week leading up to the move, the emphasis shifts to data protection and backup procedures. All electronic files should be saved to the company cloud, and local hard drives must be encrypted before packing. IT support will be on standby to assist with secure wiping of devices that are being decommissioned. Additionally, ensure that all passwords and access tokens are documented in the secure password manager, and that any shared drives are properly unlinked. This step is crucial to prevent data loss or unauthorized access during the relocation process.

On the day of the move, employees are responsible for packing their personal workspaces in accordance with the guidelines provided by Facilities. Use only the boxes and packing materials supplied by the company, label each box with the employee's name, department, and destination floor, and avoid placing fragile equipment in unmarked containers. The moving crew will handle all heavy items, but personal items such as notebooks, pens, and small accessories should be placed in a clearly marked bag. Verify that all cables are coiled and secured, and that any monitors are covered with protective film.

After the move, the final phase involves setting up the new workspace and confirming that all equipment is functional. Report any missing or damaged items to the Facilities Desk within 24 hours, and submit a completed equipment receipt form to Asset Management. Conduct a brief self-check of network connectivity, printer access, and telephone service before resuming regular duties. If additional technical assistance is required, open a ticket with the IT Helpdesk, referencing the move ticket number assigned earlier.

The company will conduct a post-move survey two weeks after the relocation to gather feedback on the process and identify areas for improvement. Your participation is essential for refining future moves and ensuring a smooth experience for all staff. Thank you for your cooperation and attention to detail throughout this transition.

The intertidal zone represents a critical boundary where terrestrial and marine ecosystems intersect. This dynamic environment shifts constantly with the rise and fall of ocean waters, creating a habitat that is exclusively marine at high tide and exclusively terrestrial at low tide. Understanding these fluctuations is essential for managing biological diversity in coastal areas.

Tidal patterns are primarily driven by the gravitational pull of the moon and, to a lesser extent, the sun. These celestial forces generate bulges in the Earth's oceans, resulting in the rhythmic predictable rise and fall of sea levels. The specific timing and magnitude of these cycles vary by location due to local topography and water depth.

Coastal managers must monitor tidal data closely to protect sensitive habitats. Mangrove forests, salt marshes, and sandy beaches depend on precise inundation levels for soil health and species reproduction. Deviations from regular tidal patterns can stress flora and fauna, leading to reduced biodiversity and altered nutrient cycles within the estuary.

Recent observations indicate a subtle shift in local tidal ranges over the past decade. While minor fluctuations are normal, sustained changes may signal broader climatic impacts or localized structural issues in the harbor. Continuous data collection is vital to distinguish between natural variation and anthropogenic influences on coastal hydrodynamics.

Staff members are encouraged to log daily high and low tide timings in the central database. Accurate records support long-term research initiatives and help inform emergency response protocols during extreme weather events. Consistent and precise documentation remains our most valuable tool for preserving the integrity of the local marine environment and ensuring regulatory compliance.

Subject: Details Regarding Your Gym Membership Terms
Dear Member,
Thank you you for choosing FitLife Gym as your health and fitness partner. We appreciate the chance to support your wellness goals and want you to understand the membership terms that govern your access to our facilities and services. This email outlines the key provisions of your contract, including payment schedules, membership tiers, renewal policies, and the procedures for pausing or ending your account. Please review the information carefully and contact us with any questions.
Your membership fee is billed monthly at the rate in your enrollment agreement. Payments are automatically withdrawn from the card on file by the first of each month. If a payment fails, we will retry within five business days and notify you. A late fee of $15 is applied after the seventh day of a missed payment. You may also opt to pay annually at a discounted rate, which will be reflected in a single charge on the anniversary of your start date.
The standard membership term is twelve months, after which the agreement automatically renews for successive twelve-month periods unless either party gives written notice of non-renewal at least thirty days before the renewal date. If you wish to upgrade to a higher tier, such as Premium Access, the change takes effect at the start of the next billing cycle, and any prorated adjustments appear on that month's invoice.
If you need to temporarily suspend your membership for medical reasons, relocation, or extended travel, you may place your account on hold for a minimum of one month and a maximum of three months per year. A $25 administrative fee applies for each hold, and the request must be submitted in writing, either by email or through our member portal, at least five business days before the hold begins.
To end your membership before the current term expires, you must submit a written cancellation request and give a thirty-day notice. Early termination incurs a fee equal to one month's dues, covering administrative costs and any prepaid balance. Any outstanding balance will be settled at the time of cancellation. After the notice period ends, we will send a confirmation email and stop all future billing.
We value your commitment to a healthier lifestyle and are here to help you with any aspect of your membership. Thank you for your attention to these details.
Sincerely,
John Doe
Membership Services Manager
FitLife Gym
