raw:
Adolf Stieler

Adolf Stieler (26 February 1775 - 13 March 1836) was a German cartographer and lawyer who worked most of his life in the Justus Perthes Geographical Institute in Gotha. Although he studied law and would serve in government for his entire career, he maintained an interest in cartography and published many famous works. His Handatlas was the leading German world atlas until the middle of the 20th century.

Stieler spent much of his early youth in Gotha, where his father was the mayor. In his adolescence, he showed an affinity for map-making, an interest he maintained throughout his adult life. However, he studied law at the University of Jena and the University of Göttingen from 1793 to 1796. He served as a legation councillor in Gotha from 1813 to 1829, and served the remainder of his career as a counsel to the local government until his retirement in 1835.

Stieler's cartographic career began with a position as a geography teacher at a girls' school in Gotha. However, he began work with Franz Xaver von Zach, the director of the Gotha Observatory. His works during this period include publishing cartographic representations of a number of von Zach's observations. Such illustrations were completed in von Zach's "Allgemeinen Geographischen Ephemeriden" or "General Geographical Ephemeris," published in 1798.

In 1804, Stieler worked in the Geographical Institute of Weimar, continuing his goal of starting a geographical publishing business. He also produced a number of regional and international maps. With von Zach, Stieler published his "Atlas Gaspari," which included maps of many European nations, including Spain, Portugal, and England. In 1806, his map of the East Indies was published. Later he would publish a 25 sheet military map of Germany that was part of a larger 204 sheet work. His maps were well known for their inclusion of new information from exploration and culture. He also incorporated a "System der fortwährenden Modernisierung," or "System of Ongoing Modernization," in his map creation and issuing. However, he began work on his most famous and long-lasting work, the Handatlas, in 1816 after a long hiatus from cartographic work. By 1826, when he completed the Handatlas, his career was nearing its end. His 1836 map of Germany would remain unfinished.

In addition to his contributions to cartography and law, Stieler also proposed mathematical methods in the insurance industry. He founded an insurance bank in 1828 with merchant and founder of Gothaer Versicherungsbank, Ernst-Wilhelm Arnoldi. Stieler died on March 13, 1836, in Gotha.

Stieler had a significant impact on his contemporaries. Johann Christoph Bär, a protégé of Stieler's who also worked at the Justus Perthes Institute, continued much of Stieler's work after his death. Stieler's "System der fortwährenden Modernisierung" for maps was incorporated into Bär's Handatlas, completed with fellow cartographer Johann Friedrich von Stülpnagel. Bär's 1833 "Das Herzogthum Gotha und umliegende Länder" (The Duchy of Gotha and Surrounding Lands) also explained much of Stieler's style. Stülpnagel also supervised the completion of an edition of Stielers Handatlas.

The Handatlas became one of his most recognized and long-lasting works. Editions remained in print as late as 1945. Other works by Stieler also remained in print. The Neue Kriegskarte, to which he contributed, had an edition in print as late as 1904.

pet adoption

Waiting in a shelter can be disheartening for animals who just want a soft place to sleep and a familiar hand to pet. Every day, thousands of dogs and cats lose their homes due to relocation, financial strain, or lifestyle changes. These animals are often healthy, vaccinated, and house-trained, ready to give unconditional love to a new family. Adopting instead of buying saves a life and frees up a kennel space for another animal in need. It is a simple act of compassion that ripples through the local community, supporting shelters that rely heavily on donations and volunteer efforts.

Before you visit, prepare by honestly assessing your daily routine, living space, and budget. Consider whether your home is secure for a curious kitten or a playful puppy. Research breeds or mixes that match your energy level and experience. Many shelters have friendly counselors who can help match you with a pet that fits your personality and lifestyle. Do not rush into a decision; take your time to ensure the bond will be a happy and lasting one for both you and the animal.

Once you bring your new companion home, patience is key. The first few weeks may involve adjustment periods for both of you. Set up a quiet space with their own bed, food, and water bowls away from high-traffic areas. Stick to a consistent feeding and walking schedule to build trust. Be gentle with training and socialization, rewarding good behavior with treats and praise. Avoid punishment, as it can erode the bond you are trying to build during this vulnerable transition phase.

Adoption is a lifelong commitment, not a temporary whim. Pet ownership brings immense joy, but it also demands time, money, and emotional energy. Prepare for vet visits, potential behavioral challenges, and the realities of aging companions. Many first-time owners underestimate the costs of emergency care or specialized diets for older pets. By planning ahead and staying informed, you ensure that your new friend receives the highest quality of life possible for many years to come.

If you encounter an animal that has already settled into homes, know that returning them is not a failure. Sometimes circumstances change, and the best thing for the animal is to find a more suitable environment. Shelters understand the complexities of human life and will work with you to find the right fit. Remember that every adoption story is unique, and success is defined by the well-being and happiness of the pet in their new forever home.

Subject: Climate Adaptation Strategies for Our Community
Dear Council Members,
Thank you for the opportunity to discuss our community's growing need for climate adaptation. Recent flood events and heat spikes have highlighted vulnerabilities that we can no longer ignore. These events also strain our local economy. Proactive planning will safeguard public health and local infrastructure.
First, we should prioritize a comprehensive risk assessment that maps flood-prone zones, heat islands, and vulnerable populations. This data will guide targeted investments, such as upgrading storm-water systems and expanding tree canopies in the downtown core. We will also model projected sea-level rise.
Second, we recommend incentivizing resilient building practices through grant programs and streamlined permitting. Homeowners and developers who incorporate flood-resistant design, cool roofs, or rain gardens should receive tangible financial support. A fast-track process for green roofs will help.
Third, community outreach must be integral to any plan. Workshops, multilingual resources, and partnerships with local schools can raise awareness and empower residents to take simple actions, like installing rain barrels or adopting native landscaping. Volunteers will act as climate ambassadors.
Finally, securing funding will require coordination with state agencies and private foundations. By presenting a unified adaptation framework, we can leverage existing climate-resilience grants and demonstrate fiscal responsibility. A public dashboard will track progress.
Sincerely,
[Your Name] 
Director of Sustainability Planning

Subject: Quick Tips for Getting Started with Photography
Hi Alex,
Hope you're having a good week. I remember you mentioning wanting to get more into photography, so I thought I'd send over a few basic tips to get you started without feeling overwhelmed.
First off, don't worry too much about fancy gear. Start by really understanding the camera you already have, even if it's just your phone. Experiment with its different modes and settings before diving into buying anything new.
One of the biggest things to pay attention to is light. Natural light is almost always your best friend. Try shooting outdoors early in the morning or late in the afternoon - that "golden hour" light makes everything look fantastic. Avoid harsh midday sun if you can.
Composition is key too. A simple concept to try is the "rule of thirds." Imagine a tic-tac-toe grid over your image and try placing your main subject along one of the lines or at an intersection. It often makes for a more balanced and interesting photo than just putting everything dead center.
Most importantly, just keep practicing. Take photos of anything and everything. Don't be afraid to take a lot of bad photos; that's how you learn what works and what doesn't. Review your shots and try to understand why some are better than others.
And finally, a little bit of editing can go a long way. You don't need complex software. Most phones have basic editing tools for adjusting brightness, contrast, and saturation. A small tweak can often elevate a good photo to a great one.
Good luck and have fun with it! Let me know if you have any questions.
Best,
Sarah

First off, don't worry too much about fancy gear. Start by really understanding the camera you already have, even if it's just your phone. Experiment with its different modes and settings before diving into buying anything new.
One of the biggest things to pay attention to is light. Natural light is almost always your best friend. Try shooting outdoors early in the morning or late in the afternoon - that "golden hour" light makes everything look fantastic. Avoid harsh midday sun if you can.
Composition is key too. A simple concept to try is the "rule of thirds." Imagine a tic-tac-toe grid over your image and try placing your main subject along one of the lines or at an intersection. It often makes for a more balanced and interesting photo than just putting everything dead center.
Most importantly, just keep practicing. Take photos of anything and everything. Don't be afraid to take a lot of bad photos; that's how you learn what works and what doesn't. Review your shots and try to understand why some are better than others.
And finally, a little bit of editing can go a long way. You don't need complex software. Most phones have basic editing tools for adjusting brightness, contrast, and saturation. A small tweak can often elevate a good photo to a great one.
Good luck and have fun with it! Let me know if you have any questions.
Best,
Sarah

Subject: Exploring different fiber optic options for our future apartment
Hi Sarah,
I finally got around to comparing the various home internet providers that offer coverage in the district where we are looking to move next spring. The last few months have been quite confusing due to the rapid changes in the market, but I wanted to share some initial findings with you before we make any long-term commitments regarding our housing arrangements. It seems that the landscape has shifted significantly toward fiber optic connections, which are now being marketed aggressively as the standard for modern households. This change is partly driven by the increasing number of remote workers who require reliable and high-speed connections for video conferencing and cloud-based applications.
The major provider currently holding nearly six percent of the local market share offers a base plan that includes up to five hundred megabits per second of symmetric speed. While this sounds impressive on paper, their data caps are extremely restrictive, allowing for only one terabyte of monthly usage before imposing heavy throttling restrictions or additional charges. This limitation could be a serious problem if we decide to stream high-definition content regularly or if we plan to download large software updates for our new laptops. Their customer service reviews have also been mixed lately, with several recent users complaining about long wait times on the phone and slow response times to technical support tickets.
On the other hand, a smaller regional utility company has introduced a new tiered plan that promises unlimited data usage for a slightly higher monthly fee. Their maximum speed sits at four hundred megabits, which is still more than enough for our current needs given that we do not plan to engage in heavy industrial data transfers or 8k video production. The key advantage here is the inclusion of free installation and a two-year price lock, which protects us from potential inflationary hikes in electricity or service costs during the pandemic recovery period. They also offer a dedicated support line that operates around the clock, which feels reassuring for someone who is not technically inclined and might struggle with basic router configurations.
We also need to consider the hardware costs involved in setting up these new connections. Most providers now recommend mesh networking systems to ensure consistent coverage throughout a two-bedroom apartment, especially if concrete walls might block standard Wi-Fi signals. These systems can add several hundred dollars to our upfront costs, which we need to factor into our moving budget alongside the security deposit and first month's rent. I have attached the detailed price quotes from both companies to this email so you can review the fine print and see if any other hidden fees are lurking in the contract terms.
Let me know your thoughts on this matter when you have a chance to sit down and read through the attached documents. I am leaning toward the regional utility because of the price stability, but I am willing to switch if you feel the speed difference is negligible for our daily habits. We should aim to finalize this decision by early next month so we can bundle the internet service with our existing cable television plan if we decide to keep it, potentially saving even more money in the long run through the provider's loyalty discount.
Best regards,
Alex

2023–24 European windstorm season

The 2023-2024 European windstorm season was the ninth season of the European windstorm naming in Europe. It comprised a year, from 1 September 2023 to 31 August 2024. This was the fifth season in which the Netherlands participated (through KNMI), alongside the United Kingdom's Met Office and Ireland's Met Éireann in the western group. The Portuguese, Spanish, French and Belgian meteorological agencies collaborated for the seventh time, joined by Luxembourg's agency (Southwestern group). This was the third season in which Greece, Israel and Cyprus (Eastern Mediterranean group), and Italy, Slovenia, Croatia, Montenegro, North Macedonia and Malta (Central Mediterranean group) named storms which affected their areas.

There is no universal definition of what constitutes a windstorm in Europe, nor is there a universally accepted system of naming storms. For example, in the Western Group, consisting of the UK, Ireland, and the Netherlands, a storm is named if one of the meteorological agencies in those countries issues an orange warning (amber in the UK), which generally requires a likelihood of widespread sustained wind speeds greater than 65 km/h (40 mph), or widespread wind gust speeds over 110 km/h (70 mph). (Required wind speeds vary slightly by agency and by season.) Both the likelihood of impact and the potential severity of the system are considered when naming a storm. The Southwest Group of Spain, Portugal, and France share a similar storm-naming scheme, though their names differ from those used by the Western Group. In Greece, however, naming criteria were established for storms when the storm's forecast winds are above 50 km/h (30 mph) over land, with the wind expected to have a significant impact to infrastructures. In Denmark, a windstorm must have an hourly average windspeed of at least 90 km/h (55 mph). The Meteorology Department of the Free University of Berlin (FUB) names all high and low pressure systems that affect Europe, though they do not assign names to any actual storms. A windstorm that is associated with one of these pressure systems will at times be recognized by the name assigned to the associated pressure system by the FUB. Named windstorms that have been recognized by a European meteorological agency are described in this article. Naming conventions used in Europe are generally based on conditions that are forecast, not conditions that have actually occurred, as public awareness and preparedness are often cited as the main purpose of the naming schemes-for example, a reference. Therefore, an assignment of a storm name does not mean that a storm will actually develop.

In 2015, the Met Office and Met Éireann announced a project to name storms as part of the "Name our Storms" project for windstorms and asked the public for suggestions. The meteorological offices produced a full list of names for 2015-2016 through 2017-2018, common to both the United Kingdom and Ireland, with the Netherlands taking part from 2019 onwards. Names in the United Kingdom will be based on the National Severe Weather Warning Service. The following names were chosen for the 2023-2024 season in the United Kingdom, Ireland, and the Netherlands. For a windstorm to be named, the United Kingdom's Met Office, Ireland's Met Eireann, or the Netherlands' Royal Netherlands Meteorological Institute (KNMI) have to issue an amber weather warning, preferably for wind, but a storm can also be named for amber warnings of rain and snow (e.g. Storm Arwen in 2021).

The Eastern Mediterranean Group works slightly differently compared to other naming lists; instead of ending a season on 31 August of that year, they end the season on 30 September of that year. These are the names that were chosen for the 2023-24 season in Greece, Israel and Cyprus.

This naming group, like the naming from the Free University of Berlin, does not use a naming list but names storms when it has not received a name by any other meteorological service in Europe and is projected to affect Denmark, Iceland, Norway or Sweden.

Like the Northern Group, the Free University of Berlin names storms based on low pressures across the continent and does not use a naming list. The storms listed below were strong enough or were anticipated to cause equal or more disruption than if it were named either by one of the other groups.

All storms named by European meteorological organisations in their respective forecasting areas, as well as Atlantic hurricanes that transitioned into European windstorms and retained the name assigned by the National Hurricane Center:

Storm Agnes was named by the UK's Met Office on 25 September 2023 and was forecast to bring strong winds and heavy rain to much of the UK and Ireland. The storm, which was also named Kilian by the Free University of Berlin and the Deutscher Wetterdienst, impacted the British Isles on 27 September.

used car buying

Buying a used car can feel like stepping into a maze of options, especially when you're trying to balance price, reliability, and personal taste. The first step is to define what you actually need-a compact commuter for city traffic, a family-sized SUV for weekend trips, or perhaps a sturdy truck for work. Knowing the primary purpose narrows the field and makes the research phase less overwhelming.

Once you have a vehicle type in mind, start gathering data from multiple sources. Online listings, local dealer inventories, and private sellers each have their own advantages, but all should be cross-checked with price guides and consumer reports. Look for patterns in the asking price, mileage, and vehicle history. A car that consistently appears at a lower price than comparable models may have hidden issues, while a slightly higher price could reflect a well-maintained history and recent service.

The next crucial stage is the physical inspection. Even if the car's paperwork looks clean, a hands-on evaluation can reveal problems that aren't obvious online. Check the exterior for rust, mismatched paint, and tire wear; examine the interior for signs of water damage or excessive wear; and listen to the engine for unusual noises. If you're not comfortable assessing mechanical condition yourself, bring a trusted mechanic along or arrange for a professional pre-purchase inspection. A modest inspection fee can save you from costly repairs later.

Financing a used car requires a different approach than buying new. Banks and credit unions often offer better rates than dealer-run finance departments, especially if you have a solid credit history. Compare loan terms, interest rates, and any prepayment penalties before committing. Remember that a larger down payment not only reduces your monthly obligation but also improves your negotiating leverage, as sellers appreciate buyers who appear financially prepared.

Finally, the paperwork should be handled with as much care as the test drive. Verify the vehicle identification number (VIN) against the title and any history reports, ensure that there are no liens, and confirm that the seller's name matches the title. Obtain a bill of sale that includes the final price, odometer reading, and any "as-is" conditions. After the transaction, promptly register the vehicle, transfer the title, and consider purchasing an extended warranty or service plan if the car is still under manufacturer coverage. A thorough, methodical approach can turn the often-daunting used-car market into a manageable, rewarding experience.

Subject: First Aid Basics - Quick Guide for Everyday Situations
Dear Team,
I wanted to share a brief refresher on first aid basics that can help us respond confidently to common injuries and medical emergencies at work or at home. Even a short pause to assess a situation and apply the right technique can make a big difference, and most of the steps rely on simple, calm actions that anyone can learn. Keeping a well-stocked first-aid kit nearby and knowing a few core principles means we're better prepared for the unexpected.
The first step in any emergency is to ensure the scene is safe for both the victim and the responder. Look for hazards such as traffic, fire, or electrical sources, and remove them if possible. Once the area is secure, check the person's responsiveness by gently tapping their shoulder and asking, "Are you okay?" If there is no response, call emergency services immediately and then begin the basic assessment: airway, breathing, and circulation. Clearing the airway by tilting the head back and lifting the chin can open the passage, while watching the chest for rise and fall tells us if the person is breathing. If breathing is absent, start chest compressions at a rate of about 100 to 120 per minute, using the heel of one hand placed over the center of the chest and interlocking the other hand on top.
For minor cuts, scrapes, or abrasions, the priority is to stop the bleeding and protect the wound from infection. Apply firm, direct pressure with a clean cloth or bandage, and maintain that pressure for several minutes until the bleeding slows. Once the bleeding is controlled, rinse the wound gently with clean water to remove debris, then apply an antiseptic if one is available. Cover the area with a sterile dressing to keep it clean and to promote healing. Encourage the injured person to keep the wound elevated when possible, as this helps reduce swelling and further bleeding.
Burns require special attention, especially if they cover a large area or involve the face, hands, or genitals. For a minor, first-degree burn, run cool (not icy) water over the affected skin for at least ten minutes to reduce heat and pain. Do not apply butter, oils, or ointments, as these can trap heat. For more severe burns, cover the area with a clean, non-adhesive dressing and seek medical help right away. If a chemical burn occurs, remove any contaminated clothing and flush the area with copious amounts of water for at least fifteen minutes before addressing pain relief.
Choking is another situation where quick action can save a life. If the person is able to cough, encourage them to continue, as this may dislodge the obstruction. When coughing is ineffective and the person cannot speak, breathe, or cough, perform the Heimlich maneuver: stand behind them, wrap your arms around the waist, make a fist above the navel, and thrust inward and upward sharply. Repeat the thrusts until the object is expelled or emergency responders arrive.
Having these basics in mind can boost our confidence and effectiveness when an emergency arises. I encourage everyone to review the attached first-aid handbook and, if possible, attend the upcoming hands-on workshop scheduled for next month. Practicing these skills regularly ensures they become second nature, which is exactly what we need when seconds count.
Best regards,
Jordan Patel 
Health & Safety Coordinator

The City of Riverton Street Food Safety and Inspection Protocol

Effective immediately, all vendors operating within the designated three-mile radius of the Central Business District must comply with the new health and safety standards outlined in this memorandum. This update is designed to ensure consistent quality for tourists and residents alike while maintaining the vibrant, informal character of our urban dining scenes. The primary goal is to bridge the gap between traditional street vending and modern public health expectations without stifling the creativity that makes our local food scene unique. Vendors should view these changes not as bureaucratic hurdles, but as professional milestones that elevate their establishments to new levels of credibility and safety.

First and foremost, hand hygiene and personal grooming represent the single most critical factor in preventing foodborne illness. All food handlers must wash their hands with soap and warm water for a minimum of twenty seconds after touching raw ingredients, waste, or their own bodies. Gloves are encouraged but not mandatory, provided that they are changed frequently and between handling different types of ready-to-eat foods. In addition, long hair must be secured with a net or cap to prevent contamination. Clean, pressed uniforms are required, and any visible tattoos or jewelry that might compromise hygiene standards should be covered or removed prior to starting service. These basic disciplinary measures form the foundation of trust between the vendor and the public.

Temperature control remains a non-negotiable aspect of food safety. Perishable foods, including cut fruits, grilled meats, and dairy-based sauces, must be kept below forty degrees Fahrenheit or above one hundred forty degrees Fahrenheit at all times. Portable refrigerators and heated holding units should be sanitized daily and protected from direct sunlight to prevent equipment failure. Vendors are strictly prohibited from keeping perishable items at room temperature for more than four hours, a practice often seen during peak afternoon rushes. Temperature logs must be maintained on-site, with readings taken every two hours and recorded on the provided flip chart. This data must be available for inspection upon request by city health officers at any time during business hours.

Proper storage and labeling of ingredients further reduce the risk of cross-contamination and spoilage. All pre-prepared or partially prepared foods must be stored in covered, food-grade containers. Ingredients that have been defrosted must be labeled with the date of preparation and must be used within forty-eight hours. Raw meat, poultry, and seafood should be stored on the bottom shelves of refrigeration units, while ready-to-eat foods rest on the top shelves. This vertical arrangement prevents potential drips from raw products from contaminating prepared dishes. Additionally, single-use condiments and packaging materials must be stored in a dry area away from open food preparation zones to maintain their integrity and cleanliness.

Compliance with these guidelines will be tested through random, unannounced inspections by the Department of Environmental Health. Failures to meet these baseline standards will result in immediate citations, with penalties escalating from written warnings to fines, and ultimately, the revocation of the temporary food service license. However, vendors who consistently maintain high standards may be eligible for the City Certified Safe Street Food Badge, a digital and physical marker that can be displayed prominently. This badge serves as a visible assurance to consumers that the food they are enjoying meets rigorous public health criteria. We encourage all stakeholders to read the full technical manual available on the city portal and to attend the upcoming workshop on advanced sanitation practices scheduled for next month. Your cooperation in maintaining the safety and reputation of Riverton's culinary heritage is greatly appreciated.

Yiannakis Gavriel

Yiannakis Gavriel (born July 17, 1961, in Deryneia, Famagusta) is a Greek Cypriot politician. He is a member of the House of Representatives representing the Famagusta District, elected with the AKEL party.

Yiannakis Gavriel was born in Deryneia on July 17, 1961. He speaks Greek, English, and Hungarian. He studied industrial engineering and wood processing at the University of Forestry and Wood Sciences in Sopron, Hungary. He works as an educator. He is married to Chrystalla Ioannou and has one son and one daughter.

He served as the secretary of the United Democratic Youth Organization (EDON) of Deryneia from 1989 to 1993. He was a member of the board of the Drug and Addict Information and Treatment Center (KENTHEA) from 2004 to 2008. He has also been a member of the Association of Scientific Engineers and the Scientific Technical Chamber of Cyprus since 1990. He has been a member of the Famagusta District Committee of AKEL since 2008 and a member of the Central Committee of AKEL since 2010. He participated in the 2006 parliamentary elections in the Famagusta District with AKEL but was not elected. However, in 2008, the AKEL Member of Parliament for Famagusta District, Costas Papacostas, was appointed Ministry of Defense in the Demetris Christofias government. As the first alternate, Yiannakis Gavriel took his place in parliament on March 6, 2008, for the 9th Parliamentary Session (Cyprus). He was re-elected in the 2011 parliamentary elections for the 10th Parliamentary Session (Cyprus). As a member of parliament, he served as Chairman of the Parliamentary Committee on Agriculture and Natural Resources and a member of the Parliamentary Committee on Commerce and Industry. He ran for re-election in the 2016 parliamentary elections but was not elected. However, following the resignation of the AKEL MP for the Famagusta District, Christakis Tziovanis, Yiannakis Gavriel took his place on October 23, 2020, as the first alternate, for the 11th Parliamentary Session (Cyprus). He was re-elected in the 2021 parliamentary elections for the 12th Parliamentary Session (Cyprus).

insurance claim steps

Filing an insurance claim can feel overwhelming, but knowing the correct sequence of actions makes the process significantly smoother for everyone involved. The very first step is to gather comprehensive documentation. This includes your policy number, driver's license, and any relevant records that prove coverage was active at the time of the incident. Do not wait until you speak with an adjuster to start collecting these items, as having them ready speeds up the initial verification phase considerably.

Next, you must report the incident promptly. Most policies require notification within a specific timeframe, often ranging from twenty-four to seventy-two hours. Call your insurance provider to open the claim file and obtain a unique reference number. This number is crucial for all future correspondence, so write it down immediately. While on the phone, provide a clear and concise summary of what happened, sticking strictly to the facts without speculation.

After reporting the incident, you will likely need to submit detailed evidence. This may include photographs of any damage, police reports, or medical bills depending on the type of claim. Ensure that all images are high-resolution and clearly show the extent of the issue. Organizing these documents into a single digital folder can help you avoid losing important files during the back-and-forth communication with your adjuster.

Once the claim is opened, an adjuster will be assigned to evaluate your case. They may ask additional questions or request further documentation. It is important to remain cooperative and honest throughout this stage, as providing false information can result in claim denial or legal consequences. Keep a log of every interaction, noting dates, names, and key points discussed, to ensure you have a clear history if disputes arise later.

Finally, wait for the assessment to be completed. The adjuster will review the evidence against your policy terms and determine the payout amount. If you agree with the decision, accept it and arrange for repairs or payment directly. If you disagree, you have the right to appeal the decision, but it is often more efficient to resolve smaller discrepancies through clarification. Patience and persistence are key to a successful resolution.

raw:
Tirax language

The name Tirax refers to 'inland person'. The original homeland of the Tirax speakers is the mountainous interior of North Central Malakula, neighbouring Big Nambas. As the Tirax speakers embraced Christianity in the early twentieth century, they began to migrate towards the east coast, where they founded the villages of Mae, Rori and Bethel.

Tirax speakers often refer to their own language as resan, "language, speech", or Resan Tirax. Tirax is called "Dirak" by the speakers of Northeast Malakula. Dirak is the name used to refer to Tirax in John Lynch and Terry Crowley's 2001, Languages of Vanuatu: A New Survey and Bibliography. Because it is the language of Mae village, the Tirax language is referred to as "Mae" in the Ethnologue listing, and also in Darrell Tryon's 1976, New Hebrides languages: An internal classification. See Mae language. Tirax speakers prefer not to use "Mae" as the language name, as it is also the language of Rori and Bethel.

Tirax has many features in common with other North Vanuatu languages. It has no tense marking, but has "obligatory subject-mood markers distinguishing realis and irrealis mood". It has "inalienable and alienable possessive marking", with a range of "possessive classifiers for alienable possession" including specific markers for food, drink and paths. Also like other Malakula languages, numbers have verbal morphology. Tirax has "nuclear verb serialisation, and a range of strategies for paratactic linkage. Several morphosyntactic processes, such as object marking and plural marking, are sensitive to the animacy of the referent".

Voiced stops are prenasalized. /s/ and /r/ are alveolar, with the rest of the column being dental. It is possible that the cluster of /d/ and /r/ is actually the unit phoneme /dr/, a dental with a trill release.

There is evidence that Tirax had an apicolabial (linguolabial consonant) series, likely borrowed from Big Nambas. The apicolabials are no longer part of the Tirax phoneme system, but have recently shifted to their dental consonant counterparts.

Until 2004, Tirax was an oral language; a writing system is a relatively recent development. Tirax narratives show previously undescribed structural features not found in written narratives. There is a linking device between paragraphs, termed "transition clauses". Transition clauses are associated with a misalignment of prosodic and discourse-semantic levels of structure. And there are a small set of circumstances in which story events are related out of chronological order, which runs counter to traditional theories of narrative.

To all team members,

Effective from the first of next month, the restaurant will adopt a revised schedule of opening hours designed to align with peak customer demand while also providing a balanced workload for staff. The new operating times will be 7:00 a.m. to 10:30 p.m. Monday through Thursday, 7:00 a.m. to 11:00 p.m. on Fridays, 8:00 a.m. to 11:30 p.m. on Saturdays, and 8:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m. on Sundays. This shift reflects data from the past twelve months, indicating higher patronage during later evening periods on weekends and a modest increase in early-morning traffic during weekdays.

All front-of-house staff are required to adhere to the new start-times for each shift, with a mandatory 30-minute pre-opening briefing at the designated time. Kitchen personnel must be on site no later than 30 minutes before service begins, ensuring that prep work and safety checks are completed before guests arrive. Any deviations from these schedules must be approved in writing by the shift manager and logged in the scheduling system no later than 24 hours prior to the requested change.

The revised hours also introduce a brief "quiet hour" each day from 3:00 p.m. to 4:00 p.m., during which the dining room will operate with reduced staffing levels. This period is intended for inventory checks, deep cleaning of high-traffic zones, and staff rotation without disrupting service. While the restaurant remains open, the menu will be limited to a selection of quick-serve items, and wait times are expected to be minimal. Managers are asked to monitor guest flow during this interval and adjust staffing as necessary to maintain a seamless experience.

Please note that the updated schedule will affect overtime calculations and shift differentials. Hours worked beyond 9:00 p.m. on weekdays will qualify for the standard evening premium, while any service extending past midnight on Fridays and Saturdays will trigger the late-night surcharge rate. Payroll will be updated accordingly, and any concerns should be directed to the Human Resources department by the end of the current pay period.

Finally, we appreciate everyone's flexibility as we transition to these new hours. The changes are expected to improve both customer satisfaction and employee well-being by reducing understaffed periods and providing clearer expectations. Should you have questions about the implementation, please attend the brief Q&A session scheduled for next Tuesday at 2:00 p.m. in the staff lounge. Thank you for your continued dedication and professionalism.

Johann Martin Boltzius

Johann Martin Boltzius (December 15, 1703 - November 19, 1765) was a German-born American Lutheran minister. He is most known for his association with the Salzburger emigrants, a group of German-speaking Protestant refugees who migrated to the British colony of Georgia in 1734. They founded the city of Ebenezer, Georgia to escape persecution in the Archbishopric of Salzburg and other Roman Catholic authorities for their religious views.

Boltzius was born at Forst in Lower Lusatia, a town southeast of Berlin, Germany. His parents, Eva Rosina Muller and Martin Boltzius worked as weavers. He was awarded a scholarship for theology from the University of Halle. conference registration

Conference registration can feel like a daunting step, especially for first-time attendees, but understanding the process helps you focus on what truly matters: the content and networking opportunities the event offers. Most organizers have moved their sign-up systems online, providing a streamlined portal where you can create an account, select your ticket type, and secure your spot with a few clicks. The key is to start early; many conferences open registration several months in advance, and early-bird pricing often disappears once the deadline passes.

When you land on the registration page, you'll typically be asked to choose between several categories: standard attendee, student, presenter, or sponsor. Each option comes with its own set of benefits, such as access to workshops, meal vouchers, or exclusive networking lounges. Be sure to read the fine print, because some tickets may exclude certain sessions or limit the number of events you can attend each day. If you're presenting a paper or leading a panel, there may be additional steps, like uploading your abstract or confirming your equipment needs.

Payment methods have also become more flexible. Credit cards remain the most common, but many platforms now accept PayPal, Apple Pay, or even direct bank transfers for larger groups. For corporate attendees, it's worth checking whether your organization has a discount code or a bulk-registration agreement that can reduce costs per person. Keep a copy of the confirmation email and the receipt; they often contain a unique registration ID that you'll need to present at check-in, as well as links to download the event app or access the virtual agenda.

After you've secured your ticket, the next step is to personalize your experience. Most conference portals allow you to build a schedule by adding sessions, meetings, and social events to a personal itinerary. You can also update your profile with a photo, a short bio, and your professional interests, which helps other attendees find you during networking breaks. Some events even offer a matchmaking service that suggests connections based on shared topics or industries, making it easier to arrange one-on-one meetings in advance.

Finally, remember to review the cancellation and refund policy before the event. Unforeseen circumstances-travel delays, health issues, or changes in work commitments-can arise, and knowing your options can save you both money and stress. Many conferences offer a partial refund or a credit toward a future event if you cancel by a specific date. By staying organized, confirming details promptly, and taking advantage of the tools provided, you can turn the registration process into a smooth prelude to a rewarding conference experience.

To: Residents of the Riverbend Community 
From: Riverbend Neighborhood Safety Committee 
Date: October 8, 2026 
Subject: Updated Guidelines and Resources for Enhancing Neighborhood Safety

The safety of our streets, sidewalks, and public spaces is a shared responsibility that benefits from clear communication and coordinated effort. Recent observations and feedback from residents have highlighted a few recurring concerns, including increased traffic speed on Oak Street, occasional loitering near the park after dusk, and occasional missed lighting maintenance on certain walkways. This notice outlines practical steps we can all take, along with the resources the committee is mobilizing, to address these issues promptly and effectively.

First, all drivers are reminded to observe the posted 25-mph speed limit on residential streets, especially during school pickup and drop-off times. Speed-monitoring devices have been installed at key intersections, and the city's traffic enforcement team will conduct regular checks during peak hours. Residents are encouraged to report any observed speeding or reckless driving through the non-emergency police line (555-123-4567) or the online portal, which will allow officers to respond quickly and issue warnings or citations as appropriate.

Second, the lighting plan for the neighborhood is being updated. The public works department has scheduled inspections of all streetlights on Main Avenue, Willow Lane, and the perimeter of Riverbend Park. Any fixture found to be malfunctioning will be replaced within 48 hours of reporting. For immediate concerns, please call the maintenance hotline at 555-987-6543 and provide the exact location and description of the lighting issue. Well-lit areas deter criminal activity and help residents feel more secure when walking after dark.

Third, community vigilance is essential in deterring loitering and other undesirable behavior. Residents are asked to report suspicious activity to the neighborhood watch email (watch@riverbend.org) or directly to the local patrol unit. The watch program has been expanded to include volunteer "safe-walk" volunteers who will patrol the park and nearby sidewalks between 8 p.m. and 10 p.m. on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Volunteers receive a brief training on how to engage respectfully with strangers and how to contact law enforcement if a situation escalates.

Lastly, we are introducing a series of safety workshops open to all residents. The first session, "Home Security Basics," will be held at the community center on October 20 at 6 p.m. Topics will include proper lock usage, alarm system options, and simple landscaping tips that increase visibility. Subsequent workshops will cover emergency preparedness, child safety, and cyber-security awareness. Attendance is free, and participants will receive a handbook summarizing the key points discussed.

The committee thanks every resident for their continued cooperation and commitment to making Riverbend a safe and welcoming place to live. By adhering to traffic rules, promptly reporting maintenance needs, staying alert, and participating in community initiatives, we can collectively reduce risks and foster a stronger sense of security. Should you have any questions or suggestions, please contact the committee at safety@riverbend.org or call the office line at 555-321-7890.

Big Backyard Beat Show

Big Backyard Beat Show is the second album by the American band BR5-49, released in 1998. It peaked at No. 38 on Billboard's Top Country Albums chart and at No. 7 on the UK Country Artists Album chart. The first single was "Wild One", a cover of the Johnny O'Keefe song; it was nominated for a Grammy Award for "Best Country Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocal". The band supported the album with North American and UK tours.

Recorded in November 1997, the album was produced by Jozef Nuyens and Mike Janas. BR5-49 wrote nine of its songs. "Georgia on a Fast Train" is a cover of the Billy Joe Shaver song. "There Goes My Love" was written by Buck Owens. "Seven Nights to Rock" is a version of the song made famous by Moon Mullican. "18 Wheels and a Crowbar" is a tale of road rage. "My Name Is Mudd" is about a town pariah. Santiago Jiménez Jr. played accordion on "Goodbye, Maria". The band considered remixing some of the tracks for a harder sound, but instead chose to have Steve Albini record live tracks for them to use on an EP, Bonus Beats.

The Baltimore Sun concluded that, "as clever as the lyrics sometimes are, the album's real allure is its blend of boogie piano, blues guitar, honky tonk twang, and Tex-Mex exuberance." The Lincoln Journal Star wrote that "Chuck Mead and Gary Bennett are both solid writers-Mead's work tends toward the rock end of things while Bennett recycles the old country feel in his hurtin' songs." USA Today noted that the originals "tend toward the dark or humorous, though guitarist Gary Bennett's 'Storybook Endings (If You Stop Believin')' has both a lyric and a meter that Roger Miller would've appreciated." The Ottawa Citizen stated that "rockabilly, one of modern country music's principal roots, is a key element in the group's recipe." The Scotsman considered the music to be "fired by a raw-edged punk sensibility and mellowed with authentic back-porch charm." The Washington Post said that Mead "has a dark, humorous streak, as heard in the paean to road rage, '18 Wheels and a Crowbar', and in 'Goodbye, Maria', a tale of suicide set to the happy-sad strains of a polka." The Atlanta Journal-Constitution opined: "Like the Stray Cats or Big Bad Voodoo Daddy, BR5-49 has plopped down in a musical era-in this case, 1950s big-twang, cigarettes-and-ashtrays country-which it excavates like an obsessed college kid in a vintage clothing store." The Los Angeles Times determined that Mead and Bennett "lack the vocal depth and character to make BR5-49 more than a particularly skilled bar band with a well-developed playful streak." The Boston Globe wrote that "BR5-49 owe a great deal of their success to a flat refusal to distill the genre for the sake of accessibility."

craft fair

Gathering around a table with a stack of handmade ceramics, I realized that the weekend ahead would be more than just a fun errand. The local Community Craft Fair is scheduled for next Saturday, and I needed to prepare carefully to ensure my small stall looked inviting and professional. There is something deeply satisfying about the tactile nature of selling handmade goods face to face, where conversations are accompanied by the clink of pottery and the rustle of paper. It is a reminder that in our digital age, physical interaction still holds immense value and potential for meaningful connection.

I started by sorting through the last few weeks of production, setting aside the pieces that did not meet my quality standards. This culling process is difficult, especially when you have invested hours in a specific design, but it is crucial for maintaining a high level of craftsmanship at the event. I selected only the items that I would be proud to give to a close friend. The final collection included twelve ceramic mugs, four sets of hand-bound journals, and a dozen personalized leather keychains. Each item has a story behind it, which helps potential buyers connect with the work on a personal level rather than viewing it as a mass-produced commodity.

Pricing was the next challenge I faced this week. I spent time calculating my material costs, labor hours, and overhead expenses to arrive at a fair price that reflected the true value of the handmade process. I knew that underpricing my work would undermine its perceived quality, while overpricing it might discourage sales in a competitive environment. After several rounds of adjustments, I settled on a pricing strategy that offered slight discounts for bulk purchases. This approach encourages customers to buy more while ensuring that I still receive fair compensation for the time and skill involved in creating each piece.

Setting up the display area is another critical aspect of preparing for a craft fair. I sketched out layouts for my folding table, ensuring that there was enough space to display items clearly without feeling cluttered. I plan to use neutral background cloths to make the colors of the ceramics pop and to create a cohesive visual theme. Lighting is also important; I will bring battery-operated clip-on lights to highlight the textures of the leather goods. A clean and organized presentation tells customers that the maker takes pride in their craft, which builds trust and confidence in the purchase.

Finally, I am preparing some simple marketing materials, such as business cards and small placards with my social media handles. This allows customers to follow my work even after the fair ends, turning a one-time transaction into a long-term relationship. I am also bringing a portable card reader to make payments seamless and efficient. All of these preparations serve one purpose: to create a smooth and memorable experience for both the seller and the buyer. The craft fair is not just about making sales; it is about community, creativity, and the shared joy of supporting local artists. I can not wait to see who stops by and what stories our handmade items will tell over the weekend.

small business accounting

Running a small business means wearing many hats, and one of the most critical roles is that of the chief financial officer. Many entrepreneurs mistakenly believe they can keep their free side projects separate from their main business without facing legal or financial repercussions. However, the moment you hire your first employee or sign a lease, the distinction between personal and business accounts becomes a matter of legal necessity, not just professional courtesy. Keeping these finances entangled endangers your personal assets and complicates your tax filing process significantly.

The first step toward healthy books is opening a dedicated business checking account. This simple act demonstrates good faith to the IRS and creditors while providing a clear audit trail. Every dollar spent on office supplies, software subscriptions, or marketing campaigns should flow through this account. It eliminates the guesswork during tax season and makes it easier to track cash flow. You no longer have to sift through personal credit card statements to find legitimate business expenses, saving you countless hours of frustrating reconciliation.

Quarterly estimated tax payments are another area where many new owners stumble. If you are a sole proprietor or LLC, you are responsible for self-employment tax, which is a substantial percentage of your net profit. Failing to remit these quarterly payments can result in steep penalties and interest charges that erode your profits. Automating these transfers directly from your business account ensures your government obligations are met without the stress of last-minute calculations.

Modern accounting software has made maintaining these records far more accessible than in previous decades. Cloud-based platforms offer real-time insights into your financial health, allowing you to see where money is coming from and where it is leaking away. These tools automatically categorize transactions based on your spending habits, reducing manual entry errors and providing instant reports that help you make informed decisions about inventory, staffing, and investments.

Finally, consider hiring a part-time bookkeeper or part-time accountant for quarterly reviews. Their fresh perspective can identify discrepancies you might overlook and suggest deductions you may have missed. This investment in professional guidance pays for itself multiple times over by preventing costly mistakes and ensuring that your business remains compliant with evolving local and federal regulations. A solid financial foundation allows you to focus on growth rather than backtracking.

To: All Employees 
From: Facilities Management 
Date: October 8 2026 
Subject: Guidelines for Maintaining Healthy Office Houseplants

The purpose of this notice is to provide clear, practical guidance for caring for the houseplants placed throughout our workspaces. Healthy plants contribute to air quality, reduce stress, and enhance the overall aesthetic of the office. Consistent, simple practices by everyone will ensure that the foliage remains vibrant and that the plants continue to thrive throughout the year, regardless of seasonal changes outside.

Watering is the most frequent source of plant stress. Each species has a specific moisture requirement, but a good rule of thumb is to check the top inch of soil before adding water. If the soil feels dry at that depth, give the pot enough water to saturate the root zone, allowing excess to drain from the bottom. Over-watering can lead to root rot, while under-watering causes wilting; both conditions are easily avoided with a quick tactile check each morning before the workday begins.

Light exposure varies considerably across the office floor plan. Plants positioned near windows receive direct or indirect sunlight, while those in interior zones depend on artificial lighting. When relocating a plant, observe the existing light level for several days; a sudden shift from bright to low light often results in leaf yellowing or slowed growth. If a plant appears to be stretching toward a light source, rotate the pot a quarter turn each week to promote balanced development and prevent one side from becoming leggy.

Fertilization should be applied sparingly, using a balanced, water-soluble formula diluted to half the recommended strength. During the active growing months of spring and summer, a monthly feed supports healthy leaf production. In autumn and winter, most houseplants enter a dormancy period and require little to no supplemental nutrients. Avoid feeding during these cooler months, as excess fertilizer can accumulate in the soil and damage the root system.

Pest monitoring is essential for early detection and control. Common indoor insects such as spider mites, aphids, and fungus gnats can appear on any plant, especially those with dense foliage or consistently moist soil. Conduct a brief visual inspection during each watering cycle, looking for webbing, discolored spots, or tiny insects on leaves and stems. If an infestation is suspected, isolate the affected plant and notify Facilities Management; we will provide appropriate treatment options while minimizing disruption to the surrounding work environment.

By following these straightforward practices-regular soil checks, appropriate lighting, measured fertilization, and vigilant pest observation-we can collectively maintain a thriving indoor garden that benefits everyone. Should you have any questions or require assistance with a specific plant, please reach out to the Facilities team at plantcare@company.com. Thank you for your cooperation in keeping our office greenery healthy and attractive.

Subject: Quick question on magma viscosity
Hi Dr. Aris,
I hope you are having a good week. I have been reviewing the recent seismic data from the Kilauea East Rift Zone and I wanted to double-check my understanding of how silica content influences eruptive behavior. Specifically, I am trying to reconcile the low-viscosity basaltic flows we observed last month with the unexpected formation of those thick, slow-moving lobes near the crater rim.
In my notes, I had assumed that the high silica content in the fractional melt would immediately increase the viscosity significantly. However, the thermal decay rates suggest the magma remained relatively fluid for longer than standard models predict. I am concerned that this might indicate a different source composition or a higher initial temperature than we originally accounted for in our risk assessment.
I recall we discussed this topic during the last geology conference, where the new research on crystal mush dynamics was a major highlight. Do you think the plagioclase crystals were acting as a slurry that prevented the melt from stiffening as quickly? Or should we be looking at the role of volatile exsolution in keeping the bubble fraction lower than expected during the final ascent phase?
The implications for our emergency response protocols are non-trivial here. If lower viscosity persists at higher elevations, the lava could travel further and speed up before cooling, which would change our evacuation buffer zones. I would appreciate any thoughts you have on whether the current monitoring data supports the slurry hypothesis or if we need to recalibrate our petrological models.
Let me know if you have time for a brief call next Tuesday or Wednesday. I can send over the raw spectrometry logs ahead of time so we can review them together. Thank you for your help in clarifying this complex dynamic.
Best regards,
Elena Vance
Junior Field Geologist
Volcanic Hazard Monitoring Team

Home | About | Contact

The Swiss League, also known as the Sky Swiss League for sponsorship reasons, is the second tier of the main professional ice hockey league in Switzerland, behind the National League. The winners of the league each season play a best-of-seven series against the bottom team of the NL, and if they win, they are promoted, while the National League team is relegated to the Swiss League. In 2024, the Swiss League changed its name to Sky Swiss League as a partnership with broadcaster Sky Switzerland. Prior to the 2017-18 season, the league was formerly called National League B. The league attendance in 2018-19 was about 2,700 spectators.

alumni newsletter

The September issue of the Cedar Valley University Alumni Quarterly has just hit subscriber inboxes, and this time, the content feels distinctly different from previous editions. Instead of relying solely on standard faculty updates and generic fundraising appeals, this semester's publication places a heavy emphasis on local impact and tangible community contributions. Editors at the university noted that feedback from last year's reader survey indicated a clear desire to see more stories about how graduates are actively using their degrees to effect change beyond their immediate corporate roles. By shifting the narrative focus, the newsletter aims to bridge the emotional gap between the academic institution and the broader societal context in which its graduates are now operating.

One of the standout features in this edition is a deep-dive profile on a 2015 graduate who has established a series of independent labs in underserved rural areas. The article chronicles her journey from a struggling student to a key player in regional public health initiatives, highlighting the specific skills she gained during her chemistry residency. This narrative approach is designed to inspire current students by showing real-world applications of their curriculum. Readers are encouraged to view the newsletter not just as a record of achievement, but as a roadmap for career possibilities that extend into specialized, niche fields often overlooked by major corporate recruiters.

Financial transparency has also been addressed more directly in this quarter's pages, a response to growing scrutiny from long-time supporters who wish to understand exactly where their donations go. A detailed breakdown of the new engineering wing renovation is included, complete with architectural renderings and cost comparisons with similar projects across the state. This level of detail speaks to the changing expectations of the modern donor, who increasingly demands accountability alongside gratitude. By providing this data, the university hopes to foster a deeper sense of partnership between the administration and the alumni community, transforming passive readers into active stakeholders in the school's physical and financial future.

Beyond the print and digital articles, this issue includes a dedicated section for professional networking tips customized for mid-career professionals. Many respondents to the internal surveys mentioned feeling isolated after moving away from their college towns, and this section aims to counter that isolation. It offers practical advice on how to leverage the shared network for mentorship opportunities, job referrals, and collaborative professional development. The inclusion of these resources signals a shift in the newsletter's role, moving it from a recreational publication to a functional tool for career management and professional growth.

Looking ahead, the editorial team is planning a digital-only series next month that will feature video interviews with notable alumni from various industries. This hybrid approach allows for richer storytelling while keeping the printed edition concise and easy to read. The goal is to create a multi-layered experience that appeals to different consumption habits within the alumni base. As the page count remains relatively stable, the quality and relevance of the content have become the primary metrics for success, ensuring that every issue remains a valuable connection point for graduates years after their final exam.

Sheila Frazier

Sheila Elaine Frazier (born November 13, 1948) is an American actress, producer, and model. Frazier is known for her role as Georgia in the 1972 crime drama film Super Fly. Frazier later reprised her role in the 1973 sequel, Super Fly T.N.T.

Sheila Elaine Frazier was born in New York City to parents Dorothy Dennis and Eugene Cole Frazier. She spent her early years living on the Lower East Side of Manhattan and attended PS 97 until the age of ten, when she relocated with her mother to Englewood, New Jersey. There, she enrolled in the Liberty School. During her childhood, Frazier experienced a stutter, which contributed to her shyness. In sixth grade, a teacher attempted to help her overcome it by addressing the class before her presentation and stating, "I don't want any laughter. Sheila has a stutter." Frazier has mentioned that this introduction heightened her anxiety about public speaking. In Englewood, her neighbors included, Clyde McPhatter, Van McCoy, The Isley Brothers, and Dolly and Jackie McLean. She went on to Dwight Morrow High School, where her classmates included Margaret Travolta, actress and sister of John Travolta. Despite Frazier's struggle with stuttering, she was inspired by Susan Hayward's performance in the film I'll Cry Tomorrow to pursue a career as an actress. After graduating from high school in 1966, aged 17, she moved to New York City, where she stayed with her godmother and found work as a secretary.

One day on the subway, a man approached Frazier and asked if she'd ever considered modelling. That chance encounter led her to do photo sessions with his boss, Bert Andrews. She began to do runway modeling and print work, but was not comfortable with that sort of attention. At some point, she met actor Richard Roundtree, who suggested she audition for the Negro Ensemble Company. Following his advice about focusing on the part she was playing, Frazier found she had overcome her stuttering. Five months later, she auditioned for the film Super Fly, winning the role of Georgia, the lead actress. She went on to work in many film and television productions, including Three the Hard Way. In 1980, she hosted a community affairs show on KNXT-TV in Los Angeles. She also worked as a story editor at Richard Pryor's Indigo Productions.

Frazier has been married twice and has one child. Frazier married evangelist minister John Atchison in early-2008 at Crenshaw Christian Center East in Manhattan, New York. Frazier's son, Derek McKeith is from her previous marriage to Sam McKeith. Frazier currently resides in New York.

Subject: Update on Adult Programs and Digital Access
Dear Friends of the Library,
I hope this message finds you well and that you have had a chance to enjoy the recent weather. We are writing to share some important updates regarding our public library services for the upcoming month. Our goal remains to provide accessible and meaningful resources for every member of our community, regardless of age or background.
We are proud to announce the expanded hours for our digital literacy workshops. These sessions are designed to help residents navigate online databases, e-book platforms, and municipal service portals. Beginners are especially welcome, and no prior experience is required to join us. Volunteers will be available to offer one-on-one assistance during these drop-in hours on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons.
Furthermore, we are increasing our collection of audiobooks and large-print materials in response to recent community requests. These additions ensure that our library remains inclusive and accessible to patrons with varying visual needs or learning styles. We have also secured new grants to support local youth initiatives, including after-school homework clubs and art programs for teenagers.
Please note that our main building will be closed for one day next week for essential HVAC maintenance. During this time, please direct any urgent inquiries to our public access terminals at the neighboring community center. We apologize for any inconvenience this brief closure may cause and appreciate your patience as we work to maintain a safe and comfortable space.
We look forward to seeing you at the library soon. Your support and engagement are vital to the success of our programs. For more information or to register for workshops, please visit our website or call our front desk during regular business hours. Thank you for being part of our library family.
Sincerely,
The Public Library Staff

raw:
baby sleep routines

Establishing a consistent sleep routine for your baby can feel like searching for the holy grail of parenthood. The quest for predictable naps and a full night's rest is a common goal for many new families, and for good reason. A well-structured routine offers numerous benefits, not just for your little one but for your entire household.

Routines provide babies with a sense of security and predictability. When they know what to expect next, it helps them wind down and prepare for sleep, reducing anxiety and making bedtime battles less likely. For parents, a routine creates much-needed structure in what can often feel like a chaotic new chapter, allowing for personal time or planning.

A typical evening routine might involve a warm bath, a gentle massage, a final feed, followed by a quiet activity like reading a board book or singing a soft lullaby. The specific elements are less important than the order and consistency. Repeating these steps nightly signals to your baby that sleep is approaching, helping their body and mind prepare.

It's vital to remember that a routine is not a rigid schedule fixed to the clock. Instead, think of it as a predictable sequence of events. Babies aren't robots; they will have off days, growth spurts, and teething issues that will disrupt even the most established patterns. Flexibility and responsiveness to your baby's unique needs are key to success.

Starting a gentle routine can begin as early as six to eight weeks, though some parents prefer to wait a little longer. The key is to introduce elements gradually and observe your baby's cues. Patience is paramount; it takes time for both you and your baby to learn and adapt to new patterns, so don't get discouraged by initial setbacks.

Ultimately, the goal of a baby sleep routine is to foster healthy sleep habits that can last for years, providing rest and peace for everyone. It's a journey of trial and error, but with consistency, warmth, and understanding, you can create a comforting bedtime ritual that benefits your entire family.

raw:
houseplant care

Many new home gardeners discover that keeping plants alive is far more nuanced than simply placing them in a pot and waiting for them to flourish. The struggle often stems from a misunderstanding of basic biological needs, leading to over-enthusiastic watering or neglect. It is essential to recognize that houseplants are miniature ecosystems that respond directly to their environment. By understanding the specific requirements of your chosen green companions, you can transform a generic living room into a thriving indoor garden. The first step toward success is educating yourself on the unique characteristics of each species, as no single care routine fits all plants.

Light is the most critical factor in determining the health and vigor of your foliage. Most houseplants do not require intense direct sunlight, which can scorch delicate leaves, but they do need a consistent source of brightness. A north-facing window provides gentle, indirect light suitable for tolerant species like snake plants or pothos. Conversely, tropical varieties such as monsteras or philodendrons thrive in bright, filtered light. If you notice your plants stretching toward the window with long, sparse growth, this is a clear signal that they are hungry for more illumination. Rotating your pots weekly ensures even growth and prevents the plant from leaning awkwardly toward the light source.

Watering is perhaps the most common cause of houseplant death, usually due to excess rather than deficiency. Overwatering suffocates the roots by depriving them of oxygen, leading to rot that kills the plant from the inside out. Before you reach for the watering can, always check the top two inches of soil. If it feels dry, it is time to water. However, if it remains damp, wait another day. Proper drainage is non-negotiable for this process. Ensure your pots have holes in the bottom and use a well-aerated potting mix designed specifically for indoor plants. Standard garden soil compacts too densely and retains too much moisture, creating a perfect environment for mold and bacterial growth.

Feeding your plants does not mean pouring a bucket of fertilizer into the soil every week. Houseplants generally require nutrients on a seasonal schedule that mirrors their natural growth cycles. During the spring and summer, when plants are actively producing new leaves and stems, a balanced liquid fertilizer applied once a month is usually sufficient. Fertilizer contains salt, and over-application causes these salts to accumulate in the potting mix, burning the root tips. In contrast, during the fall and winter months, many plants enter a dormant phase. During this time, they need very little to no additional nutrients, as they are focusing energy on maintenance rather than expansion. Forgetting to fertilize during the active growing season leads to pale, weak growth, while over-fertilizing during dormancy wastes resources and risks damaging the plant.

Pruning and dusting are often overlooked aspects of care that significantly impact plant health and aesthetics. Dead or yellowing leaves do not heal; they become points of entry for pests and diseases. Regularly trimming these back with clean shears encourages the plant to direct its energy toward healthy new growth. Additionally, dust accumulation on leaf surfaces blocks stomata, the tiny pores that allow the plant to breathe and exchange gases. A gentle wipe with a damp cloth or a quick rinse under lukewarm shower water cleans the leaves and helps the plant photosynthesize more efficiently. These simple maintenance tasks, when performed consistently, create a resilient plant that can better withstand minor environmental fluctuations and thrive year after year.

Regularly trimming these back with clean shears encourages the plant to direct its energy toward healthy new growth. Additionally, dust accumulation on leaf surfaces blocks stomata, the tiny pores that allow the plant to breathe and exchange gases. A gentle wipe with a damp cloth or a quick rinse under lukewarm shower water cleans the leaves and helps the plant photosynthesize more efficiently. Alex

vaccine schedule overview

Vaccines are one of the most effective tools for protecting public health, and understanding the recommended schedule helps families keep children and adults safe from preventable diseases. The routine immunization program begins shortly after birth and continues through adolescence, with each dose timed to maximize immune response while minimizing side effects. Health authorities such as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention regularly review data to adjust timing and composition, ensuring that the schedule reflects the latest scientific evidence.

For infants, the first series of shots typically starts at two months of age, covering diseases like diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and the first doses of the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine. A second set follows at four months, and a third at six months, each reinforcing immunity as the child's immune system matures. The schedule also includes the rotavirus vaccine, administered orally, which protects against severe gastroenteritis in the first year of life.

By the time a child reaches their first birthday, a booster dose of measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) is usually given, along with the final dose of the varicella (chickenpox) vaccine and a fourth pneumococcal dose. The pre-school period, around four to six years of age, often includes another MMR booster and a dose of the DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis) vaccine. These boosters help sustain protection until the adolescent schedule begins.

Adolescents receive vaccines that address risks specific to teenage years, such as human papillomavirus (HPV) and meningococcal disease. The HPV series is typically started at age 11 or 12, with two doses spaced several months apart, while the meningococcal conjugate vaccine is given around the same age, with a booster at 16. Many schools also require a tetanus booster at age 11, known as Tdap.

Adults are not exempt from immunizations; boosters for tetanus and diphtheria are recommended every ten years, and a single dose of shingles vaccine is advised for those over 50. Seasonal influenza shots should be received annually, especially for people with chronic health conditions. By following the schedule and staying up to date with boosters, individuals contribute to community immunity and reduce the likelihood of outbreaks.

.

Dong Hong

Dong Hong (Chinese: 董宏; pinyin: Dǒng Hóng; born November 1953) is a former Chinese politician. He was investigated by China's top anti-graft agency in October 2020. He was a senior disciplinary inspector under Wang Qishan until 2017, when Wang was chief of China's top anti-corruption agency, the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI).

Home | About | Contact

Dong was born in Haicheng, Liaoning, in November 1953. After graduating from the Renmin University of China, he joined the Central Advisory Commission as a secretary of Bo Yibo, the then vice chairman. In 1992, he was transferred to Foshan, Guangdong and appointed assistant mayor. One year later, he was transferred back to Beijing and became deputy director and then director of the Institute of Contemporary China Studies. In 1998, he was deputy director of the Development Research Center of Guangdong Provincial People's Government. Ta Kung Pao reported in 2014 that Dong had a long-term working relationship with Wang Qishan beginning in 1998, sharing stints in Guangdong, Hainan and Beijing, and at the now defunct State Council General Office of Economic Reform. In March 2006 he was promoted to become deputy director of the Party Documents Research Office of Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party. After Wang Qishan became Secretary of the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, Dong became one of the group leaders of central inspection groups during Xi Jinping's first term.

On October 2, 2020, he was under investigation for "suspected serious violation of laws and party rules", according to a terse statement by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI), the party's internal disciplinary body, and the National Supervisory Commission, the highest anti-corruption agency of China. On April 25, 2021, he was detained by the Supreme People's Procuratorate. On June 8, he was indicted on suspicion of accepting bribes. On August 26, he stood trial at the Intermediate People's Court of Qingdao on charges of taking bribes. The public prosecutors accused him of abusing his multiple positions between 1999 and 2020 in Guangdong, Hainan and Beijing to seek favor on behalf of certain organizations and individuals in matters of project contracting, project development and job promotions. In return, he accepted money and gifts worth more than 460 million yuan ($71 million) directly or through his relatives. On January 28, 2022, he was sentenced to death with a two-year reprieve for bribery by Qingdao Intermediate People's Court. He was also deprived of his political rights for life, and ordered by the court to have all his personal assets confiscated and turn over all illicit gains and their interests to the state.
