Sincerely, John the Ghost

Sincerely, John the Ghost is the debut extended play recorded by American indie rock singer John O'Callaghan under his alias John the Ghost. He released the EP on April 29, 2016. "Sour Grapes" was released as the first and only single from the EP.

O'Callaghan began going under the moniker John the Ghost in 2016. He wrote and recorded Sincerely, John the Ghost in his bedroom. "Sour Grapes" was released as the first single from the EP on April 12, 2016. To accompany the record, O'Callaghan also released a book of poetry titled the same name of his EP.

Jenna Romaine of idobi Radio gave the EP an A+ rating. She stated, "unsurprisingly, what shines the most are the lyrics." She also stated that the EP feels "candid and sincere," and is bound to "capture listeners and keep them wanting more." She ended off remarking, "this is a debut EP you'll want to be able to keep re-living and re-playing." Alternative Press named the EP as one of the solo projects to check out in 2016.

warranty terms

Understanding warranty terms is essential whenever you buy a new product, from electronics to home appliances. A warranty is a promise from the maker or seller to repair or replace a defective item within a set period, and the wording determines how that promise is applied.

Most standard warranties last twelve months from the purchase date, though premium models may enjoy longer coverage. The agreement will state whether it is a limited or full warranty and if it covers parts, labor, or both. Some brands also sell extended plans for an extra fee.

Coverage typically excludes damage caused by misuse, accidents, or unauthorized repairs, as well as cosmetic blemishes and normal wear and tear. Consumable components such as batteries are often not covered. Reading the fine print early helps you avoid surprises when a claim is needed.

To file a claim you usually need the original receipt, the product's serial number, and a clear description of the defect. Contact the manufacturer's support line or submit an online request, then follow any instructions to ship the item to an authorized service center.

Keep records of all communications, register the product promptly, and note the warranty expiration date. Understanding the specific terms turns a potential headache into a straightforward resolution, ensuring you receive the protection you paid for without hidden surprises in the future.

Subject: A New Friend Awaits - Adopt a Pet Today
Dear [Recipient Name],
I hope this message finds you well. As we approach the spring season, our shelter is experiencing an influx of animals looking for a permanent home, and I wanted to share a few stories that might inspire you.
First, meet Bella, a three-year-old Labrador mix who was rescued from a busy road. She's gentle, well-trained, and loves long walks in the park. Families who have adopted her say she instantly became the heart of their home.
Next is Milo, a shy kitten who arrived with a litter of four. After two weeks of quiet observation, he began to trust his caregivers, now following them from room to room and purring loudly when you sit down.
Adopting a pet is more than a simple transaction; it creates a lasting bond that benefits both animal and owner. Studies show that companionship reduces stress, encourages daily exercise, and even improves cardiovascular health over time.
If you feel ready to welcome a new friend, please visit our website or stop by the shelter during open hours. Our volunteers are happy to answer any questions, arrange a meet-and-greet, and guide you through the adoption process.
Thank you for considering adoption and giving a deserving animal a second chance at a happy life. I look forward to hearing from you and helping you find the perfect match.
Warm regards,
[Your Name]
Animal Welfare Coordinator

Subject: Update on Weekend Trail Conditions and Safety Alerts
Hi Friends,
I am writing this quick update to share the latest information regarding the trail conditions for the upcoming weekend. Since the heavy rains from last Tuesday, the lower sections of the ridge have become significantly more unstable than usual. We have received several reports from early morning hikers indicating that the mud has turned into slick, deep muck, particularly near the river crossing at mile marker four. If you are planning to attempt the main loop, please be aware that the usual solid footing is no longer available, and traction will be your primary concern for the first few miles of the ascent.
The upper switchbacks remain relatively dry due to the rocky terrain, but caution is still advised. A small section of the boardwalk near the overlook was damaged by the recent storms and is currently under repair by the park crew. You will need to take the designated detour path marked with bright orange ribbons. This alternate route adds approximately twenty minutes to your hike but is safe and well-maintained. Please do not attempt to bypass this closure, as the ground beneath is soft and poses a risk of injury if fallen.
Regarding wildlife, we have seen an increase in deer activity in the middle meadows. This is not a safety threat, but keep in mind that maintaining a standard distance is best for both your safety and theirs. The forest floor is noisy with the sound of moving water, so if you are hiking with small children, please ensure they remain within arm's reach near the ravine edges where the ground is eroded. The official rescue team has noted that response times may be longer than usual due to the waterlogged access roads for their vehicles.
Weather forecasts suggest clear skies for Saturday, with highs in the mid-eighties, which will help dry out the trails slightly. However, Sunday morning is expected to bring a light shower, which will likely turn the wooden stairs into a slip-and-fall hazard. I would strongly recommend scheduling your long hike for Saturday if at all possible. If you do choose to go on Sunday, bring non-slip hiking shoes and consider using trekking poles for extra stability on the wet surfaces.
Please share this information with any group members who may have missed the official park newsletter. For the most current real-time updates, check the local trail conditions board or the park's radio channel before you head out. Let's all enjoy the fresh air and beautiful scenery while prioritizing our safety and respecting the fragile environment we are so lucky to explore.
Safe trails,
Alex

Bi Community News

Bi Community News (commonly shortened to BCN) is a bimonthly magazine, and the United Kingdom's only magazine serving the bisexual population. It is published bimonthly and includes many articles reflecting bisexual life and media representation as well as news from the bisexual community. Resulting from a workshop at the UK BiCon in 1995, it started as a zine moving to being a full-colour glossy magazine around 2010. It has been consistently published since October 1995. The current editor is Jen Yockney MBE. Previous UK bisexual journals were BiFrost (1991-1995) and Bi Monthly in the 1980s.

Each issue of Bi Community News has a mixture of regular columns and topical or one-off articles, interviews and features. A "serialised short story", Fixation, ran for two years.

This appears every issue and reports on bi representation on television and in film, in newspaper articles and on radio. It is mostly focused on UK media but includes items from the rest of the world in some editions.

This is a regular column since 2015, highlighting new research on bisexuality, and exploring the bi data within general and LGBT research. The title was the draft working name for the 2012 Bisexuality Report, which brought together research on bisexuality in the UK.

Each edition lists national and local bi or bi-relevant organisations in the UK and Ireland. There is also a section on popular resources on research and advice, and upcoming bisexual community events dates.

When Bi Community News switched from a newsletter/zine format to mainstream magazine in style it changed from text covers to photo covers. Featured "cover bis" include both members of the UK bisexual community and people in the public eye who are either out as bisexual or have played bi characters in TV and film.

In 2001 BCN published "An A-Z of Bi Group Running", a resource for helping build local community support. It was written by Jen Yockney based on five years of organising Manchester-based bisexual community group BiPhoria and BiCon workshops about bi group organising. A fundraising erotic stories compilation, "Salacious Stories for Boys and Girls" in 2005, was followed in 2006 by a one-off fundraising calendar with photos of activists from around the UK working on different parts of advancing bi representation and support. In 2007 BCN published "Both Directions", a 20-page guide to the UK bisexual scene and its history, as well as bi books, films and other resources. Further editions were published each year until 2011 when BiPhoria published "Getting Bi In A Gay / Straight World". BCN's website recommended that over their own Both Directions title as more accessible.

BCN was shortlisted for Community Group or Organisation of the Year in the 2011 Homo Hero Awards, alongside Outdoor Lads and the Albert Kennedy Trust.

Bi Community News (commonly shortened to BCN) is a bimonthly magazine, and the United Kingdom's only magazine serving the bisexual population. It is published bimonthly and includes many articles reflecting bisexual life and media representation as well as news from the bisexual community. Resulting from a workshop at the UK BiCon in 1995, it started as a zine moving to being a full-colour glossy magazine around 2010. It has been consistently published since October 1995. The current editor is Jen Yockney MBE. Previous UK bisexual journals were BiFrost (1991-1995) and Bi Monthly in the 1980s.
Each issue of Bi Community News has a mixture of regular columns and topical or one-off articles, interviews and features. A "serialised short story", Fixation, ran for two years.
This appears every issue and reports on bi representation on television and in film, in newspaper articles and on radio. It is mostly focused on UK media but includes items from the rest of the world in some editions.
This is a regular column since 2015, highlighting new research on bisexuality, and exploring the bi data within general and LGBT research. The title was the draft working name for the 2012 Bisexuality Report, which brought together research on bisexuality in the UK.
Each edition lists national and local bi or bi-relevant organisations in the UK and Ireland. There is also a section on popular resources on research and advice, and upcoming bisexual community events dates.
When Bi Community News switched from a newsletter/zine format to mainstream magazine in style it changed from text covers to photo covers. Featured "cover bis" include both members of the UK bisexual community and people in the public eye who are either out as bisexual or have played bi characters in TV and film.
In 2001 BCN published "An A-Z of Bi Group Running", a resource for helping build local community support. It was written by Jen Yockney based on five years of organising Manchester-based bisexual community group BiPhoria and BiCon workshops about bi group organising. A fundraising erotic stories compilation, "Salacious Stories for Boys and Girls" in 2005, was followed in 2006 by a one-off fundraising calendar with photos of activists from around the UK working on different parts of advancing bi representation and support. In 2007 BCN published "Both Directions", a 20-page guide to the UK bisexual scene and its history, as well as bi books, films and other resources. Further editions were published each year until 2011 when BiPhoria published "Getting Bi In A Gay / Straight World". BCN's website recommended that over their own Both Directions title as more accessible.
BCN was shortlisted for Community Group or Organisation of the Year in the 2011 Homo Hero Awards, alongside Outdoor Lads and the Albert Kennedy Trust.

Paul Edwin Hinrichs (August 31, 1925 - April 9, 2023) was an American baseball player who was briefly a relief pitcher for the Boston Red Sox of Major League Baseball during the 1951 season. After his baseball career, Hinrichs became a Lutheran minister.

Hinrichs was born to a family of German descent in Marengo, Iowa, the son of a Lutheran pastor, on August 31, 1925. He attended Concordia College in Saint Paul, Minnesota, and enrolled at Concordia Seminary in Clayton, Missouri in 1943. He married Frances Rauscher in 1948, and they had five children, one of whom predeceased him.

Hinrichs was signed to the Detroit Tigers organization in 1946, and first played in the West Texas-New Mexico League before going to the Dallas Rangers, the Tigers' Double A team. In 1948, ten minor league players within the Tigers farm system, including Hinrichs, were declared free agents after an investigation by Baseball Commissioner Happy Chandler found that the organization was keeping more players in their farm system than they were permitted to. Hinrichs then signed with the New York Yankees, and was the first player to be given a signing bonus by the team. The bonus was reported to be $75,000 at the time, though later estimates varied, and in a 2015 interview, Hinrichs only said that it was above $50,000. He played for their Double-A affiliate, the Kansas City Blues. However, his performance was hampered by an injury, and in the Rule 5 draft after the 1950 season, he was drafted by the Boston Red Sox. In four appearances for the Red Sox in the 1951 season, Hinrichs posted a 21.60 earned run average with one strikeout and four walks in 31⁄3 innings pitched, without recording a decision. In the months after his last major league game on June 21, 1951, he was optioned to the San Francisco Seals, before he decided to leave baseball at the end of the year.

Hinrichs followed his father's career and became a Lutheran minister. He was ordained at Our Redeemer Lutheran Church in Augusta, Georgia, on September 14, 1952. Hinrichs was sent to open a church in Aiken, South Carolina, followed by one in La Puente, California, before returning to St. Louis. He opened a congregation in Litchfield, Illinois, before retiring at age 63 and moving to Kentucky. Hinrichs died at a hospital in Greenville, Kentucky, on April 9, 2023, at age 97.

The chemical industry in Bangladesh is a small part of the overall industrial base of the country. Major sectors of chemical production in Bangladesh include pharmaceutical production, fertilizers, refineries, inorganic chemicals and some specialty chemicals.

Bangladesh has quite a few government run as well as private fertilizer factories. These include: Triple Super Phosphate Complex Limited, DAP Fertilizer Company Limited etc.

The biggest chemical industry in terms of contribution to GDP is the pharmaceutical industry in Bangladesh. The industry has many state of the art pharmaceutical production plants. There are also a few API plants with others in construction.

This employee handbook section outlines the fundamental responsibilities of staff members regarding workplace safety and immediate incident response. While our primary goal is to prevent accidents through proper protocols and maintenance, every employee must be prepared to act in the initial moments following an injury. Adequate training in first aid is not merely a compliance requirement but a critical component of a safe work environment. By understanding basic techniques, you can stabilize an injured colleague, prevent further harm, and buy valuable time for professional medical teams to arrive on the scene.

The first step in any emergency is to ensure your own safety before approaching the victim. Assess the area for hazards such as electrical wires, chemical spills, or unstable structures. Do not become a secondary victim. Once the scene is secure, check the responsiveness of the injured person. If they are unconscious, call for emergency services immediately, specifically instructing the dispatcher to send an ambulance. If the person is conscious, ask detailed questions about the nature of the injury and any known allergies or medical conditions.

For minor cuts and abrasions, cleanliness is the most important factor in preventing infection. Remove any visible debris gently, rinse the wound with clean water, and apply a sterile dressing. Do not attempt to wash deep wounds with high-pressure water, as this can damage tissue further. For bleeding that is not arterial, apply direct pressure with a clean cloth or bandage. Continue applying firm pressure for several minutes. If the blood soaks through, add more layers on top; do not remove the initial layer to check the wound.

In cases of suspected burns, do not apply ice, butter, or other home remedies that can cause additional tissue damage. Instead, run cool running water over the burn for at least ten minutes to lower the skin temperature and reduce pain. Cover the area loosely with a sterile, non-adhesive cloth or保鲜膜. If the burn is extensive or involves the face, hands, or genitals, seek immediate professional medical attention regardless of its apparent severity. Never remove clothing that is stuck to the skin, as this can cause further injury and exacerbate the situation.

Regular refreshers on these procedures are mandatory for all staff members. We will hold quarterly workshops where employees can practice these skills under supervision. Stay alert, remain calm, and act with purpose during emergencies. Your quick and correct response can significantly improve recovery outcomes and save lives. Familiarize yourself with the location of the nearest first aid kit, AED, and emergency exits in your specific work area. Preparedness is continuous, and maintaining knowledge is just as important as the physical ability to perform these tasks when needed.

Preparation is the cornerstone of a successful job interview. Candidates who arrive unprepared often find themselves struggling to connect their past experiences with the specific requirements of the role they are seeking. It is essential to spend at least two full days researching the company before the interview takes place. This goes beyond skimming the "About Us" page on the corporate website. You should delve into recent press releases, industry news articles, and the company's social media channels to understand their current strategic initiatives, major challenges, and corporate culture. Knowing who your interviewer is and what they have achieved in their own career also allows you to tailor your responses in a way that resonates with their professional interests and management style. This depth of knowledge demonstrates genuine interest and helps you move beyond generic answers that hiring managers hear repeatedly from other applicants.

When formulating your responses, structure them using proven frameworks such as the Situational, Task, Action, and Result model. This approach ensures that every answer you provide is grounded in concrete evidence rather than vague assurances of your capabilities. Start by briefly describing the specific situation you faced at a previous job, outlining the exact task you were assigned. Then, focus heavily on the actions you personally took to resolve the issue, using active verbs to highlight your agency. Finally, conclude with a measurable result, such as a percentage increase in efficiency, a cost saving figure, or a customer satisfaction metric. This method not only organizes your thoughts logically but also provides the interviewer with a clear narrative that showcases your problem-solving skills and tangible impact on business outcomes.

Dressing appropriately for the interview is a non-negotiable aspect of making a strong first impression. While every industry has its own norms, the general rule is to dress one level above the daily attire of the employees you will be working with. For most corporate environments, this means wearing tailored business formal wear for men and professional business attire for women. Ensure that your clothing is clean, pressed, and free of visible wrinkles. Pay close attention to grooming standards, as neat hair, trimmed nails, and subtle fragrance convey attention to detail and professionalism. If the company culture appears very casual based on their online presence, you might opt for smart casual, but it is always safer to err on the side of formality. Your appearance should support your message, not distract from it, so avoid overly bright colors or flashy accessories that might draw the eye away from your qualifications.

During the actual conversation, active listening is just as important as speaking. Many candidates focus too much on what they want to say next, effectively tuning out the interviewer's nuances. Instead, maintain steady, comfortable eye contact and nod occasionally to show engagement. If you do not understand a question, it is perfectly acceptable to ask for clarification rather than guessing at the intent. This demonstrates intellectual honesty and confidence. Additionally, be mindful of your body language. Sit up straight, keep your hands visible on the table, and avoid fidgeting or crossing your arms tightly, which can be interpreted as defensive or closed off. Your physical presence should mirror the confidence and openness you aim to convey in your verbal responses, creating a cohesive and trustworthy impression.

Finally, the question of "Do you have any questions for us" is a critical opportunity that is often wasted. Never say you have no questions, as this suggests a lack of curiosity or genuine interest in the position. Prepare three to five insightful questions that reflect your research. Ask about the team's dynamic, the specific goals for the first ninety days in the role, or the biggest challenge the department is currently facing. These types of questions show that you are thinking about your contribution to the team and the long-term success of the department. Avoid asking about salary, benefits, or vacation time in the first interview, as these topics are better suited for a later stage of the hiring process when a verbal offer has been extended. Ending the meeting on a high note with meaningful inquiries leaves a lasting positive impression and reinforces your candidacy.

Changan UNI-V

The Changan UNI-V is the third product of the UNI-series, and also the first fastback of the series. It was first unveiled to the public during the 2021 Guangzhou Auto Show. The Changan UNI-V was developed on the new lightweight Modular Platform Architecture, also called as Ark Architecture. The platform is the base of the highly rigid and lightweight body of the UNI-V according to Changan Automobile. The Ark architecture also offers six airbags and the white body chassis is 70% high-strength steel.

The Changan UNI-V is powered by a 1.5 liter turbo engine developed by Changan Automobile inhouse with a maximum power of 138 kW (185 hp; 188 PS) and a maximum speed of 205 km/h (127 mph).

The interior design of the UNI-V adopts a 3+1 quadruple screen layout design. The hovering instrument panel is placed above the steering wheel, displaying high-frequency interactive information such as speed and navigation from the instrument panel with a 10° eye movement when looking at the road ahead.

The Changan UNI-V iDD launched in April 2024 is the plug-in hybrid version of the Changan UNI-V sedan featuring an upgraded powertrain and redesigned bumpers. The UNI-V iDD was originally planned to be a rebadged model sold under the Changan Nevo brand, called the A06. Images of the A06 were published, but plans were changed before launch and was sold as a variant of the UNI-V instead. The iDD plug-in hybrid system powertrain of the UNI-V iDD is composed of a 1.5 liter engine and a front positioned electric motor, mated to an E-CVT gearbox. The 1.5 liter engine has a maximum power output of 81 kW and a peak 143 Nm while the front positioned electric motor develops 158 kW and 330 Nm. The top speed of the UNI-V iDD is 185 km/h and the 0 to 100 km/h acceleration time is 6.9 seconds. The battery is a 18.99kWh or 18.4kWh lithium iron phosphate providing a CLTC pure electric range of 136 km while the combined CLTC range is 1,160 km. Charge the battery from 30% to 80% takes 30 minutes under DC fast charging.

Subject: Weekly Roundup: Digital Minimalism and Sustainable Travel
Hi everyone,
It is absolutely wonderful to see so many of you joining us for another edition of the newsletter. This week feels particularly special as we navigate through a busy period for several of our industry partners. We have curated a selection of stories, tips, and insights that we believe offer genuine value to your professional and personal lives. Whether you are looking to streamline your workflow or seeking inspiration for your next project, this issue is packed with content designed to save you time and spark new ideas. We read through dozens of sources to pick the best, so you don't have to wade through the noise.
One of the standout articles this week comes from a prominent tech publication discussing the rise of digital minimalism. The piece argues that our constant connectivity is not only draining our mental Energy but also hindering our creative output. The author suggests practical steps for implementing a digital fast, such as turning off non-essential notifications and dedicating specific hours to deep work without screen interruptions. I found this resonant because, as you know, we often talk about productivity, but true efficiency comes from focused attention. It is a concept worth revisiting, especially if you feel like your day is being chopped into unmanageable fragments by endless pings and alerts.
On the sustainability front, there is fascinating news coming out of the travel sector. A major airline has announced a significant investment in sustainable aviation fuel, aiming to reduce carbon emissions by a substantial percentage over the next decade. While critics argue that this is still not enough to meet urgent climate targets, the scale of the commitment is undeniable. The article details the technical challenges of producing bio-fuel at scale and the logistical hurdles of integrating it into existing fueling infrastructure. For professionals in logistics or energy, this report offers a detailed breakdown of the supply chain implications that are often overlooked in higher-level sustainability discussions.
We also wanted to highlight a small business success story that caught our attention. A local bakery that started with a simple Instagram account has grown into a multi-location brand without ever having to take on venture capital. The founder shared her philosophy on slow growth and building direct relationships with customers. It is a refreshing counter-narrative to the big-tech hype that dominates much of our coverage. Her approach emphasizes quality over quantity and values long-term community engagement over viral marketing tactics. This perspective is highly relevant for any entrepreneur or small business owner who might feel pressured to scale rapidly at the expense of their core values.
Finally, we have a few quick resources for those interested in remote work ergonomics and home office setup. There is a comprehensive guide on optimizing lighting for video calls and a breakdown of affordable standing desk options that do not sacrifice comfort. These small adjustments can make a notable difference in reducing fatigue during long working hours. Please feel free to share this issue with colleagues or friends who might find these insights helpful. We always welcome your feedback and story suggestions for future editions. Thank you for reading and staying connected with us through another busy week.
Best regards,
The Editorial Team

Netted Ware culture

The Netted Ware culture (also called Textile Ceramic culture) was a Bronze Age culture in northeastern Europe that extended from Finland to the upper Volga region in Russia.

The Netted Ware culture emerged around 1900 BCE with the arrival of the Seima-Turbino phenomenon in the upper Volga region, replacing the earlier Volosovo cultures, and soon expanded to the west to Karelia and eastern and central Finland. The Netted Ware culture did not reach southwestern Finland, the area of the Kiukainen culture and later the Nordic Bronze culture. The subsistence of the Netted Ware culture was based on small-scale swidden agriculture and animal husbandry.

The spread of the Netted Ware culture has been linked to the dispersal of early forms of the Finno-Volgaic languages, especially Finnic languages and Saami languages.

restaurant opening hours

Few pieces of information are as crucial to a potential diner as a restaurant's opening hours. It's the very first filter people apply when deciding where to eat, often before even considering the menu or price point. A quick search on a phone, a glance at a website, or a peek at a storefront sign can either guide a hungry customer to your door or send them searching elsewhere.

Today's diners expect instant and accurate information. They aren't likely to call a restaurant just to ask about hours. Instead, they consult Google Maps, the restaurant's official website, social media pages, and various third-party listing sites. The expectation is that wherever they look, the information will be correct and consistent, ensuring their journey ends with a delicious meal, not a closed door.

For restaurant owners, managing opening hours isn't always as straightforward as it seems. Holidays, special events, private bookings, seasonal changes in demand, and even unexpected staffing challenges can all necessitate adjustments to regular schedules. The dynamic nature of the hospitality industry means that what was true last week might not be true today, requiring constant vigilance.

The real challenge often lies in disseminating these changes across all the platforms customers might check. Updating a website is one thing, but ensuring your Google Business Profile, Facebook page, Instagram bio, and any other relevant listing sites are also current requires a disciplined approach. A single outdated entry can lead to significant frustration for an eager customer.

The consequences of inaccurate opening hours can be surprisingly severe. A customer who arrives to find a restaurant unexpectedly closed doesn't just miss a meal; they often feel misled and disappointed. This can lead to negative online reviews, a damaged reputation, and, most importantly, the loss of potential repeat business. Trust is hard to earn and easy to lose.

To foster a positive customer experience, restaurants should prioritize clear and consistent communication regarding their hours. This means regularly auditing all online listings, prominently displaying hours on their physical premises, and utilizing social media to announce any temporary changes or special holiday schedules well in advance. Proactive updates build reliability.

Ultimately, accurate opening hours are more than just a logistical detail; they are a fundamental component of customer service. They streamline the dining experience, build trust, and ensure that when a customer decides to visit, they are met with a welcoming, open door, ready to serve them. It's a small effort with a massive impact on both satisfaction and success.

Subject: Water Quality Report - Findings and Recommendations
Dear Team,
Our latest water quality analysis for the municipal supply covering the period from July 1 to September 30 has been completed. The data indicate that most parameters remain within the EPA's safe drinking water standards, with turbidity and pH levels showing slight fluctuations but staying within acceptable limits.
However, we observed a modest increase in nitrate concentrations at three monitoring sites, reaching 9.5 mg/L, which approaches the maximum contaminant level of 10 mg/L. This rise appears correlated with recent agricultural runoff following heavy rains. While the current levels are not yet hazardous, they warrant close observation and possibly preventive measures.
In contrast, bacterial counts, including E. coli, were undetectable across all samples, confirming the continued efficacy of our disinfection processes. Chlorine residuals were stable at 0.5 mg/L, providing a reliable barrier against microbial contamination throughout the distribution network.
Based on these findings, I recommend that we enhance runoff mitigation strategies in the affected watershed, such as buffer strips and timed fertilizer applications, to curb nitrate inputs. Additionally, a follow-up sampling campaign should be scheduled for early next year to verify trends and assess the impact of any remedial actions.
Please review the attached detailed report and let me know if you have any questions or need further clarification. I look forward to discussing the next steps at our upcoming operations meeting.
Best regards,
Laura Martinez 
Environmental Compliance Officer 
City Water Services

tenant association meeting

The annual tenant association meeting at the Oakwood Apartments complex took place on a rainy Tuesday evening, drawing a surprisingly robust crowd of residents from the four buildings. The community room, usually reserved for quarterly check-ins, was packed with neighbors who had been waiting for the new property management team to outline their plans for the upcoming fiscal year. Tension was palpable as attendees settled into the rows of folding chairs, eager to voice concerns that had simmered for months regarding maintenance response times and parking enforcement.

Mayor of the association, Sarah Jenkins, opened the session by acknowledging the prolonged backlog of repair requests. She emphasized that while the previous administration struggled with staffing constraints, the new directors have already initiated a partnership with an external HVAC specialist to address the frequent heating complaints. This immediate action was met with cautious optimism, though many residents remained skeptical, citing past promises that rarely materialized into tangible improvements within the stipulated deadlines.

A significant portion of the agenda was dedicated to the proposed increase in the monthly amenity fee. The board explained that the current revenue stream was insufficient to maintain the swimming pool and fitness center, which had fallen into disrepair. Residents questioned why these facilities were not included in the base rent, arguing that they had effectively subsidized these services for years. The discussion grew heated as several tenants pointed out that the breakage of the treadmills and the outdated sauna equipment had reduced the perceived value of their lease agreements.

The motion to approve the $15 monthly surcharge was put to a vote, resulting in a narrow majority in favor. Proponents argued that the additional funds would ensure the long-term sustainability of the shared spaces, preventing further deterioration. Opponents, however, expressed deep disappointment, suggesting that if the fee were to be raised, it should be accompanied by strict service level agreements that guarantee prompt repairs and regular maintenance schedules to justify the extra cost.

As the meeting wound down, the board agreed to release a detailed timeline for the upcoming renovations within the next two weeks. Residents were encouraged to submit written feedback on the parking policy changes before the next scheduled session in three months. The atmosphere at the conclusion was more one of reluctant acceptance than celebration, with many neighbors heading home with a heightened awareness of their collective leverage in future negotiations with the property manager.

chess openings

Home | About | Contact

Chess openings are the first phase of a game, the moment when players lay the foundation for everything that follows. Though the opening can last anywhere from a few moves to a dozen or more, its purpose remains the same: to develop pieces efficiently, control the centre of the board, and safeguard the king. For beginners, learning a handful of solid, well-tested openings can provide a reliable roadmap and boost confidence, while more experienced players use opening theory as a springboard for deeper strategic battles.

One of the most popular openings for White is the Ruy Lopez, a classical system that begins with 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5. By pinning the black knight on c6, White puts immediate pressure on the e5 pawn and prepares to dominate the centre with d4 later on. The Ruy Lopez has been employed by countless world champions, and its many variations-from the quiet Berlin Defense to the sharp Marshall Attack-offer a rich playground for study. Even a simple understanding of the main ideas-rapid development, early castling, and maintaining central tension-can make a big difference in a casual game.

For Black, the Sicilian Defense stands as the most combative response to 1.e4. After 1...c5, Black immediately challenges White's central pawn and invites asymmetrical positions that often lead to sharp, tactical play. The Sicilian branches into numerous lines such as the Najdorf, Dragon, and Scheveningen, each with its own characteristic pawn structures and piece placements. While the sheer volume of theory can be intimidating, focusing on the core concepts-counter-attacking on the queenside, using the half-open c-file, and keeping the king safe-helps players navigate the opening without memorising endless move orders.

When White opts for 1.d4, the Queen's Gambit has enjoyed a renaissance thanks to recent popular culture, but its strategic depth has been appreciated for centuries. By offering the c4 pawn, White aims to tempt Black into accepting a temporary material deficit while White gains rapid piece activity and control over the centre. Declining the gambit with ...e6 or ...c6 leads to the Slav and the Orthodox lines, both of which provide Black with solid, resilient structures. Mastering the basic plans-central breaks with e4 or c5, piece coordination on the long diagonals, and timely exchanges-allows players to handle the opening confidently regardless of Black's choice.

The modern player does not need to memorize dozens of variations to succeed; instead, a focus on universal opening principles pays dividends. Developing knights before bishops, avoiding premature queen moves, and ensuring the king's safety by castling early are timeless guidelines. Moreover, studying model games by strong masters can reveal how strategic ideas emerge from the opening and transition into the middlegame. By integrating a few reliable openings into one's repertoire and consistently applying the underlying principles, any chess enthusiast can turn the opening phase from a source of anxiety into a solid platform for creative and victorious play.

Mark

garden pest control

Dealing with unwanted insects and animals in your landscape can quickly turn a sanctuary into a source of frustration. Whether it is aphids clustering on rose stems, rabbits chewing on young root vegetables, or Japanese beetles decimating foliage, the damage accumulates faster than most homeowners expect. The first step toward effective management is strict identification. Misidentifying a pest often leads to the application of the wrong remedy, which wastes time and money, and can sometimes harm beneficial insects that are actually helping to keep your garden in check. Look closely at the damage patterns and the invaders themselves, perhaps using a magnifying glass or a local extension service guide, to ensure you are targeting the correct organism before making any moves.

Once you know exactly what you are facing, consider integrated pest management techniques that prioritize prevention and minimal chemical intervention. Physical barriers remain one of the most reliable tools in this arsenal. Floating row covers can protect brassicas from cabbage moths, while chicken wire fencing effectively keeps deer and rabbits away from tender growth. For smaller insects, introducing natural predators such as ladybugs or lacewings can tip the ecological balance in your favor. These biological controls are safe for pets and children and help establish a healthier, more resilient ecosystem within your garden beds.

If biological and physical methods are insufficient due to the severity of the infestation, consider using targeted organic treatments. Neem oil, for instance, acts as both a systemic pesticide and an insect repellent, effective against a wide range of soft-bodied insects. Insecticidal soap is another excellent option for aphids and mites, working by dehydrating the pests upon contact. When applying any subduing agent, strictly adhere to the label instructions and apply them during the evening or early morning hours. This timing is crucial because it minimizes contact with pollinators like bees, which are primarily active during the heat of the day, and reduces the rapid volatilization of the product due to direct sunlight.

Consistency is the key to long-term success in garden protection. Pests rarely disappear after a single treatment; populations need to be managed over time to prevent rebound outbreaks. Regularly inspect your plants for early signs of stress or new colonies. Remove any heavily infested plant parts promptly to prevent spread, and maintain a tidy garden free of fallen fruit and standing water, which often attract flies and fungi. Monitoring the environment allows you to react quickly with low-impact solutions before a minor issue escalates into a full-blown crisis that requires harsher chemical interventions.

Finally, view pest presence as a normal part of gardening rather than a failure. Even pristine landscapes will occasionally host insects, and a certain level of biodiversity is natural. By focusing on a balanced approach that combines physical barriers, biological agents, and careful, targeted chemical use when necessary, you can enjoy a thriving vegetable patch or flower bed. The goal is not eradication, which is rarely achievable and often unnecessary, but rather control. With patience and persistent observation, you can cultivate a garden that is vibrant, productive, and largely free from destructive pressure.

raw:
British Borneo

British Borneo comprised the four northern parts of the island of Borneo, which are now the country of Brunei, two Malaysian states of Sabah and Sarawak, and the Malaysian federal territory of Labuan. During the British colonial rule before World War II, Sarawak was known as the Raj of Sarawak (1841-1946), Sabah was known as North Borneo (1881-1946), and Labuan was known as the Crown Colony of Labuan (1848-1946). Between World War II and their independence from Britain, Sarawak became the Crown Colony of Sarawak (1946-1963) whereas Sabah and Labuan combined to form the Crown Colony of North Borneo (1946-1963). The Kingdom of Brunei (1888/1906-1984) was a protectorate of the United Kingdom since the 1888/1906 Protectorate Agreement, and was known as British Protectorate State of Brunei.

Around 1322, the first Christian mission to arrive in northern Borneo was by the Italian Odoric of Pordenone (also mentioned variously as Odorio, Odoric or Odorico Mattiussi). Further, in 1567, North Borneo received another two Jesuit missionaries from the Kingdom of Portugal but was interrupted by the Dutch in 1600, and in 1587, another two Franciscan missionaries from the Spanish East Indies. In 1687, a Theatine missionary named Antonino Ventimiglia was commissioned by Pope Innocent XI to preach Christianity in Borneo, he further lived on the eastern coast of northern Borneo for five years, marking the further chapter of Christian missions within northern Borneo despite earlier struggles to reach the local indigenous natives. The Congregation for the Evangelisation of Peoples decreed on 27 August 1855 the erection of the northern part of the island of Borneo into an independent prefecture of North Borneo and Labuan and entrusted it to Carlos Cuarteroni, a Spaniard. Cuarteron was originally a sea-captain and had vowed, after escaping great peril, to devote himself to the evangelisation of Borneo. He landed at Labuan in 1857, in company with several missionaries who deserted him in 1860. Although alone in the island of Labuan, Cuarteroni continued his labours. At length, seeing that isolation made him powerless, he went to Rome in 1879 to request that the Propaganda place the mission in charge of an institute. From Rome, Cuarteroni went to Spain, where he soon died. The island of Labuan has an area of 30 square miles (78 km2) and contains 6,800 inhabitants; it is an important shipping station between Singapore and Hong Kong. The prefect Apostolic lives at Labuan. The stations served are Labuan and Kuching (Sarawak), the two most important towns. Outside of these two places where the missionaries live ten stations are visited: Sibu, Kanowit, Igan, Oya, Mukah, Baram, Papar, Jesselton, Putatan, and Sandakan. According to the "Missions-Atlas" of P. Streit, the statistics of the Catholic mission in the early 20th century were: 19 regular priests, 2 lay brothers, 15 sisters; 8 churches; 20 chapels; 16 catechists; 14 schools with 740 pupils; 2,600 baptisms; about 1,000 catechumens.

.

The British had obtained the island of Labuan in 1846; they gradually extended their power over the petty rulers of the northern part of Borneo until, in 1888, the British protectorate of North Borneo was formally acknowledged. English speaking missionaries being desired in the British part of Borneo, the Propaganda (19 March 1881) confided the mission of North Borneo and Labuan to the Society for Foreign Missions of Mill Hill, from England. The first prefect Apostolic appointed under the new administration was Thomas Jackson. The society continued in charge of the mission. During the Second World War, the British realised they were unable to defend the colony from the powerful Imperial Japanese Navy. They destroyed the airfields, and especially the oil fields there and in Brunei before the Japanese landed on 16 December 1941. The small British forces surrendered. In 1943, the Chinese population of about 50,000 rebelled against Japan and seized some towns. They were overwhelmed with many executed. Australia sent special operation forces, which trained and armed local militia units and aided the landing of an Australian division in June 1945. Japanese forces numbered about 31,000, and held out until October 1945, long after the Emperor had surrendered.

In 1687, a Theatine missionary named Antonino Ventimiglia was commissioned by Pope Innocent XI to preach Christianity in Borneo, he further lived on the eastern coast of northern Borneo for five years, marking the further chapter of Christian missions within northern Borneo despite earlier struggles to reach the local indigenous natives. The Congregation for the Evangelisation of Peoples decreed on 27 August 1855 the erection of the northern part of the island of Borneo into an independent prefecture of North Borneo and Labuan and entrusted it to Carlos Cuarteroni, a Spaniard. Cuarteron was originally a sea-captain and had vowed, after escaping great peril, to devote himself to the evangelisation of Borneo. He landed at Labuan in 1857, in company with several missionaries who deserted him in 1860. Although alone in the island of Labuan, Cuarteroni continued his labours. At length, seeing that isolation made him powerless, he went to Rome in 1879 to request that the Propaganda place the mission in charge of an institute. From Rome, Cuarteroni went to Spain, where he soon died. The island of Labuan has an area of 30 square miles (78 km2) and contains 6,800 inhabitants; it is an important shipping station between Singapore and Hong Kong. The prefect Apostolic lives at Labuan. The stations served are Labuan and Kuching (Sarawak), the two most important towns. Outside of these two places where the missionaries live ten stations are visited: Sibu, Kanowit, Igan, Oya, Mukah, Baram, Papar, Jesselton, Putatan, and Sandakan. According to the "Missions-Atlas" of P. Streit, the statistics of the Catholic mission in the early 20th century were: 19 regular priests, 2 lay brothers, 15 sisters; 8 churches; 20 chapels; 16 catechists; 14 schools with 740 pupils; 2,600 baptisms; about 1,000 catechumens.
.
The British had obtained the island of Labuan in 1846; they gradually extended their power over the petty rulers of the northern part of Borneo until, in 1888, the British protectorate of North Borneo was formally acknowledged. English speaking missionaries being desired in the British part of Borneo, the Propaganda (19 March 1881) confided the mission of North Borneo and Labuan to the Society for Foreign Missions of Mill Hill, from England. The first prefect Apostolic appointed under the new administration was Thomas Jackson. The society continued in charge of the mission. During the Second World War, the British realised they were unable to defend the colony from the powerful Imperial Japanese Navy. They destroyed the airfields, and especially the oil fields there and in Brunei before the Japanese landed on 16 December 1941. The small British forces surrendered. In 1943, the Chinese population of about 50,000 rebelled against Japan and seized some towns. They were overwhelmed with many executed. Australia sent special operation forces, which trained and armed local militia units and aided the landing of an Australian division in June 1945. Japanese forces numbered about 31,000, and held out until October 1945, long after the Emperor had surrendered.

Aviat Eagle

The Christen Eagle is an aerobatic sporting biplane aircraft that has been produced in the United States since the late 1970s. In the 1990s, it became known as the Aviat Eagle after Aviat Aircraft purchased rights from Christen Industries. As of 2025, the airplane title has reverted back to the Christen Eagle after a newly formed Christen Industries renewed production.

The aircraft was intended to compete with the Pitts Special. Designed by Frank Christensen, originally of Salt Lake City, the Eagle II is marketed in kit form for homebuilding. The Eagle II is a small aircraft of conventional configuration with single-bay, equal-span staggered biplane wings braced with streamlined flying and landing wires and an I-strut to form a box truss. The pilot and a single passenger sit in tandem underneath a large bubble canopy. The tailwheel undercarriage is fixed, with the mainwheels mounted on spring aluminum legs. The main wheels are housed in streamlined fairings. The fuselage and tail are constructed of chromoly steel welded tube, with the forward fuselage skinned in aluminum and the rear fuselage and tail covered in fabric. The wing structure is Sitka spruce wood and fabric covered. The engine cowling is fiberglass. By 2011 over 350 aircraft were flying.

In 1979, the Eagles Aerobatic Team (Charlie Hillard, Tom Poberezny, and Gene Soucy) chose the Christen Eagle as a replacement for their Pitts Special airshow act "The Red Devils". The act continued until 1995. All three Christen Eagles hang from the lobby of the EAA Airventure Museum in Oshkosh, Wisconsin.

Christen Eagle I Single seat variant. Lycoming AEIO-540 260 hp (190 kW). First design model, built at the San Carlos Airport. Four airframes built, one is now based in Dallas Texas, the other 3 are in the EAA Museum in Oshkosh WI. Christen/Aviat Eagle II Most common variant, two seat dual controls. Lycoming AEIO-360.200 hp (150 kW) The first Eagle II produced (Serial #001) is on display at the Connecticut Air & Space Center in Stratford, CT.

Christen Super Eagle I 540 Two built. Lycoming AEIO-540 300 hp (220 kW). Formerly flown by the Iron Eagles aerobatic team, now owned by Professional Pilots based in Texas and Alaska. Christen Super Eagle II Several examples built, two seats, limited fuel tanks.

Data from Jane's All the World's Aircraft 2003-2004General characteristics Crew: Two Length: 17 ft 11 in (5.46 m) Wingspan: 19 ft 11 in (6.07 m) Height: 6 ft 6 in (1.98 m) Wing area: 125.0 sq ft (11.61 m2) Empty weight: 1,025 lb (465 kg) Max takeoff weight: 1,578 lb (716 kg) Fuel capacity: 24 US gal (20 imp gal; 91 L) usable Powerplant: 1 x Textron Lycoming AEIO-360-A1D air-cooled flat-four, 200 hp (150 kW) Propellers: 2-bladed Hartzell HC-C2YK-4/C7666A-2 constant-speed propeller, 6 ft 4 in (1.93 m) diameter Performance

Maximum speed: 184 mph (296 km/h, 160 kn) Cruise speed: 165 mph (266 km/h, 143 kn) Stall speed: 58 mph (93 km/h, 50 kn) Never exceed speed: 210 mph (340 km/h, 180 kn) Range: 437 mi (703 km, 380 nmi) Service ceiling: 17,000 ft (5,200 m) g limits: +9, -6 Roll rate: 187 degree per sec Rate of climb: 2,100 ft/min (11 m/s)

Jackson, Paul, ed. (2003). Jane's All the World's Aircraft 2003-2004. Coulsdon, UK: Jane's Information Group. ISBN 0-7106-2537-5. Taylor, Michael J. H. (1989). Jane's Encyclopedia of Aviation. London: Studio Editions. p. 254. Jane's All the World's Aircraft 1987-88. London: Jane's Yearbooks. pp. 585-85. Manufacturer's website Cavanaugh Flight Museum's Christen Eagle II

poetry workshop

Our upcoming evening session focuses on the delicate art of imagery and sound. Participants will explore how specific sensory details can anchor an abstract emotion, making the poem tangible for the reader. We will spend the first hour analyzing three short works by contemporary poets, identifying the precise nouns and verbs that create resonance. This analytical phase is crucial because it transforms passive reading into active understanding of craft.

The second half of the workshop is dedicated to guided writing. You will receive a prompt centered on a single object found in your immediate surroundings. The goal is not to write a complete poem, but to draft a stanza that captures the texture and weight of that object. Many writers struggle with concrete description, often drifting into cliché. By focusing on one small detail, you avoid the trap of overwriting and discover the natural rhythm of your own voice.

Between sessions, we encourage you to share your draft with at least one peer. Feedback should be specific, asking questions rather than dictating changes. Did the image land? Does the rhythm feel natural? This collaborative environment fosters a sense of community that supports your continued growth. You will learn to receive critique with grace and offer constructive insight to others.

Materials provided include printed copies of selected readings and a comprehensive handout on line breaks and enjambment. No prior experience is required, but a willingness to let go of perfectionism is essential. Bring a notebook and a pen you enjoy using, as the tactile act of writing by hand can unlock different thought processes than typing on a screen.

Registration opens next Monday at eight in the morning. Seats are limited to ensure meaningful discussion for each participant. If you have been feeling stuck or creatively stagnant, this workshop offers a safe space to experiment and refine your technique. Join us for an afternoon dedicated to honoring the power of the written word.

Park am Gleisdreieck

The Park am Gleisdreieck is an inner city public park on former railway land between Kreuzberg and Schöneberg in Berlin, Germany. Developed in stages between 2011 and 2014, it comprises the Ostpark (East Park), the Westpark, and the southern Dora-Duncker Park (formerly "Flaschenhalspark"). The design by Atelier LOIDL integrates lawns and recreational facilities with preserved railway relics and ruderal habitats. The combined area is about 31.5 hectares.

The park stretches from the Landwehr Canal near Potsdamer Platz south to the Yorckbrücken / Monumentenbrücke corridor. A north-south mainline railway divides the site into Ostpark (east) and Westpark (west); Dora-Duncker Park continues the park towards Schöneberger Südgelände Nature Park. Ostpark and Dora-Duncker Park carry long axial paths used by cyclists and walkers, while Westpark opens to adjoining residential streets and includes lawns and multiuse courts.

The park occupies parts of the former Anhalter and Potsdamer freight yards and the historic "railway triangle" (Gleisdreieck). After freight operations declined in the post-war decades, the area became an overgrown wasteland with disused tracks and infrastructure. In the late 1990s the State of Berlin and rail property owners agreed to develop a public park as compensation for nearby redevelopment around Potsdamer and Leipziger Platz.

A two-stage landscape competition (2005-2006) selected the final concept. Works for Ostpark (approx. 17 ha) began in 2008-2009, with opening in September 2011; Westpark (approx. 9-10 ha) was inaugurated on 31 May 2013; and the southern strip, renamed Dora-Duncker Park (approx. 5.5 ha; formerly Flaschenhalspark), opened on 21 March 2014.

The design retains rails, signal posts and sleepers as historic markers within a contemporary framework of meadows, terraces and long benches. Ruderal zones were integrated to support urban biodiversity.

Beach volleyball (Beach61): A large sand-sports complex with numerous courts and supporting facilities operates at Westpark; the "Beach61" brand traces its origins to 2005 and moved to the present site around 2010. Skate elements and plazas: Ostpark includes paved skate features and a pool-style bowl near the former postal signal box; design documentation and reviews note integrated sport tracks and skateable areas. Playgrounds and courts: Facilities include children's play areas, boules lanes and multiuse courts, distributed among meadows and path networks. Paths and cycling: Long paths connect to city cycling routes. Citizens' preferences were taken into account for planning

WTBU (FM)

WTBU (95.3 MHz, "The Bull") is an FM radio station licensed to York Center, Maine, United States. Established in 1987, WTBU is owned by iHeartMedia and serves York County, Maine, and the New Hampshire Seacoast. The station broadcasts a country music format.

The station went on the air in June 1987 as WQMI with a middle of the road format. In 1989, it became WCQL-FM as "Cool 95.3" with an oldies format. That was dropped in August 1996 in favor of a contemporary hit radio format, WXHT ("Heat 95.3"), which placed a heavy emphasis on 1980s new wave hits. That lasted until May 1998, when it went modern rock as "95-3 The Heat" via Radio One Networks. In March 1999, the station changed to a country format, becoming WUBB ("B95.3"). However, WUBB was faced with strong competition from country leader WOKQ, which also had a much stronger signal. WUBB also had a limited local presence when compared to WOKQ. As a result, WUBB never became a big ratings success. On January 10, 2008, the station dropped its country format and began simulcasting sister station WQSO; WUBB's website stated "Coming Soon! Sports Radio" with a link to MSN's Fox Sports page, implying that the new format would be Fox Sports Radio. However, this never happened, and this was thought to be put on the website only to throw people off. The following day, the stunt shifted to TV theme songs; in between the songs, there was a message saying "We are building a new station just for you," promoting a new format that would be launched at 6 a.m. on the 14th. At the announced time, the station relaunched as "Kiss 95.3", initially simulcasting WXKS-FM from Boston. Soon after, the call letters changed to WSKX. By August of the following year, WSKX ended the simulcast and ran its own CHR format.

On October 4, 2012, sister station WERZ adopted 95.3's old format, and the station began stunting with sounds of ocean waves and occasional bells, along with voiceover Chad Erickson (as well as its website) redirecting Kiss listeners to WERZ, and advising them to tune in the following Tuesday, October 9, at Noon. At that time, the station flipped to adult hits as "95.3 The Coast", launching with Journey's "Don't Stop Believin'". In November 2013, WSKX flipped to Christmas music for the holiday season, letting listeners choose online the music to be played; this feature was also used for the station's regular variety hits programming. On August 29, 2014, at 1 p.m., the station flipped back to country as 95.3 The Bull. The last song on "The Coast" was "Closing Time" by Semisonic, while the first song on "The Bull" was "This Is How We Roll" by Florida Georgia Line. It shares a common coverage area with market-leading WOKQ, as well as WBQQ, a York County simulcast of WTHT from the Portland area. On September 16, 2014, WSKX changed its call letters to WTBU to go with "The Bull" branding.

WTBU's second HD Radio subchannel carries a classic country format; the format had been carried on sister station WMYF (1380 AM) until its 2015 shutdown.

Facility details for Facility ID 35218 (WTBU) in the FCC Licensing and Management System WTBU in Nielsen Audio's FM station database WUBB format change noted

WTBU (95.3 MHz, "The Bull") is an FM radio station licensed to York Center, Maine, United States. Established in 1987, WTBU is owned by iHeartMedia and serves York County, Maine, and the New Hampshire Seacoast. The station broadcasts a country music format.
The station went on the air in June 1987 as WQMI with a middle of the road format. In 1989, it became WCQL-FM as "Cool 95.3" with an oldies format. That was dropped in August 1996 in favor of a contemporary hit radio format, WXHT ("Heat 95.3"), which placed a heavy emphasis on 1980s new wave hits. That lasted until May 1998, when it went modern rock as "95-3 The Heat" via Radio One Networks. In March 1999, the station changed to a country format, becoming WUBB ("B95.3"). However, WUBB was faced with strong competition from country leader WOKQ, which also had a much stronger signal. WUBB also had a limited local presence when compared to WOKQ. As a result, WUBB never became a big ratings success. On January 10, 2008, the station dropped its country format and began simulcasting sister station WQSO; WUBB's website stated "Coming Soon! Sports Radio" with a link to MSN's Fox Sports page, implying that the new format would be Fox Sports Radio. However, this never happened, and this was thought to be put on the website only to throw people off. The following day, the stunt shifted to TV theme songs; in between the songs, there was a message saying "We are building a new station just for you," promoting a new format that would be launched at 6 a.m. on the 14th. Toshihide Matsui

Toshihide Matsui (松井 俊英, Matsui Toshihide; born 19 April 1978) is a professional Japanese tennis player. On 12 June 2006, he reached his highest ATP singles ranking of No. 261. He achieved his highest doubles ranking of No. 123 in February 2024. He is currently the oldest active singles player in the ATP world doubles rankings.

He was the runner-up in men's singles at the Japanese National Championships in 2006 when he lost the final against Satoshi Iwabuchi. He won 6 Japanese national championship titles in men's doubles category: 4 titles with Satoshi Iwabuchi (2005, 2007-09) and 2 titles with Kaito Uesugi (2021-22). When he played at the 2019 Shenzhen Longhua Open against 18-year-old Chun-hsin Tseng as a lucky loser, it was the largest age difference ever in a Challenger match, with Matsui being the oldest player at 41 years old, with an ATP ranking. He represented Japan in three Davis Cup ties between 2006 and 2010, his win-loss record is 4-1. Plus Matsui participated in the first 2 editions of ATP Cup in 2020-2021 as a member of Team Japan. Matsui holds the record as the oldest player in ATP Cup history. In February 2024, Matsui achieved his highest ranking in doubles, No.123, at the age of 45; he later improved this to No. 121 on 27 May 2024, aged 46.

.

Based in Kashiwa, Matsui speaks Japanese and English fluently. In 2010, he was married to a former professional tennis player Tomoyo Takagishi, they have 2 children.

raw:
vaccine schedule overview

Navigating the pediatric vaccine schedule can feel overwhelming for new parents and caregivers. The timeline is designed to protect infants from serious diseases during the most vulnerable months of their lives. Most vaccines are administered in a specific order, often combining multiple protections into single shots to minimize discomfort. It is crucial for parents to understand that these recommendations are based on extensive scientific data regarding immune system development and disease risk, ensuring maximum safety and efficacy for the child.

Between birth and two months of age, the focus is on immediate protection. Hepatitis B vaccination begins shortly after birth, providing a critical first line of defense against liver infection. If the mother is not immune to Hepatitis B, the infant may also receive a passive immunization injection for extra immediate coverage. This early intervention is vital because newborns have high exposure risks in hospital settings if the source of infection is unknown or if family members carry the virus unknowingly.

From two to six months, the schedule intensifies with a series of doses for diseases like DTaP, which prevents diphtheria, tetanus, and whooping cough. Simultaneously, parents are introduced to the Rotavirus vaccine, typically given orally to protect against severe diarrhea and dehydration. Polio, Hib, and PCV vaccines are also introduced during this window. These monthly visits are common, and while the number of injections can be concerning, combining vaccines during each visit has been proven safe and significantly reduces the total number of appointments required.

By seven to eighteen months, the schedule shifts to boosting initial immunity and introducing new protections. The first MMR shot, which safeguards against measles, mumps, and rubella, is usually administered around one year of age. Varicella, or chickenpox, follows a similar timeline. This stage is important because maternal antibodies that provided temporary protection after birth begin to wane, necessitating the child's own immune system to build long-lasting memory through active vaccination.

Finally, the preschooler phase, spanning from four to six years of age, serves as the ultimate booster period. At this stage, children receive additional doses of DTaP, MMR, varicella, and Hepatitis A to solidify their defense before entering school environments. Keeping up with this final set ensures that children are fully protected as they age into adolescence. Healthcare providers use digital tracking systems to monitor these milestones, making it easy for families to stay on schedule and maintain full compliance with national health guidelines.

raw:
hospital visiting hours

Hospital visiting hours are a small but essential part of the patient experience, offering families a chance to provide emotional support while allowing medical staff to maintain a controlled environment. Most hospitals publish a schedule that outlines when relatives and friends may enter patient rooms, and the rules can differ from one facility to another. Understanding these guidelines helps prevent misunderstandings, reduces the risk of disruptions, and ensures that both patients and caregivers benefit from the interaction.

Typical visiting windows start early, often at 8 a.m., and run until about 8 p.m. on weekdays. Weekends usually have a shorter block, sometimes only three hours in the late afternoon. Intensive care, neonatal, and transplant units have stricter limits, with shorter daily windows and a requirement to sign in at a central desk. A few hospitals offer open-visiting periods for stable patients without infection precautions, but these exceptions are clearly noted on the facility's website.

The reasons behind these schedules are rooted in patient safety and comfort. Rest is a critical component of healing, and constant traffic can interfere with sleep cycles and medication schedules. Infection control is another major concern; limiting the number of people entering a ward reduces the chance of transmitting pathogens. Staff also need predictable patterns to coordinate rounds, procedures, and cleaning tasks, and a defined visiting window helps keep the unit's workflow orderly and efficient.

Before you visit, check the hospital's specific policy. Most facilities post their hours online, and a quick call to the main desk can clarify any special restrictions for intensive care or isolation rooms.

raw:
Tel Yitzhak

Tel Yitzhak (Hebrew: תֵּל יִצְחָק, lit. 'Isaac Hill') is a kibbutz in central Israel. Located in the coastal plain to the south-east of Netanya, it falls under the jurisdiction of Hof HaSharon Regional Council. In 2024 it had a population of 1,055.

The region of Tel Yitzhak, bordering the wetlands of the Poleg stream, has been inhabited intermittently since the Middle Paleolithic age, with peak periods of settlement during the Middle and Late Bronze Age (17th-13th centuries BCE), the Byzantine (4th-7th centuries CE) and Late Ottoman periods (19-early 20th centuries CE). Before the 20th century the area formed part of the Forest of Sharon and was part of the lands of the village of Ghabat Kafr Sur. It was an open woodland dominated by Mount Tabor Oak, which extended from Kfar Yona in the north to Ra'anana in the south. The local Arab inhabitants traditionally used the area for pasture, firewood and intermittent cultivation. The intensification of settlement and agriculture in the coastal plain during the 19th century led to deforestation and subsequent environmental degradation. The kibbutz was established in 1938 by General Zionist immigrants from Galicia as part of the tower and stockade settlement campaign. It was named after Yitzhak Steiger, a leader of HaNoar HaTzioni in Galicia. During the 1936-1939 Arab revolt in Palestine, the area was one of several sites selected by the Jewish National Fund for rapid fortified settlement in order to establish a Jewish presence in the Sharon plain and protect nearby roads. The first pioneers combined agriculture with defense duties, and for several years the kibbutz maintained a watchtower and stockade enclosure. In the 1940s Tel Yitzhak hosted one of the printing presses of the newspaper Haaretz. After the establishment of the State of Israel, it developed mixed farming, including citrus orchards, poultry, and dairy production. Masua (Massuah), a center for Holocaust research, commemoration, and youth education, was established on the kibbutz in the 1970s and later became an official institution supported by the Israeli Ministry of Education. It serves as a major Holocaust education center for school groups and soldiers.

Like many kibbutzim, Tel Yitzhak underwent processes of privatization from the 1990s onward, introducing differential wages and leasing agricultural land to private farmers. Today its economy combines agriculture, light industry, and services, while also hosting cultural and educational programs connected with Masua.

Southwest of the kibbutz is an 8-dunam nature reserve established in 1968 to protect flora and fauna native to the Sharon plain. Flora includes Ceratonia siliqua, Calicotome villosa, Thymelaea hirsuta, Prasium majus, Anagyris, and Lavandula stoechas. The reserve preserves remnants of the once extensive oak woodlands of the Sharon.

raw:
research grant timeline

A research grant timeline begins with the announcement of a funding opportunity, often posted on agency websites, newsletters, or academic portals. Applicants typically have between four and six weeks to review the scope, assess eligibility, and decide whether to compete.

During the preparation phase, investigators gather collaborators, draft budgets, and compose the narrative sections required by the solicitation. Institutions usually provide internal deadline checkpoints, such as a pre-submission review by the Office of Research, to ensure compliance with formatting and policy requirements before the external deadline.

The official submission deadline marks the end of the application window; once the electronic file is uploaded, the system locks the proposal and sends a receipt confirmation. After this point, reviewers are assigned, and the peer-review process can take anywhere from eight to twelve weeks, depending on the funding body's schedule and the complexity of the proposal.

Following the review, agencies issue a summary statement that includes scores, critiques, and funding recommendations. Principal investigators receive the decision letter a few weeks later, at which time they may need to revise budgets, address reviewer comments, or negotiate terms with the program officer before a formal award is issued.

The award notice triggers the start of the project period, which is commonly twelve to thirty-six months. Researchers must submit a detailed work plan, set up financial controls, and begin data collection or experimental work according to the agreed schedule.

At the conclusion of the grant, a final report summarizing outcomes, expenditures, and impact is required. Many agencies also request a post-award progress report twelve months after the project ends to capture longer-term effects and inform future funding decisions.

raw:
composting

Turning kitchen scraps into dark, nutrient-rich soil is one of the most effective ways to reduce household waste while boosting garden health. Many people overlook the simplicity of this process because they believe it requires expensive equipment or large outdoor spaces. In reality, a simple three-bin system or even a single worm bin can handle the volume of food waste produced by an average family. The key to success lies in understanding the balance between different types of materials, often referred to as greens and browns. This balance ensures that the pile heats up correctly, breaks down efficiently, and remains free from unpleasant odors that often deter newcomers.

Greens are nitrogen-rich materials such as vegetable peels, fruit cores, coffee grounds, and fresh grass clippings. These items contain high moisture content and decompose relatively quickly, providing the energy needed for microbial activity. Browns, on the other hand, are carbon-rich items like dried leaves, shredded cardboard, and wood chips. They provide structure and aeration to the pile, preventing it from becoming a compacted, anaerobic mess. Ideally, you should aim for a ratio of roughly three parts brown to one part green by volume. If your compost smells like rotten eggs, you likely have too much moisture and nitrogen, so add some dry leaves or shredded paper to absorb the excess.

Layering these materials correctly is crucial for successful decomposition. Start with a base layer of coarse browns to improve airflow, then alternate thin layers of greens and browns as you add new waste. Each layer should be about an inch or two thick to ensure proper mixing. After adding fresh materials, mix the pile gently with a pitchfork or turn it to introduce oxygen. Aerobic decomposition is significantly faster and cleaner than anaerobic breakdown, which produces sulfur compounds and foul smells. Regular turning, perhaps once every week or two, keeps the bacteria active and accelerates the curing process.

Patience is a virtue in composting, as natural cycles take time rather than minutes. Depending on the method used and ambient temperatures, a finished compost pile can take anywhere from three to six months to mature. The final product should look like dark, crumbly earth and smell sweet and pleasant, similar to forest soil. This material, often called humus, is a goldmine for gardeners, improving soil structure, water retention, and nutrient availability for plants. Unlike synthetic fertilizers that can burn roots or leach into waterways, compost provides a slow-release steady stream of essential nutrients that encourages healthy microbial communities in the soil.

Starting small is the best way to build confidence in your composting routine. If you live in an apartment, focus on dry scraps that can be stored in a sealed container until you can drop them off at a community collection site. For those with yards, a standard wood pallet bin or a manufactured tumbler works well. Consistency is more important than volume; adding scraps daily to your designated bin creates a habit that seamlessly integrates into your weekly cleaning routine. By viewing food waste as a resource rather than trash, you participate in a circular system that benefits both your immediate environment and the broader ecosystem.

They provide structure and aeration to the pile, preventing it from becoming a compacted, anaerobic mess. Ideally, you should aim for a ratio of roughly three parts brown to one part green by volume. If your compost smells like rotten eggs, you likely have too much moisture and nitrogen, so add some dry leaves or shredded paper to absorb the excess.
Layering these materials correctly is crucial for successful decomposition. Start with a base layer of coarse browns to improve airflow, then alternate thin layers of greens and browns as you add new waste. Each layer should be about an inch or two thick to ensure proper mixing. After adding fresh materials, mix the pile gently with a pitchfork or turn it to introduce oxygen. Aerobic decomposition is significantly faster and cleaner than anaerobic breakdown, which produces sulfur compounds and foul smells. Regular turning, perhaps once every week or two, keeps the bacteria active and accelerates the curing process.

Patience is a virtue in composting, as natural cycles take time rather than minutes. Depending on the method used and ambient temperatures, a finished compost pile can take anywhere from three to six months to mature. The final product should look like dark, crumbly earth and smell sweet and pleasant, similar to forest soil. This material, often called humus, is a goldmine for gardeners, improving soil structure, water retention, and nutrient availability for plants. Unlike synthetic fertilizers that can burn roots or leach into waterways, compost provides a slow-release steady stream of essential nutrients that encourages healthy microbial communities in the soil.
Starting small is the best way to build confidence in your composting routine. If you live in an apartment, focus on dry scraps that can be stored in a sealed container until you can drop them off at a community collection site. For those with yards, a standard wood pallet bin or a manufactured tumbler works well. Consistency is more important than volume; adding scraps daily to your designated bin creates a habit that seamlessly integrates into your weekly cleaning routine. By viewing food waste as a resource rather than trash, you participate in a circular system that benefits both your immediate environment and the broader ecosystem.
